anatomy-and-physiology/basic-structures.title: Basic Structures
anatomy-and-physiology/basic-structures.content:
Overview
The human body is organized into increasingly complex levels, from individual cells to organ systems that work together to maintain life.
Each level builds on the structures and functions of the level below it.
Levels of Biological Organization
Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ System → Organism

Cell: Smallest living structural and functional unit of the body.
Tissue: Group of similar cells and associated material working together.
Organ: Structure composed of multiple tissue types performing specific functions.
Organ System: Group of organs working together to perform major body functions.
Organism: The complete living individual.

Example — The Heart

Cells: Cardiac muscle cells contract.
Tissues: Cardiac muscle, connective tissue, nervous tissue, and epithelial tissue contribute to heart function.
Organ: The heart pumps blood.
Organ System: The cardiovascular system circulates blood throughout the body.
Organism: Circulation supports the needs of the entire person.

Four Basic Tissue Types






























TissuePrimary FunctionExamplesEpithelialCovers surfaces, lines cavities, and forms glandsEpidermis, intestinal liningConnectiveSupports, binds, protects, and transportsBone, blood, cartilage, adipose tissueMuscleProduces movement through contractionSkeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscleNervousReceives, processes, and transmits informationBrain, spinal cord, peripheral nerves
Clinical Connections

Integumentary System — epithelial tissue provides a protective skin barrier.
Musculoskeletal System — muscle and connective tissues enable movement and structural support.
Cardiovascular System — cardiac muscle produces the force needed for circulation.
Nervous System — nervous tissue coordinates and regulates body functions.

Flashcards
What are the five levels of biological organization?01-foundations / anatomy-physiology / foundationsAnswerCell, tissue, organ, organ system, and organism.
What are the four basic tissue types?01-foundations / anatomy-physiology / foundationsAnswerEpithelial, connective, muscle, and nervous.
What is the difference between a tissue and an organ?01-foundations / anatomy-physiology / foundationsAnswerA tissue is a group of cells working together; an organ contains multiple tissue types performing specific functions.
Which tissue type forms protective surfaces and organ linings?01-foundations / anatomy-physiology / foundationsAnswerEpithelial tissue.
Which tissue type supports, binds, and protects body structures?01-foundations / anatomy-physiology / foundationsAnswerConnective tissue.

anatomy-and-physiology/cardiovascular-sy.title: Cardiovascular System
anatomy-and-physiology/cardiovascular-sy.content:
Overview
The cardiovascular system circulates blood throughout the body to deliver oxygen and nutrients, remove carbon dioxide and other waste products, and maintain blood pressure and tissue perfusion.
It consists of the heart, blood vessels, and blood.
The right side of the heart pumps blood to the lungs, while the left side pumps oxygen-rich blood throughout the body.
Major Structures
Heart
The heart is a muscular organ containing four chambers and four valves that maintain one-way blood flow.

Right Atrium: Receives oxygen-poor blood returning from the body.
Right Ventricle: Pumps oxygen-poor blood to the lungs through the pulmonary arteries.
Left Atrium: Receives oxygen-rich blood returning from the lungs.
Left Ventricle: Pumps oxygen-rich blood to the body through the aorta.
Heart Valves: Prevent backward blood flow.

Tricuspid Valve: Right atrium → right ventricle.
Pulmonary Valve: Right ventricle → pulmonary artery.
Mitral (Bicuspid) Valve: Left atrium → left ventricle.
Aortic Valve: Left ventricle → aorta.


Coronary Arteries: Supply oxygen-rich blood to the heart muscle itself.

Blood Vessels

Arteries: Carry blood away from the heart, generally under higher pressure.
Arterioles: Small arteries that regulate blood flow into capillary networks and contribute to vascular resistance.
Capillaries: Microscopic vessels connecting arterioles and venules, allowing exchange of gases, nutrients, and waste products.
Venules: Small vessels that collect blood from capillaries and drain into larger veins.
Veins: Return blood toward the heart, often containing valves that prevent backward flow, particularly in the limbs.

Important: Arteries and veins are defined by the direction of blood flow, not oxygen content. Pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood, while pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood.
Blood
Blood is a specialized connective tissue consisting of plasma and formed elements.

Red Blood Cells (Erythrocytes): Transport oxygen using hemoglobin and carry some carbon dioxide.
White Blood Cells (Leukocytes): Support immune defense and fight infection.
Platelets (Thrombocytes): Help form blood clots to stop bleeding.
Plasma: Liquid portion of blood, mostly water, containing proteins, electrolytes, nutrients, hormones, and waste products.

Key Processes


Pulmonary Circulation: Blood travels from the right side of the heart to the lungs for gas exchange, then returns to the left side.


Systemic Circulation: Oxygen-rich blood travels from the left side of the heart to the body, and oxygen-poor blood returns to the right side.


Cardiac Cycle: Repeated contraction and relaxation of the heart.

Systole: Ventricles contract and eject blood.
Diastole: Ventricles relax and fill with blood.



Heart Rate: Number of heartbeats per minute.


Stroke Volume: Amount of blood pumped by one ventricle with each heartbeat.


Cardiac Output: Volume of blood pumped by one ventricle per minute.
Cardiac Output = Heart Rate × Stroke Volume


Blood Pressure: Force exerted by circulating blood against vessel walls, typically measured in the arteries.


Systemic Vascular Resistance: Resistance to blood flow through the systemic circulation, influenced strongly by arteriolar diameter.


Tissue Perfusion: Delivery of blood to tissues to supply oxygen and nutrients.


Hemostasis: Process of stopping bleeding through vessel responses, platelet activity, and coagulation.


Effects of Aging

Increased Arterial Stiffness: Large arteries become less elastic, contributing to higher systolic blood pressure.
Reduced Cardiac Reserve: The heart may be less able to increase its pumping performance during exertion or illness.
Changes in Heart Muscle: Heart walls may thicken, and ventricular relaxation and filling may become less efficient.
Changes in Heart Valves: Valves may thicken or stiffen, increasing the likelihood of valve dysfunction.
Reduced Blood Pressure Regulation: Less sensitive pressure receptors can contribute to dizziness or Orthostatic Hypotension when changing positions.
Increased Susceptibility to Arrhythmias: Changes in the heart’s electrical conduction system can increase the risk of abnormal heart rhythms.

Clinical Implications

Increased vulnerability to cardiovascular disease.
Greater risk of dizziness and falls when changing positions.
Reduced exercise tolerance and increased fatigue during activity.
Greater importance of monitoring blood pressure, pulse, and changes from baseline.
Observe swelling, shortness of breath, chest discomfort, and reduced activity tolerance.

Important: Anemia, markedly reduced white blood cell counts, uncontrolled hypertension, and heart failure are not inevitable consequences of normal aging. New abnormalities require evaluation.
Common Diseases & Disorders

Important: CNAs observe and report cardiovascular abnormalities rather than independently diagnosing conditions, adjusting medications, or determining treatments.
Important Distinctions

Arteriosclerosis vs. Atherosclerosis: Arteriosclerosis is a broad term for arterial thickening or hardening. Atherosclerosis specifically involves plaque buildup within artery walls and is one form of arteriosclerosis.
Angina vs. Myocardial Infarction: Angina is a symptom of temporary myocardial ischemia, typically without heart muscle death. Myocardial infarction involves heart muscle injury or death caused by prolonged ischemia. New chest discomfort requires prompt evaluation; CNAs should not attempt to distinguish these conditions independently.
Peripheral Artery Disease vs. Chronic Venous Insufficiency: PAD reduces arterial blood delivery to tissues and can produce cool extremities or arterial ulcers. Chronic venous insufficiency impairs blood return and can cause edema, skin discoloration, and venous stasis ulcers.
Heart Failure vs. Heart Attack: Heart failure involves impaired pumping or filling of the heart. A heart attack causes acute heart muscle injury due to insufficient blood supply. A heart attack can lead to heart failure.

When to Report

Blood pressure or pulse outside prescribed parameters.
New dizziness, weakness, or fainting.
New or worsening swelling of the legs or feet.
Unusual shortness of breath, fatigue, or reduced activity tolerance.
New irregular pulse or palpitations.
Changes in skin color, temperature, or circulation.
Unexplained bruising or bleeding.
Sudden weight gain in a resident being monitored for fluid retention.

Emergency signs: New chest pain or pressure, severe breathing difficulty, sudden one-sided weakness, loss of consciousness, or sudden severe chest, back, or abdominal pain require immediate emergency response.
Study Notes

Blood Pressure
Cardiac Output
Systemic Vascular Resistance

Clinical Connections

Hypertension: Persistent elevation of arterial blood pressure can increase cardiovascular risk.
Hypotension: Low blood pressure may reduce tissue perfusion.
Orthostatic Hypotension: Postural blood pressure changes can contribute to dizziness and falls.
Blood Loss: Reduced circulating blood volume can impair tissue perfusion.
Dehydration: Fluid loss can contribute to low blood pressure and an increased heart rate.
Vital Signs: Blood pressure and pulse provide important cardiovascular observations.
Fall Risk: Dizziness, fainting, and impaired circulation can increase fall risk.
Recognizing Patient Distress: Chest discomfort and sudden circulation changes may signal emergencies.

anatomy-and-physiology/cardiovascular/bl.title: Blood Pressure
anatomy-and-physiology/cardiovascular/bl.content:
Blood pressure is the force exerted by circulating blood against blood vessel walls.
Mean arterial pressure is approximately determined by Cardiac Output and Systemic Vascular Resistance.

Increasing cardiac output generally increases arterial pressure, all else being equal.
Increasing systemic vascular resistance generally increases arterial pressure, all else being equal.

Dehydration and Blood Loss can reduce circulating blood volume, potentially reducing venous return, cardiac output, and blood pressure.
Flashcards
What two variables primarily determine mean arterial pressure?01-foundations / anatomy-physiology / cardiovascularAnswerCardiac output and systemic vascular resistance.
How might dehydration reduce blood pressure?02-mechanisms / anatomy-physiology / cardiovascularAnswerLower blood volume can reduce venous return and cardiac output.

anatomy-and-physiology/cardiovascular/ca.title: Cardiac Output
anatomy-and-physiology/cardiovascular/ca.content:
What is it?
Cardiac output (CO) is the volume of blood pumped by one ventricle of the heart per minute.
It depends on:

Heart Rate (HR): Number of heartbeats per minute.
Stroke Volume (SV): Amount of blood ejected by one ventricle with each heartbeat.

How does it work?
Formula:
CO = HR × SV
Example:

Heart rate = 70 beats/min.
Stroke volume = 70 mL/beat.
Cardiac output = 70 × 70 = 4,900 mL/min = 4.9 L/min.
A typical resting adult cardiac output is approximately 4–8 L/min, although it varies with body size, activity, and health.

Factors Affecting Cardiac Output
Heart Rate:

Increasing HR can increase CO.
Extremely high HR may reduce ventricular filling and lower stroke volume.
Stroke Volume:
Preload: Ventricular filling and stretch before contraction.
Contractility: Strength of heart muscle contraction.
Afterload: Resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject blood.

Relationship to Blood Pressure

Higher CO generally increases arterial pressure when other factors remain constant.
Lower CO may contribute to hypotension.
Blood pressure also depends on Systemic Vascular Resistance.

Why does it matter clinically?
Cardiac output helps determine whether enough blood reaches the body’s tissues.
Reduced cardiac output may contribute to:

Dizziness or weakness.
Reduced organ perfusion.
Cool extremities.
Low blood pressure.
Altered mental status.
These findings have multiple possible causes and do not independently establish low cardiac output.

What is the cardiac output formula?01-foundations / anatomy-physiology / cardiovascularAnswerHeart rate × stroke volume.

What is stroke volume?01-foundations / anatomy-physiology / cardiovascularAnswerBlood ejected by one ventricle per beat.

anatomy-and-physiology/cardiovascular/sy.title: Systemic Vascular Resistance
anatomy-and-physiology/cardiovascular/sy.content:
What is it?
Systemic vascular resistance (SVR) is the resistance to blood flow through the systemic circulation.
It is influenced primarily by the diameter and tone of small arteries and arterioles.
How does it work?
Vasoconstriction:

Blood vessels narrow.
Resistance to blood flow increases.
Blood pressure generally increases if cardiac output remains constant.
Vasodilation:
Blood vessels widen.
Resistance to blood flow decreases.
Blood pressure generally decreases if cardiac output remains constant.

Factors Affecting SVR

Vessel Diameter: Narrower vessels create greater resistance.
Blood Viscosity: Thicker blood increases resistance.
Vessel Length: Greater vessel length increases resistance.
Autonomic Nervous System: Sympathetic stimulation commonly increases arteriolar constriction.
Hormones: Angiotensin II and other vasoactive substances regulate vascular tone.

Relationship to Blood Pressure
Simplified relationship:
Mean Arterial Pressure ≈ Cardiac Output × Systemic Vascular Resistance
This approximation assumes central venous pressure is small relative to arterial pressure.

Higher SVR generally increases blood pressure when CO remains constant.
Lower SVR generally decreases blood pressure when CO remains constant.
Blood pressure depends on the interaction between SVR, CO, and other physiological factors.

Why does it matter clinically?
Changes in SVR contribute to blood pressure regulation.
Increased SVR may occur with:

Sympathetic nervous system activation.
Vasoconstriction associated with cold or stress.
Some forms of hypertension.
Decreased SVR may occur with:
Certain medications.
Widespread vasodilation during distributive shock.
Some causes of hypotension.
These conditions may affect SVR through several mechanisms.

Related

Blood Pressure
Cardiac Output
Hypertension

Flashcards
What happens to SVR when arterioles constrict?02-mechanisms / anatomy-physiology / cardiovascularAnswerResistance increases.
What happens to pressure when SVR rises and cardiac output stays constant?02-mechanisms / anatomy-physiology / cardiovascularAnswerArterial pressure generally increases.
What vessel property has a major influence on SVR?01-foundations / anatomy-physiology / cardiovascularAnswerArteriolar diameter and tone.

anatomy-and-physiology/digestive-system.title: Digestive System
anatomy-and-physiology/digestive-system.content:
Overview
The digestive system (gastrointestinal system) breaks down food, absorbs nutrients and water, and eliminates undigested waste.
It provides the body with nutrients needed for energy, growth, tissue repair, and normal cellular function.
The digestive system consists of two major groups:

Alimentary Canal (Gastrointestinal Tract): Continuous tube through which food passes, from the mouth to the anus.
Accessory Digestive Organs: Structures that assist digestion, including the salivary glands, liver, gallbladder, and pancreas.

Major Structures
Alimentary Canal

Mouth (Oral Cavity): Begins digestion through chewing and mixing food with saliva.

Teeth: Mechanically break food into smaller pieces.
Tongue: Moves food during chewing and forms a bolus for swallowing.
Salivary Glands: Produce saliva containing digestive enzymes, including salivary amylase.


Pharynx (Throat): Passageway for swallowed food and liquids toward the esophagus.
Esophagus: Muscular tube transporting food from the pharynx to the stomach through peristalsis.
Stomach: Muscular organ that stores, mixes, and partially digests food using gastric acid and enzymes, producing chyme.
Small Intestine: Primary site of chemical digestion and nutrient absorption.

Duodenum: First segment; receives chyme, bile, and pancreatic digestive secretions.
Jejunum: Middle segment; major site of nutrient absorption.
Ileum: Final segment; absorbs remaining nutrients, including vitamin B12 and bile salts.


Large Intestine (Colon): Absorbs water and electrolytes and forms feces.

Cecum: First portion of the large intestine.
Ascending Colon: Travels upward along the right side of the abdomen.
Transverse Colon: Crosses the upper abdomen.
Descending Colon: Travels downward along the left side.
Sigmoid Colon: S-shaped portion leading to the rectum.


Rectum: Stores feces before elimination.
Anus: Opening through which feces leave the body, controlled by anal sphincters.

Accessory Digestive Organs

Liver: Large organ in the upper right abdomen.

Produces bile to assist fat digestion.
Processes absorbed nutrients.
Stores glycogen, vitamins, and minerals.
Metabolizes medications and toxins.
Produces important blood proteins.


Gallbladder: Stores and concentrates bile produced by the liver, releasing it into the small intestine during digestion.
Pancreas: Organ behind the stomach with digestive and endocrine functions.

Exocrine Function: Produces digestive enzymes and bicarbonate delivered into the duodenum.
Endocrine Function: Produces insulin and glucagon to regulate blood glucose.



Intestinal Lining

Villi: Fingerlike projections in the small intestine that increase surface area for nutrient absorption.
Microvilli: Microscopic projections on intestinal epithelial cells that further increase absorptive surface area.
Intestinal Capillaries: Absorb many nutrients into the bloodstream.
Lacteals: Specialized lymphatic vessels within villi that absorb dietary fats.

Important: Villi are characteristic of the small intestine, not the entire digestive tract.
Key Processes
Digestion
Digestion involves mechanically and chemically breaking food into smaller components that can be absorbed.

Mastication: Chewing food to break it into smaller pieces.
Salivation: Saliva moistens food and begins starch digestion.
Swallowing (Deglutition): Coordinated movement of food from the mouth through the pharynx into the esophagus.
Airway Protection: The epiglottis and other swallowing mechanisms help protect the airway.
Peristalsis: Coordinated, wave-like smooth muscle contractions that move material through the digestive tract.
Mechanical Digestion: Physical breakdown and mixing of food.
Chemical Digestion: Enzymes and digestive secretions break nutrients into absorbable components.

Pathway of Food Through the Digestive Tract

Mouth: Food is chewed, mixed with saliva, and formed into a bolus.
Pharynx: Swallowing moves the bolus toward the esophagus.
Esophagus: Peristalsis transports food into the stomach.
Stomach: Gastric acid and enzymes begin significant protein digestion; muscular contractions produce chyme.
Small Intestine: Bile and pancreatic enzymes assist digestion; most nutrients are absorbed.
Large Intestine: Water and electrolytes are absorbed, and feces are formed.
Rectum: Stores feces before defecation.
Anus: Feces are eliminated during a bowel movement.

Nutrient Absorption

Carbohydrates: Broken down into simple sugars, such as glucose.
Proteins: Broken down into amino acids and small peptides.
Fats: Bile helps emulsify fats, allowing digestive enzymes to break them down for absorption.
Vitamins and Minerals: Absorbed primarily in the small intestine, with specific absorption sites depending on the nutrient.
Water: Absorbed throughout the intestines, predominantly in the small intestine, with additional absorption in the colon.

Elimination

Feces Formation: Undigested material, bacteria, water, and other substances form stool.
Defecation: Coordinated contractions and relaxation of the rectum and anal sphincters allow stool to leave the body.
Mucus Secretion: Helps lubricate intestinal contents and protect the intestinal lining.

Effects of Aging

Changes in Oral Health: Tooth loss, reduced chewing efficiency, dry mouth, and dental problems may interfere with eating.
Changes in Swallowing: Some age-related changes in swallowing physiology may reduce swallowing reserve, especially during illness.
Changes in Gastrointestinal Motility: Motility patterns may change, but significant slowing and constipation are not inevitable consequences of aging.
Increased Constipation Risk: Reduced mobility, inadequate fluid or fiber intake, and medication effects can make constipation more likely.
Changes in Liver Physiology: Liver size and blood flow may decrease with age, potentially affecting the metabolism of certain medications.
Changes in Appetite: Taste, smell, medications, illness, and social factors can influence food intake.

Clinical Implications

Increased vulnerability to poor nutritional intake.
Dental problems and swallowing difficulties may affect safe eating.
Reduced mobility and certain medications can increase constipation risk.
Dehydration may worsen constipation.
Medication effects may be more pronounced because of changes in metabolism.
Greater importance of observing food intake, swallowing, bowel patterns, and changes from baseline.

Important: Persistent constipation, unexplained weight loss, difficulty swallowing, gastrointestinal bleeding, and significantly impaired digestion are not normal consequences of aging and require evaluation.
See Effects of Aging - Systems & Clinical Implications.

Important Distinctions

Constipation vs. Fecal Impaction: Constipation involves difficult or infrequent bowel movements; impaction involves stool that has become lodged and cannot be passed normally.
GERD vs. Peptic Ulcer Disease: GERD involves reflux into the esophagus; ulcers involve open sores in the stomach or duodenal lining.
Diverticulosis vs. Diverticulitis: Diverticulosis means diverticula are present; diverticulitis means they have become inflamed.
Gallstones vs. Cholecystitis: Gallstones are hardened deposits in the gallbladder or bile ducts; cholecystitis is inflammation of the gallbladder, often due to gallstone obstruction.
Diarrhea vs. Overflow Diarrhea: Liquid stool may leak around a fecal impaction, so loose stool does not always mean constipation is absent.

Important: CNAs observe and report gastrointestinal abnormalities rather than independently diagnosing conditions, performing disimpaction, or administering bowel treatments without appropriate authorization.
When to Report

New or persistent constipation or diarrhea.
Significant changes in bowel movement frequency, appearance, or consistency.
New abdominal pain, swelling, or distention.
Nausea, vomiting, or inability to tolerate food or fluids.
Difficulty chewing or swallowing.
Coughing, choking, or a wet-sounding voice during meals.
Blood in stool or unusually dark, tarry stools.
Poor appetite, unexpected weight loss, or decreased fluid intake.
New bowel incontinence or suspected fecal impaction.
Signs of dehydration.

Emergency signs: Severe sudden abdominal pain, vomiting blood, substantial gastrointestinal bleeding, inability to breathe from choking, or signs of shock require immediate emergency response.
Study Notes

Fluid Balance
Effects of Aging - Systems & Clinical Implications

Clinical Connections

Assisting with Feeding: Proper meal assistance supports nutrition and safe swallowing.
Dysphagia & Aspiration Precautions: Swallowing problems can increase choking and aspiration risk.
Elimination Care: Bowel patterns and continence are important aspects of resident care.
Constipation: Mobility, fluids, diet, and medications influence bowel function.
Dehydration: Vomiting, diarrhea, and poor fluid intake can disturb fluid balance.
Hand Hygiene: Certain gastrointestinal infections can spread through contaminated hands and surfaces.
Vital Signs: Changes in temperature, pulse, and blood pressure may accompany dehydration, bleeding, or infection.
Patient Positions: Appropriate positioning supports comfort, feeding, and aspiration precautions.

anatomy-and-physiology/endocrine-system.title: Endocrine System
anatomy-and-physiology/endocrine-system.content:
Overview
The endocrine system is a network of glands and organs that produce and release hormones, chemical messengers that regulate body functions.
Hormones generally travel through the bloodstream and act on target cells containing the appropriate receptors.
The endocrine system helps regulate:

Metabolism and energy use.
Growth and development.
Blood glucose levels.
Fluid and electrolyte balance.
Stress responses.
Reproduction and sexual function.
Sleep, mood, and other aspects of homeostasis.

The endocrine system works closely with the Nervous System. Nervous-system signals are often rapid, while many hormonal responses develop more gradually and last longer.
Major Structures







































































Gland / OrganLocationMajor HormonesPrimary FunctionsHypothalamusBrain, below the thalamusReleasing and inhibiting hormones; synthesizes ADH and oxytocinLinks nervous and endocrine systems; controls pituitary activity, water balance, and other functionsPituitary GlandBase of brain, beneath hypothalamusGH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin; releases ADH and oxytocin from posterior pituitaryRegulates growth, reproduction, stress responses, and other endocrine glandsPineal GlandNear the center of the brainMelatoninHelps regulate sleep-wake cyclesThyroid GlandFront of neck, below the larynxT3, T4, calcitoninRegulates metabolism, growth, and development; calcitonin participates in calcium regulationParathyroid GlandsUsually four small glands behind the thyroidParathyroid hormone (PTH)Raises blood calcium levels and helps regulate calcium and phosphorus balanceAdrenal GlandsOn top of each kidneyCortisol, aldosterone, epinephrine, norepinephrineRegulate stress responses, blood pressure, fluid balance, and metabolismPancreasUpper abdomen, behind the stomachInsulin, glucagon, somatostatinRegulates blood glucose levelsThymusUpper chest, behind the sternumThymic hormonesSupports T-lymphocyte development, especially earlier in lifeOvariesPelvic cavityEstrogens, progesteroneRegulate reproductive functions, menstrual cycles, and sexual developmentTestesScrotumTestosterone, inhibinSupport sperm production and male sexual development
Hypothalamus & Pituitary Gland
The hypothalamus and pituitary form a major control center for the endocrine system.

Hypothalamus: Detects internal conditions and releases signals that regulate pituitary activity.
Anterior Pituitary: Produces and releases several hormones, including growth hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and adrenocorticotropic hormone.
Posterior Pituitary: Stores and releases ADH and oxytocin, which are produced in the hypothalamus.

The pituitary is often called the master gland, although its activity is regulated by the hypothalamus and feedback from other glands.
Adrenal Glands
Each adrenal gland has two main regions:

Adrenal Cortex (Outer):

Cortisol: Helps regulate metabolism and the body’s response to stress.
Aldosterone: Promotes sodium retention and potassium excretion, helping regulate blood volume and pressure.


Adrenal Medulla (Inner):

Epinephrine and Norepinephrine: Support the fight-or-flight response.



Pancreas
The pancreas has both endocrine and digestive (exocrine) functions.

Beta Cells: Produce insulin, which lowers blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake and storage.
Alpha Cells: Produce glucagon, which raises blood glucose by stimulating glucose release from the liver.

Key Processes
Hormonal Signaling

Hormone Secretion: Glands release hormones in response to internal signals.
Hormone Transport: Many hormones travel through the bloodstream to target tissues.
Hormone Receptors: Only cells with appropriate receptors respond to a particular hormone.
Feedback Regulation: Hormone production is adjusted according to the body’s needs.

Negative Feedback
Negative feedback counteracts a change to help maintain homeostasis.
Example — Blood Glucose Regulation:

Blood glucose rises after eating.
The pancreas releases insulin.
Insulin promotes glucose uptake and storage.
Blood glucose decreases toward its normal range.
Insulin secretion decreases as the stimulus resolves.

When blood glucose falls, the pancreas increases glucagon secretion, helping the liver release glucose into the bloodstream.
Key Principle: Negative feedback is the most common endocrine regulatory mechanism.
Positive Feedback
Positive feedback amplifies a response until a particular event or endpoint occurs.
Example — Childbirth:

The baby’s head stretches the cervix.
Nerve signals stimulate oxytocin release.
Oxytocin increases uterine contractions.
Contractions increase cervical stretching.
The cycle continues until delivery.

Oxytocin also causes milk ejection (let-down) during breastfeeding in response to suckling. Milk production itself is primarily stimulated by prolactin.
Other Important Functions

Metabolic Regulation: Thyroid hormones influence energy use and heat production.
Stress Response: Cortisol and catecholamines help the body respond to physical and emotional stress.
Fluid Balance: ADH reduces water loss through the kidneys; aldosterone supports sodium and fluid retention.
Calcium Regulation: PTH and vitamin D help maintain calcium balance.
Growth and Development: Growth hormone, thyroid hormones, and sex hormones influence body development.
Circadian Regulation: Melatonin helps coordinate sleep-wake timing.

Effects of Aging

Changes in Hormonal Regulation: Hormone levels and tissue sensitivity may change with age; not all hormones decrease.
Reduced Growth Hormone Secretion: May contribute to changes in body composition, alongside activity, nutrition, and other factors.
Reduced Insulin Sensitivity: Can increase the risk of type 2 diabetes.
Changes in Thyroid Regulation: Thyroid function and hormone metabolism may change, although significant thyroid disease is not inevitable.
Changes in Sex Hormones: Estrogen and progesterone decrease substantially after menopause; testosterone may decline gradually in some men.
Changes in Melatonin Secretion: May contribute to altered sleep-wake patterns.
Changes in Fluid Regulation: Altered thirst and ADH responses can increase vulnerability to fluid imbalance.

Clinical Implications

Greater vulnerability to abnormal blood glucose levels.
Changes in energy, weight, temperature tolerance, and sleep.
Increased importance of monitoring food and fluid intake when indicated.
Increased vulnerability to dehydration in some older adults.
Hormonal disorders may present with fatigue, weakness, confusion, or changes in daily functioning.

Important: Diabetes, thyroid disorders, severe hormonal deficiencies, and unexplained changes in weight or mental status are not inevitable consequences of aging.
Common Diseases & Disorders

































































ConditionDescriptionCommon Causes / Risk FactorsCNA ConsiderationsType 1 Diabetes MellitusAutoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, resulting in little or no insulin productionAutoimmune processes, genetic susceptibility; often begins in childhood but can occur at any ageObserve and report signs of abnormal blood glucose; follow prescribed meal, monitoring, and care plansType 2 Diabetes MellitusInsulin resistance combined with inadequate insulin secretion, causing elevated blood glucoseFamily history, age, excess body fat, physical inactivity, history of gestational diabetesObserve thirst, frequent urination, fatigue, wounds, and changes from baselineHypoglycemiaAbnormally low blood glucose, often defined as below 70 mg/dL in people with diabetesInsulin or certain diabetes medications, missed meals, increased activity, alcohol, illnessRecognize sweating, shakiness, hunger, weakness, confusion, or altered consciousness; follow facility protocol and summon helpHyperglycemiaElevated blood glucose above the appropriate target rangeDiabetes, missed medication, illness, stress, certain medicationsReport excessive thirst, frequent urination, fatigue, blurred vision, or changes in consciousnessHypothyroidismUnderactive thyroid gland producing insufficient thyroid hormoneHashimoto’s thyroiditis, thyroid surgery, radioactive iodine treatment, certain medicationsObserve fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, and reduced activityHyperthyroidismExcess thyroid hormone production causing increased metabolic activityGraves’ disease, overactive thyroid nodules, some thyroid disordersObserve heat intolerance, sweating, rapid pulse, weight loss, tremor, and restlessnessCushing SyndromeProlonged exposure to excessive cortisolLong-term glucocorticoid medications, cortisol-producing tumors, excess ACTHObserve fragile skin, bruising, muscle weakness, increased infection risk, and functional changesAdrenal Insufficiency (e.g., Addison’s Disease)Inadequate production of adrenal hormones, particularly cortisolAutoimmune adrenal damage, pituitary disease, abrupt withdrawal of prolonged steroid treatmentObserve weakness, dizziness, low blood pressure, nausea, and unusual fatigue; report promptlyHyperparathyroidismExcess PTH secretion, often causing elevated blood calcium and possible bone lossParathyroid adenoma, gland enlargement, chronic kidney disease in some formsObserve weakness, constipation, bone pain, kidney-stone symptoms, or confusion; report changes
Important Distinctions:

Type 1 vs. Type 2 Diabetes: Type 1 involves autoimmune insulin deficiency; type 2 involves insulin resistance and progressive impairment of insulin secretion.
Hypoglycemia vs. Hyperglycemia: Hypoglycemia means low blood glucose; hyperglycemia means high blood glucose.
Hypothyroidism vs. Hyperthyroidism: Hypothyroidism generally slows metabolic processes; hyperthyroidism generally accelerates them.
Cushing Syndrome vs. Adrenal Insufficiency: Excess cortisol versus insufficient cortisol.

CNAs observe and report endocrine abnormalities rather than independently diagnosing conditions or adjusting medications. Blood glucose testing or treatment assistance must follow the CNA’s authorized scope, training, and facility policy.
When to Report

New or worsening excessive thirst or frequent urination.
Sweating, shakiness, weakness, or sudden confusion.
Unexpected changes in appetite or body weight.
Unusual fatigue or declining activity tolerance.
Heat or cold intolerance.
New tremors or rapid heartbeat.
Dizziness, fainting, or changes in consciousness.
Blood glucose measurements outside prescribed parameters, when monitoring is an authorized assigned task.

Emergency signs: Severe confusion, seizure, unresponsiveness, or signs of a serious diabetic or adrenal emergency require immediate emergency response.
If hypoglycemia is suspected, follow the facility’s emergency protocol. Do not give food or liquids by mouth to someone who is unconscious or unable to swallow safely.
Study Notes

Nervous System
Fluid Balance
Effects of Aging - Systems & Clinical Implications

Clinical Connections

Vital Signs: Hormonal disorders may affect pulse, blood pressure, and temperature regulation.
Fluid Balance: ADH and aldosterone help regulate fluid balance.
Dehydration: Excessive urination or impaired fluid regulation can increase dehydration risk.
Assisting with Feeding: Meal timing and adequate intake are particularly important for residents with diabetes.
Recognizing Patient Distress: Severe glucose abnormalities can cause acute changes in consciousness.
Skin Integrity & Breakdown Prevention: Diabetes can increase vulnerability to slow-healing wounds.
Fall Risk: Weakness, dizziness, or hypoglycemia may increase fall risk.

Questions

How do hormones differ from nerve impulses?
What are the locations and functions of the major endocrine glands?
How does the hypothalamus regulate the pituitary gland?
What is the difference between the anterior and posterior pituitary?
What are the functions of insulin and glucagon?
What is the difference between negative and positive feedback?
How do cortisol and epinephrine contribute to stress responses?
How do ADH and aldosterone affect fluid balance?
How does aging affect endocrine regulation?
What distinguishes type 1 and type 2 diabetes?
What are common signs of hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia?
How do hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism differ?
What endocrine symptoms require urgent reporting?

What are hormones?01-foundations / anatomy-physiology / endocrineAnswerChemical messengers that act on cells with appropriate receptors.

anatomy-and-physiology/fluid-balance.title: Fluid Balance
anatomy-and-physiology/fluid-balance.content:
Overview
Fluid balance is the regulation of water and electrolytes within the body.
The body must maintain appropriate fluid volume, distribution, and electrolyte concentrations to support circulation, cellular function, temperature regulation, and waste removal.
Fluid balance depends on the interaction of the kidneys, cardiovascular system, endocrine system, and thirst mechanisms.
How It Works
Fluid Compartments
Body water is distributed between two major compartments:

Intracellular Fluid (ICF): Fluid inside cells.
Extracellular Fluid (ECF): Fluid outside cells, including blood plasma and interstitial fluid between cells.

Water moves between compartments primarily through osmosis, the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane toward the side with greater effective solute concentration.
Electrolytes, including sodium and potassium, help regulate fluid distribution, electrical signaling, and normal cellular function.
Fluid Intake & Output
Fluid Intake:

Beverages and water contained in foods.
Water generated during metabolism.

Fluid Output:

Urine.
Sweat and evaporation from skin.
Water lost through breathing.
Stool.
Additional losses from vomiting, diarrhea, drains, or bleeding.

Fluid balance depends on replacing losses appropriately, not simply consuming a fixed amount of water.
Regulation by the Kidneys & Hormones

Kidneys: Adjust water and electrolyte excretion through urine.
Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH): Promotes water reabsorption by the kidneys, reducing water loss.
Aldosterone: Promotes sodium retention and potassium excretion, influencing extracellular fluid volume.
Thirst: Encourages additional water intake when fluid or osmotic regulation requires it.

These mechanisms work together through feedback systems to maintain homeostasis.
Relationship to Blood Pressure
Fluid volume influences the amount of blood returning to the heart.

Reduced circulating volume may decrease venous return.
Reduced venous return can lower stroke volume.
Lower stroke volume may reduce Cardiac Output.
Reduced cardiac output can contribute to Hypotension.

The body may compensate through increased heart rate, vasoconstriction, thirst, and fluid conservation.
Blood pressure also depends on Systemic Vascular Resistance and other physiological factors.
Why It Matters Clinically
Fluid Deficit
Dehydration occurs when the body loses more water than it replaces.
Possible consequences include:

Thirst and dry mouth.
Reduced urine output.
Weakness or dizziness.
Changes in mental status.
Abnormal electrolyte concentrations.

Significant circulating volume depletion can impair tissue perfusion.
Important Distinction: Dehydration refers specifically to a body-water deficit. Hypovolemia refers to reduced circulating extracellular fluid volume. They often overlap but are not identical.
Fluid Excess
Excess fluid may accumulate in body tissues or circulation.
Possible consequences include:

Peripheral edema.
Rapid weight increase.
Increased cardiovascular workload.
Breathing difficulty when fluid accumulates in the lungs.

Fluid overload may occur with Heart Failure (CHF), kidney dysfunction, or other conditions.
Important: A person can have peripheral edema while still having inadequate effective circulating blood volume.
Recognition & Assessment
Relevant observations include:

Changes in fluid intake.
Changes in urine output.
Unexpected weight changes.
Thirst or dry mouth.
Dizziness or weakness.
New swelling.
Breathing difficulty.
Changes in alertness or usual functioning.

No single observation independently establishes a fluid-balance disorder.
Care Considerations

Record intake and output when assigned.
Measure weights consistently according to the care plan.
Follow prescribed fluid allowances or restrictions.
Assist residents in obtaining permitted fluids.
Observe and report changes from baseline.
Report new swelling, reduced urine output, dizziness, or unusual weight changes.
Seek immediate help for severe breathing difficulty, unresponsiveness, or other emergency findings.

CNAs do not independently prescribe fluid restrictions or modify treatment plans.

anatomy-and-physiology/integumentary-sys.title: Integumentary System
anatomy-and-physiology/integumentary-sys.content:
Overview
The integumentary system consists of the skin, hair, nails, sweat glands, and sebaceous (oil) glands.
It protects the body from injury, pathogens, and water loss while helping regulate temperature and detect sensations.
The skin consists of two main layers: the epidermis and dermis. Beneath the skin lies the hypodermis (subcutaneous tissue), which provides insulation, cushioning, and energy storage.

Hair and nails: Made primarily of keratin, a tough structural protein.
Sweat glands: Produce perspiration to help regulate body temperature.
Sebaceous glands: Release sebum (oil) to lubricate skin and hair.


Major Structures

Epidermis: Outermost skin layer. Forms a protective, water-resistant barrier. Contains keratinocytes and melanocytes, which produce melanin.
Dermis: Middle layer containing blood vessels, nerves, sensory receptors, hair follicles, and sweat and oil glands. Provides strength and elasticity.
Hypodermis (Subcutaneous Tissue): Layer beneath the skin, containing primarily fat and connective tissue. Provides insulation, cushioning, and energy storage.
Hair: Keratin-containing structures that provide protection and contribute to sensation.
Nails: Hard keratin structures that protect the tips of fingers and toes.
Sweat Glands: Produce sweat, which cools the body through evaporation.
Sebaceous Glands: Produce sebum to lubricate and protect the skin and hair.

Key Processes

Protection: Creates a barrier against pathogens, physical damage, and excessive water loss.
Immune Defense: Skin cells and resident immune cells help recognize pathogens and coordinate local inflammatory responses.
Thermoregulation: Sweating and changes in skin blood flow help regulate body temperature.
Sensation: Sensory receptors detect touch, pressure, pain, and temperature.
Wound Healing: Damaged tissue undergoes inflammation, repair, and remodeling.
Vitamin D Synthesis: UVB exposure initiates vitamin D production in the skin.
Skin Renewal: New epidermal cells replace older cells shed from the surface.

Effects of Aging

Thinner skin: Increases susceptibility to skin tears and injury.
Reduced elasticity: Skin becomes more fragile and less resilient.
Decreased sweat and oil production: Can contribute to dry skin and reduced temperature regulation.
Slower wound healing: Skin repair may take longer.
Reduced subcutaneous fat: Less cushioning over bony prominences.

Clinical Implications

Thinner, less elastic skin is more susceptible to injury during transfers, repositioning, and adhesive removal.
Reduced cushioning over bony prominences can increase vulnerability to pressure-related tissue damage.
Slower wound healing may prolong recovery from skin injuries.
Reduced sweating and changes in skin blood flow may impair temperature regulation.
Dry or fragile skin requires gentle hygiene and careful observation.

CNA Focus: Follow the individualized skin-care and repositioning plan, minimize friction and shear, and report new wounds, redness, bruising, or skin breakdown.
See Skin Integrity & Breakdown Prevention and Pressure Injuries.
Common Diseases & Disorders

Important: CNAs observe and report skin abnormalities rather than independently diagnosing skin diseases or selecting treatments.
When to Report

New or unexplained bruising or skin injuries.
Open wounds, blisters, or new skin breakdown.
Spreading redness, warmth, swelling, or drainage.
New painful or itchy rashes.
Suspected contagious skin conditions.
Significant changes in existing wounds or skin conditions.

Sudden widespread rash with breathing difficulty or facial/tongue swelling requires emergency response.
Study Notes

Effects of Aging - Systems & Clinical Implications
Fluid Balance

Clinical Connections

Skin Integrity & Breakdown Prevention: Gentle hygiene, skin observation, and individualized repositioning help prevent injury.
Wound Dressings & Bandage Care: Appropriate dressings protect wounds and support healing.
Incontinence Care: Prolonged moisture exposure and irritants can damage the skin.

Questions

Why does the epidermis not contain blood vessels?
How do sweat glands and skin blood vessels regulate temperature?

anatomy-and-physiology/lymphatic-and-imm.filePath: Anatomy and Physiology/Lymphatic and Immune System.md
anatomy-and-physiology/lymphatic-and-imm.title: Lymphatic and Immune System
anatomy-and-physiology/lymphatic-and-imm.content:
Overview
The lymphatic system is a network of vessels, fluid, tissues, and organs that helps maintain fluid balance, defend against infection, and absorb dietary fats.
It consists of lymph, lymphatic vessels, lymph nodes, lymphatic ducts, and lymphoid organs such as the spleen, thymus, tonsils, and bone marrow.
The lymphatic system has three primary functions:

Fluid Balance: Collect excess fluid from body tissues and return it to the bloodstream.
Immune Defense: Transport immune cells and help recognize and fight pathogens.
Fat Absorption: Absorb dietary fats and fat-soluble vitamins from the small intestine.

Unlike the Cardiovascular System, the lymphatic system has no central pump. Lymph flows primarily in one direction, from body tissues toward the bloodstream.
Major Structures
Lymphatic Vessels & Fluid

Interstitial Fluid: Fluid located in the spaces surrounding body cells.
Lymph: Interstitial fluid that has entered lymphatic vessels. Contains water, proteins, immune cells, and other substances.
Lymphatic Capillaries: Tiny, blind-ended vessels that collect excess interstitial fluid from tissues.
Lymphatic Vessels: Transport lymph toward larger lymphatic ducts. Many contain one-way valves to prevent backward flow.
Lymphatic Ducts: Return lymph to the venous bloodstream.

Right Lymphatic Duct: Drains the right side of the head and neck, right arm, and right upper chest.
Thoracic Duct: Drains lymph from the remainder of the body.


Lymph Nodes: Small, bean-shaped structures that filter lymph and contain immune cells. Commonly found in the neck, armpits, and groin.

Lymphoid Organs

Bone Marrow: Produces blood cells, including immune cells. B lymphocytes mature here.
Thymus: Located behind the sternum. Supports T lymphocyte maturation, especially during childhood.
Spleen: Located in the upper left abdomen.

Filters blood rather than lymph.
Removes aged or damaged red blood cells.
Helps recognize and respond to bloodborne pathogens.


Tonsils: Lymphoid tissues near the throat that help detect pathogens entering through the mouth or nose.
Adenoids: Lymphoid tissue in the nasopharynx, behind the nasal cavity.
Gut-Associated Lymphoid Tissue (GALT): Immune tissue in the digestive tract, including Peyer’s patches in the small intestine.

Important Immune Cells

White Blood Cells (Leukocytes): Cells that protect the body against infection and other threats.
Lymphocytes: White blood cells involved in immune defense.

B Cells: Produce antibodies through their differentiated plasma cells.
T Cells: Coordinate immune responses or destroy infected cells.
Natural Killer (NK) Cells: Destroy certain infected or abnormal cells.


Neutrophils: Respond rapidly to many infections, particularly bacterial infections.
Macrophages: Engulf pathogens, debris, and damaged cells through phagocytosis.
Dendritic Cells: Help activate adaptive immune responses by presenting antigens to T cells.

Key Processes
Lymph Formation & Circulation

Blood capillaries exchange fluid with surrounding tissues.
Excess interstitial fluid enters lymphatic capillaries and becomes lymph.
Lymph travels through progressively larger lymphatic vessels.
Lymph passes through lymph nodes, where immune cells monitor for pathogens and abnormal material.
Lymphatic ducts return lymph to the venous bloodstream near the collarbones.

Lymph Pathway: Interstitial Fluid → Lymphatic Capillaries → Lymphatic Vessels → Lymph Nodes → Lymphatic Ducts → Venous Bloodstream.
Movement of Lymph
Because there is no central lymphatic pump, lymph moves through several mechanisms:

Skeletal Muscle Contractions: Movement compresses nearby lymphatic vessels and helps move lymph forward.
Respiratory Movements: Pressure changes during breathing help propel lymph.
Smooth Muscle Contractions: Larger lymphatic vessels contract rhythmically.
One-Way Valves: Prevent backward flow.

Clinical Connection: Permitted mobility and muscle activity can support lymph return. However, edema has many causes, and movement alone does not treat every form of swelling.
Immune Defense
The immune system protects the body through two major forms of immunity.
Innate Immunity
The body’s rapid, nonspecific defense against pathogens.

Physical barriers such as the skin and mucous membranes.
Inflammatory responses.
Phagocytic cells such as neutrophils and macrophages.
Natural killer cells.
Complement proteins.

Innate immune responses begin quickly and do not require previous exposure to a particular pathogen.
Adaptive Immunity
A targeted immune response that develops after exposure to specific antigens.

B Lymphocytes: Can develop into plasma cells that produce antibodies.
T Lymphocytes: Help coordinate immune responses and destroy infected cells.
Memory Cells: Allow faster and stronger responses to certain pathogens after previous exposure or vaccination.

Inflammation
Inflammation is a protective response to injury, infection, or other harmful stimuli.
Common local signs include:

Redness.
Warmth.
Swelling.
Pain.
Sometimes loss of function.

Inflammation is part of immune defense and tissue repair, but excessive or persistent inflammation can damage healthy tissues.
Dietary Fat Absorption

Specialized lymphatic capillaries called lacteals are located within intestinal villi.
Lacteals absorb many dietary fats packaged as chylomicrons, along with fat-soluble vitamins.
The fat-rich lymph, called chyle, travels through lymphatic vessels before entering the bloodstream.

Effects of Aging

Immunosenescence: Age-related changes in immune function may reduce the effectiveness of some responses to infections and vaccines.
Reduced Thymic Activity: The thymus gradually shrinks after puberty, reducing the production of new naive T cells.
Altered Adaptive Immunity: Changes in T-cell and B-cell function can affect responses to unfamiliar pathogens.
Chronic Low-Grade Inflammation: Aging is sometimes associated with persistent low-level inflammatory activity, called inflammaging.
Changes in Lymphatic Function: Lymphatic vessel function and tissue-fluid regulation may change with age, although effects vary.

Clinical Implications

Greater vulnerability to certain infections.
Some infections may present with less typical symptoms.
Wounds may heal more slowly due to multiple age-related factors.
Illness may cause sudden functional decline.
Mobility limitations may worsen dependent swelling in some residents.
Infection prevention and vaccination remain important.

Important: Significant immune deficiency, recurrent serious infections, and persistent edema are not inevitable consequences of aging.
See Effects of Aging - Systems & Clinical Implications.
Common Diseases & Disorders

Important Distinctions

Edema vs. Lymphedema: Edema means excess fluid in tissues; lymphedema specifically results from impaired lymphatic drainage.
Lymphadenopathy vs. Lymphadenitis: Lymphadenopathy describes abnormal lymph nodes; lymphadenitis specifically describes inflammation of lymph nodes.
Lymphoma vs. Leukemia: Both are blood-related cancers; lymphoma commonly involves lymphoid tissues, while leukemia generally involves blood-forming tissues and bone marrow. Some diseases overlap.
Innate vs. Adaptive Immunity: Innate immunity is rapid and broadly targeted; adaptive immunity recognizes specific antigens and develops immunological memory.
Infection vs. Inflammation: Infection involves invasion by pathogens; inflammation is the body’s response to injury or harmful stimuli and does not always mean infection.

Important: CNAs observe and report abnormalities rather than independently diagnosing infections, immune disorders, or causes of swelling.
When to Report

New or worsening swelling of an arm, leg, or other body area.
Enlarged, tender, or persistently swollen lymph nodes.
Redness, warmth, pain, or drainage suggesting infection.
Fever, chills, or new signs of illness.
Red streaks extending from a wound or infected area.
Unexplained night sweats, fatigue, or weight loss.
New skin breakdown in an area affected by swelling.
Sudden confusion or functional decline that may accompany acute illness.
Symptoms of an allergic reaction.

Emergency signs: Difficulty breathing, throat or tongue swelling, fainting with suspected anaphylaxis, rapidly progressing severe infection symptoms, or sudden severe illness require immediate emergency response.

Clinical Connections

Chain of Infection: Infection occurs when pathogens move through a chain of transmission.
Hand Hygiene: Hand hygiene reduces the spread of infectious organisms.
Standard Precautions: Routine precautions help prevent exposure to infectious materials.

Fluid Balance: Lymphatic drainage helps return excess tissue fluid to circulation.
Limited Mobility: Reduced activity may contribute to dependent swelling and other complications.

anatomy-and-physiology/musculoskeletal-s.title: Musculoskeletal System
anatomy-and-physiology/musculoskeletal-s.content:
Overview
The musculoskeletal system provides structural support, protects internal organs, maintains posture, and enables movement.
It consists of bones, skeletal muscles, joints, tendons, ligaments, cartilage, and other connective tissues.
The system also supports mineral storage, blood cell production, and heat generation.
Major Structures
Skeletal System

Bones: Provide support, protect organs, store minerals such as calcium and phosphorus, and contain bone marrow.

Axial Skeleton: Skull, vertebral column, ribs, and sternum. Supports the body’s central axis and protects vital organs.
Appendicular Skeleton: Arms, legs, shoulders, and pelvic girdle. Supports movement and locomotion.


Joints: Connections between bones that provide stability and, depending on the joint, permit movement.
Tendons: Connect muscles to bones, transmitting force to produce movement.
Ligaments: Connect bones to other bones, helping stabilize joints.
Cartilage: Flexible connective tissue that cushions joints and supports structures such as the rib cage.
Bone Marrow: Tissue within bones. Red marrow produces blood cells; yellow marrow primarily stores fat.

Muscular System

Skeletal Muscle: Attached to bones through tendons. Produces voluntary movement and maintains posture.
Smooth Muscle: Involuntary muscle found in structures such as blood vessels, the digestive tract, and bladder.
Cardiac Muscle: Specialized involuntary muscle that contracts to pump blood through the heart.

Vertebral Column
The spine supports the body, protects the spinal cord, and allows movement.





























RegionStructureCervical7 vertebrae in the neckThoracic12 vertebrae in the upper and middle backLumbar5 vertebrae in the lower backSacrum5 fused vertebrae connecting the spine to the pelvisCoccyxTailbone, typically formed from 3–5 fused vertebrae
Intervertebral Discs: Fibrocartilaginous structures between most adjacent movable vertebrae that absorb shock and permit movement.
Other Important Structures

Temporomandibular Joint (TMJ): Connects the mandible (lower jaw) to the temporal bone of the skull, allowing chewing and speaking.
Pelvis: Connects the spine to the lower limbs, supports body weight, and protects pelvic organs.
Hip Joint: Ball-and-socket joint connecting the femur to the pelvis.

Key Processes

Muscle Contraction: Produces movement, maintains posture, and stabilizes joints.
Joint Movement: Includes flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and rotation.
Weight Bearing: Bones, muscles, and joints support body weight during standing, walking, and transfers.
Bone Remodeling: Continuous breakdown and replacement of bone tissue.
Thermoregulation: Muscle activity generates heat; shivering produces heat through repeated involuntary contractions.
Blood Cell Production (Hematopoiesis): Red bone marrow produces red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.
Mineral Storage: Bones store calcium and phosphorus and help regulate their availability.
Support of Elimination: Skeletal and smooth muscles help control urination and defecation.

Effects of Aging

Reduced Bone Density: Bone mass may decline, increasing vulnerability to fractures.
Reduced Muscle Mass (Sarcopenia): Loss of muscle mass and strength can impair mobility and balance.
Reduced Flexibility: Changes in connective tissues and joints may limit range of motion.
Slower Muscle Responses: Changes in muscle and nervous-system function can affect coordination and reaction time.
Reduced Physical Endurance: Fatigue may occur more easily during prolonged activity.

Clinical Implications

Increased risk of falls and fractures.
Greater difficulty with transfers, walking, and ADLs.
Increased vulnerability to deconditioning during prolonged bed rest.
Greater importance of appropriate mobility, exercise, and restorative care.
Encourage independence while following individualized mobility restrictions.

Important: Osteoporosis, severe weakness, and inability to walk are not inevitable consequences of aging. New functional decline should be reported.
Common Diseases & Disorders



























































ConditionDescriptionCommon Causes / Risk FactorsCNA ConsiderationsOsteoarthritisDegenerative joint disease involving cartilage and other joint tissues, causing pain and stiffnessAging, previous joint injuries, obesity, repetitive joint stress, geneticsObserve pain, stiffness, and mobility limitationsRheumatoid ArthritisAutoimmune inflammatory disease causing joint pain, swelling, and stiffnessImmune system attacks joint tissues; genetic susceptibility and smoking increase riskFollow joint-protection precautions and report worsening symptomsOsteoporosisReduced bone density and strength, increasing fracture risk; may cause kyphosis following vertebral fracturesAging, hormonal changes after menopause, inactivity, low calcium or vitamin D, certain medicationsFollow fall-prevention precautions and safe transfer techniques; encourage prescribed weight-bearing activityFracturesPartial or complete breaks in a boneFalls, trauma, osteoporosis, repetitive stressAvoid unnecessary movement and immediately report suspected fracturesSprainsStretching or tearing of ligamentsTwisting a joint, falls, sudden movements, sports injuriesObserve swelling, bruising, pain, and impaired movementStrainsStretching or tearing of muscles or tendonsOverexertion, improper lifting, repetitive movements, sudden stretchingReport pain, weakness, or difficulty movingContracturesPersistent shortening or tightening of muscles, tendons, or other tissues that restrict joint movementProlonged immobility, neurological conditions, muscle imbalance, scar tissueFollow prescribed positioning and range-of-motion plansMuscle AtrophyReduction in muscle size and massImmobility, disuse, aging, malnutrition, neurological diseaseEncourage permitted activity and report functional decline
Important: CNAs observe and report musculoskeletal problems rather than independently diagnosing injuries or determining treatment.
Important Distinctions

Osteoarthritis vs. Rheumatoid Arthritis: Osteoarthritis involves degenerative changes affecting cartilage and other joint tissues. Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune inflammatory disease that can affect multiple joints and other organs.
Sprain vs. Strain: A sprain involves ligaments; a strain involves muscles or tendons.
Osteopenia vs. Osteoporosis: Osteopenia means bone mineral density is lower than normal; osteoporosis involves more substantial skeletal fragility and increased fracture risk.
Muscle Atrophy vs. Contracture: Atrophy is loss of muscle mass. A contracture is persistent shortening or tightening of tissues that restricts joint movement.

When to Report

New or worsening joint or muscle pain.
Sudden difficulty walking, standing, or transferring.
Swelling, bruising, or visible deformity after an injury.
Reduced range of motion or increasing stiffness.
New weakness or unexpected functional decline.
Signs of injury following a fall.

Suspected fractures, sudden severe pain after injury, or new one-sided weakness require urgent evaluation. Follow emergency-response procedures when indicated.

anatomy-and-physiology/nervous-system.title: Nervous System
anatomy-and-physiology/nervous-system.content:
Overview
The nervous system receives sensory information, processes it, and coordinates the body’s responses.
It controls movement, sensation, thinking, memory, emotions, and involuntary functions such as breathing, heart rate, and digestion.
The two main anatomical divisions are:

Central Nervous System (CNS): Brain and spinal cord.
Peripheral Nervous System (PNS): Nerves and ganglia outside the CNS that carry information between the CNS and the body.

The nervous system works closely with the Sensory Organs to detect and interpret changes in the environment.
Major Structures
Central Nervous System (CNS)

Brain: Main control center responsible for processing information and coordinating body functions.

Cerebrum: Conscious thought, memory, language, sensory interpretation, and voluntary movement.
Cerebellum: Coordination, balance, posture, and motor learning.
Brainstem: Connects the brain with the spinal cord and helps regulate essential functions.

Midbrain: Movement control and visual and auditory reflexes.
Pons: Breathing regulation, sleep, and communication between brain regions.
Medulla Oblongata: Breathing, heart rate, blood pressure, and protective reflexes.


Diencephalon: Region containing structures including the thalamus and hypothalamus.

Thalamus: Relays most sensory information to the cerebral cortex.
Hypothalamus: Regulates temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep, and endocrine activity.




Spinal Cord: Transmits signals between the brain and body and coordinates many reflexes.
Meninges: Three protective membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord.
Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF): Cushions the CNS and helps maintain its environment.

Peripheral Nervous System (PNS)

Cranial Nerves: Twelve pairs of nerves associated with the brain and brainstem that support functions such as facial sensation, vision, eye movement, hearing, and swallowing.
Spinal Nerves: Thirty-one pairs of nerves connecting the spinal cord to the body.
Sensory (Afferent) Nerves: Carry information from receptors toward the CNS.
Motor (Efferent) Nerves: Carry commands from the CNS toward muscles and glands.

Functional Divisions

Somatic Nervous System: Supports conscious sensation and voluntary skeletal muscle movement.
Autonomic Nervous System (ANS): Regulates involuntary functions such as heart rate, digestion, and blood vessel diameter.

Sympathetic: Supports the fight-or-flight response.
Parasympathetic: Supports rest-and-digest functions.
Enteric Nervous System: Network of neurons within the gastrointestinal tract that helps regulate digestion.



Nervous Tissue

Neurons: Cells specialized for transmitting electrical and chemical signals.

Dendrites: Receive incoming information.
Cell Body: Contains the nucleus and supports the neuron.
Axon: Conducts nerve impulses away from the cell body.
Myelin Sheath: Insulates many axons and increases signal conduction speed.


Synapses: Junctions where neurons communicate with other cells.
Neurotransmitters: Chemical messengers used for communication at many synapses.
Glial Cells: Cells that support, protect, nourish, and insulate neurons.

Key Processes

Sensory Reception: Specialized receptors detect stimuli such as light, sound, touch, temperature, and pain.
Sensory Processing: The CNS interprets information received from sensory receptors.
Motor Control: Nerve signals activate muscles to produce movement.
Reflexes: Rapid, often automatic responses to stimuli; some involve the spinal cord without requiring initial conscious processing.
Nerve Impulse Transmission: Electrical signals called action potentials travel along neurons.
Synaptic Transmission: Signals pass between cells through neurotransmitters or electrical connections.
Autonomic Regulation: Controls many involuntary activities.
Homeostasis: Helps maintain stable internal conditions.
Learning and Memory: Neural networks acquire, retain, and retrieve information.
Neuroplasticity: Neural connections can change through experience, learning, and recovery.

Effects of Aging

Slower Reaction Times: Responses to stimuli may take longer.
Changes in Sensation: Some people experience reduced sensitivity to touch, vibration, or temperature.
Changes in Balance: Altered sensory processing and motor control may affect stability.
Sleep Changes: Sleep patterns and circadian rhythms may change.
Changes in Memory Processing: Some forms of recall and information processing may become slower.
Reduced Autonomic Responsiveness: Blood pressure regulation during position changes may become less effective.

Clinical Implications

Increased risk of falls when balance, coordination, or reaction time is impaired.
More time may be needed for communication and movement.
Sensory impairments may affect safety and independence.
Changes in position may increase dizziness in some residents.
Acute illness can increase vulnerability to delirium.

Important: Dementia, sudden confusion, new paralysis, and major neurological deficits are not normal consequences of aging.
See Effects of Aging - Systems & Clinical Implications and Sensory Organs.
Common Diseases & Disorders

follow established mobility precautionsTraumatic Brain Injury (TBI)Brain injury caused by external force; may be penetrating or nonpenetratingFalls, collisions, blows to the head, penetrating injuriesReport head injuries and changes in consciousness, behavior, speech, or movement; follow emergency procedures
Important Distinctions

Dementia vs. Alzheimer’s disease: Dementia is a syndrome; Alzheimer’s is one possible cause.
Delirium vs. dementia: Delirium develops acutely and often fluctuates; dementia usually progresses more gradually.
Stroke vs. TIA: Stroke causes brain infarction or hemorrhage; TIA causes transient ischemic symptoms without acute infarction. Both require emergency evaluation.
SCI vs. TBI: Spinal cord injury primarily affects spinal nerve pathways; traumatic brain injury affects the brain. Trauma can cause both.
Seizures: Not all seizures involve convulsions; some involve staring, altered awareness, or unusual movements.

Important: CNAs observe, support, and report rather than independently diagnosing neurological disorders.
When to Report

New confusion, disorientation, or unexpected behavior.
New weakness, numbness, tingling, or loss of sensation.
Changes in walking, balance, or coordination.
New tremors, unusual movements, or seizure activity.
Changes in speech, vision, or swallowing.
Severe or unusual headaches.
Changes in level of consciousness.
Sudden decline in normal function.

Emergency signs: Sudden facial drooping, one-sided weakness, speech difficulty, sudden severe neurological symptoms, unresponsiveness, or a prolonged seizure require immediate emergency response.
Study Notes

Sensory Organs

Clinical Connections

Dementia Care: Cognitive changes may affect memory, communication, and independence.
Neurological Observations: Changes in alertness, speech, movement, or sensation may indicate neurological illness.
Fall Risk: Impaired balance, coordination, or sensation can increase fall risk.
Recognizing Patient Distress: Sudden neurological symptoms may indicate an emergency.
Vital Signs: Neurological illness may affect or accompany changes in vital signs.
Therapeutic Communication: Adapt communication for cognitive, language, or sensory difficulties.
Safe Patient Transfers: Weakness and impaired coordination affect mobility safety.
