What is the difference between sensory and motor nerves?02-mechanisms / anatomy-physiology / nervousAnswerSensory nerves carry signals toward the CNS; motor nerves carry commands away.

How do sympathetic and parasympathetic activity differ?02-mechanisms / anatomy-physiology / nervousAnswerSympathetic supports fight-or-flight; parasympathetic supports rest-and-digest.
What is the function of the myelin sheath?01-foundations / anatomy-physiology / nervousAnswerInsulates axons and speeds nerve impulse transmission.
What are neurotransmitters?01-foundations / anatomy-physiology / nervousAnswerChemical messengers that transmit signals between cells.
What is a reflex?01-foundations / anatomy-physiology / nervousAnswerA rapid, often automatic response to a stimulus.
How does aging commonly affect the nervous system?02-mechanisms / anatomy-physiology / nervousAnswerReaction times may slow, and some sensory and balance functions may decline.
How does delirium differ from dementia?02-mechanisms / anatomy-physiology / nervousAnswerDelirium develops acutely and often fluctuates; dementia usually develops gradually.
How does Alzheimer's disease relate to dementia?02-mechanisms / anatomy-physiology / nervousAnswerAlzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia.
What is the difference between stroke and TIA?02-mechanisms / anatomy-physiology / nervousAnswerStroke causes brain infarction or hemorrhage; TIA causes transient ischemic symptoms without acute infarction.
What does FAST stand for in stroke recognition?01-foundations / anatomy-physiology / nervousAnswerFace drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services.

What is Parkinson's disease associated with?02-mechanisms / anatomy-physiology / nervousAnswerLoss of dopamine-producing neurons and movement difficulties.
What is peripheral neuropathy?01-foundations / anatomy-physiology / nervousAnswerDamage to peripheral nerves causing sensory changes, pain, or weakness.
What should a CNA do during a seizure?03-application / anatomy-physiology / nervousAnswerProtect from injury, time the event, summon help, and never restrain or place objects in the mouth.
What is the difference between a spinal cord injury and a traumatic brain injury?02-mechanisms / anatomy-physiology / nervousAnswerSCI damages spinal nerve pathways; TBI damages the brain.
What should a CNA do if an acute spinal injury is suspected?03-application / anatomy-physiology / nervousAnswerSummon emergency help and avoid unnecessary movement unless required for immediate safety.

anatomy-and-physiology/nutrition-and-ess.filePath: Anatomy and Physiology/Nutrition and Essential Nutrients.md
anatomy-and-physiology/nutrition-and-ess.title: Nutrition and Essential Nutrients
anatomy-and-physiology/nutrition-and-ess.content:
What is it?
Nutrition is the process of obtaining and using nutrients to support energy production, growth, tissue maintenance, and normal body function.
Nutritional requirements differ based on age, activity, medical conditions, and individual needs.
Essential Nutrients








































NutrientPrimary FunctionsFood SourcesCarbohydratesProvide energy; fiber supports digestionGrains, fruits, vegetables, legumesProteinsBuild and repair tissues; support muscles and enzymesMeat, fish, eggs, beans, nuts, soyFatsSupply energy and support cell membranes and vitamin absorptionOils, nuts, seeds, fishVitaminsSupport metabolism and normal body functionsFruits, vegetables, animal and fortified foodsMineralsSupport bones, nerves, oxygen transport, and other functionsDairy, vegetables, legumes, meatsWaterSupports circulation, temperature control, and waste removalWater, beverages, water-containing foods
Calories: Units of energy supplied by foods and beverages.
Carbohydrates

Sugars and starches can provide glucose for energy.
Fiber supports bowel regularity and can help regulate cholesterol and blood glucose.
Different carbohydrate sources have different nutritional characteristics.

Proteins

Made from amino acids.
Required for tissue repair, muscle maintenance, and many body functions.
Particularly important when supporting residents at risk of malnutrition or delayed wound healing.

Fats

Unsaturated fats are found in foods such as nuts, seeds, and many plant oils.
Saturated fats are found in some animal products and tropical oils.
Excess LDL cholesterol is associated with cardiovascular risk.
Dietary cholesterol and blood LDL cholesterol are related but are not the same thing.

Vitamins
Water-Soluble Vitamins:

Vitamin C.
B vitamins, including thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3), B6, folate (B9), and B12.

Fat-Soluble Vitamins:

A, D, E, and K.

Fat-soluble vitamins can accumulate in the body; excessive supplementation may cause toxicity.
Important Minerals





























MineralFunctionCalciumBone health, muscle contraction, nerve signalingIronHemoglobin formation and oxygen transportMagnesiumMuscle and nerve functionZincImmune function and wound healingFolate (vitamin B9)DNA synthesis and red blood cell development
Note: Folate is a vitamin, not a mineral, but is included here to connect with your course’s nutrient table.
Food Groups
USDA MyPlate includes:

Fruits.
Vegetables.
Grains.
Protein foods.
Dairy and fortified alternatives.

Portions and food choices depend on individualized nutritional needs rather than one serving target for every adult.
Why Does It Matter Clinically?
Inadequate nutrition may contribute to:

Unintentional weight loss.
Weakness and reduced muscle mass.
Poor wound healing.
Reduced functional ability.
Nutrient deficiencies and malnutrition.

Recognition and Assessment
Observe and report:

Reduced appetite or persistent poor intake.
Unexpected weight changes.
Difficulty chewing or swallowing.
Problems accessing or handling food.
Nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Changes in ability to feed independently.

Care Considerations

Encourage food and fluid intake according to the care plan.
Support independence and food preferences.
Observe and document intake when assigned.
Follow prescribed diets and swallowing precautions.
Do not independently prescribe supplements or modify the diet.
Report persistent poor intake or suspected malnutrition.

Connections

Fluid Balance
Dehydration
Therapeutic Diets
Assisting with Feeding
Skin Integrity & Breakdown Prevention

Sources

CNA Module 11 — Nutrition
USDA — MyPlate
MedlinePlus — Nutrition
Resident-specific nutrition and hydration care plan

Flashcards
What are the six major nutrient categories?01-foundations / anatomy-physiology / foundationsAnswerCarbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, and water.
What is the primary function of dietary protein?01-foundations / anatomy-physiology / foundationsAnswerBuilding, maintaining, and repairing body tissues.
Which vitamins are fat-soluble?01-foundations / anatomy-physiology / foundationsAnswerA, D, E, and K.
Which vitamins are water-soluble?01-foundations / anatomy-physiology / foundationsAnswerB vitamins and vitamin C.
Why is nutrition important for wound healing?02-mechanisms / anatomy-physiology / foundationsAnswerTissue repair requires adequate energy, protein, and nutrients.
What should a CNA do when a resident has persistent poor intake?03-application / anatomy-physiology / foundationsAnswerDocument observations and notify the nurse.

anatomy-and-physiology/reproductive-syst.title: Reproductive System
anatomy-and-physiology/reproductive-syst.content:
Overview
The reproductive system produces reproductive cells (sperm and eggs), enables fertilization and reproduction, and produces sex hormones.
It works closely with the Endocrine System to regulate puberty, sexual development, fertility, pregnancy, and reproductive aging.
The reproductive system has three major functions:

Reproduction: Produces sperm and eggs and enables fertilization.
Hormone Production: Produces hormones such as testosterone, estrogen, and progesterone.
Sexual Development: Supports puberty, reproductive maturation, and secondary sex characteristics.

The female reproductive system also supports pregnancy, childbirth, and, through associated mammary glands, breastfeeding.
Major Structures
Male Reproductive System
Primary Reproductive Organs

Testes (Testicles): Two organs located in the scrotum.

Produce sperm through spermatogenesis.
Produce testosterone, the primary androgen involved in male sexual development.


Scrotum: External pouch that protects the testes and helps regulate their temperature.

Accessory Reproductive Structures

Epididymis: Coiled tube along each testis where sperm mature and are stored.
Vas Deferens: Muscular tube transporting sperm from the epididymis toward the ejaculatory ducts.
Seminal Vesicles: Glands producing fructose-rich fluid that nourishes sperm and contributes to semen.
Prostate Gland: Located below the bladder and surrounding part of the urethra; produces fluid that contributes to semen.
Bulbourethral (Cowper’s) Glands: Produce lubricating mucus released into the urethra.
Urethra: Tube carrying urine and, at different times, semen to the outside of the body.
Penis: External organ containing erectile tissue; enables sexual intercourse and ejaculation.

Sperm Pathway: Testes → Epididymis → Vas Deferens → Ejaculatory Ducts → Urethra → Outside the body.
Male Secondary Sex Characteristics
During puberty, increasing androgen activity contributes to:

Deepening of the voice.
Growth of facial, pubic, axillary, and sometimes chest hair.
Increased muscle mass and strength.
Broader shoulders and changes in body composition.

Female Reproductive System
Primary Reproductive Organs

Ovaries: Two organs located on either side of the uterus.

Contain developing egg cells (oocytes).
Release an oocyte during ovulation.
Produce estrogen and progesterone.



Internal Reproductive Structures

Fallopian (Uterine) Tubes: Transport the oocyte toward the uterus; fertilization most commonly occurs in the ampulla of a uterine tube.
Uterus: Muscular organ where an embryo may implant and develop during pregnancy.

Endometrium: Inner lining that changes during the menstrual cycle and is shed during menstruation.
Myometrium: Thick muscular layer that contracts during menstruation and childbirth.
Cervix: Lower portion of the uterus that opens into the vagina.


Vagina: Muscular canal connecting the cervix to the outside of the body; allows menstrual flow, intercourse, and childbirth.

External Reproductive Structures
The external female genital structures are collectively called the vulva.

Labia Majora: Outer skin folds that help protect the external genital structures.
Labia Minora: Inner folds surrounding the vestibule and openings.
Clitoris: Highly sensitive erectile organ involved in sexual arousal.
Vaginal Opening: External opening of the vaginal canal.
Urethral Opening: Separate opening through which urine exits the body.
Perineum: Region between the external genitalia and anus.

Associated Structures

Mammary Glands (Breasts): Produce milk after childbirth under hormonal regulation.

Female Secondary Sex Characteristics
During puberty, increasing estrogen activity contributes to:

Breast development.
Widening and development of the pelvis.
Increased fat distribution around the hips, thighs, and breasts.
Changes in body composition.
Pubic and axillary hair growth, primarily influenced by androgens.

Key Processes
Hormonal Regulation
The reproductive system is regulated by the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis.

The hypothalamus releases gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH).
The anterior pituitary gland releases follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH).
The testes or ovaries respond by producing sex hormones and supporting reproductive cell development.
Hormone feedback helps regulate this process.

Major Reproductive Hormones

Testosterone: Supports sperm production, sexual development, and male reproductive function.
Estrogen: Supports female reproductive development and regulates the menstrual cycle.
Progesterone: Helps prepare and maintain the uterine lining for pregnancy.
FSH: Supports ovarian follicle development and sperm production.
LH: Triggers ovulation and stimulates testosterone production in the testes.

Sperm Production & Ejaculation

Spermatogenesis: Production of sperm in the testes.
Sperm Maturation: Sperm mature in the epididymis.
Ejaculation: Muscular contractions propel semen through the urethra.
Semen: Mixture of sperm and fluids from reproductive glands.

Menstrual Cycle
The menstrual cycle prepares the female reproductive system for a possible pregnancy.

Menstruation: Shedding of the uterine lining when pregnancy has not occurred.
Follicular Phase: Ovarian follicles develop, and estrogen levels generally rise.
Ovulation: An oocyte is released from an ovary, triggered by an LH surge.
Luteal Phase: The corpus luteum produces progesterone to support the uterine lining.

If pregnancy does not occur, estrogen and progesterone levels fall, and menstruation begins.
Fertilization & Pregnancy

Fertilization: Sperm and oocyte combine, usually within a fallopian tube, forming a zygote.
Implantation: The developing embryo attaches to the uterine lining.
Pregnancy: The uterus supports fetal development, while the placenta facilitates nutrient, gas, and waste exchange between maternal and fetal circulations.
Childbirth: Uterine contractions help deliver the baby through the cervix and vagina.

Breastfeeding

Prolactin: Stimulates milk production.
Oxytocin: Causes milk ejection (let-down) and contributes to uterine contractions.

Effects of Aging
Male Reproductive Changes

Changes in Testosterone: Testosterone levels may gradually decline with age, although changes vary considerably.
Changes in Sexual Function: Erectile function and ejaculation may change due to vascular, neurological, hormonal, or medication-related factors.
Changes in Sperm Production: Sperm production can continue later in life, although fertility may decline.
Prostate Enlargement: Benign prostatic hyperplasia becomes more common with age and may affect urination.

Female Reproductive Changes

Perimenopause: Transitional period during which menstrual cycles and hormone levels become increasingly variable.
Menopause: Permanent cessation of menstrual periods, confirmed after 12 consecutive months without menstruation when no other cause is present.
Reduced Estrogen: Can contribute to vaginal dryness, thinning of vulvovaginal tissues, and changes in urinary symptoms.
Changes in Bone Health: Reduced estrogen after menopause contributes to increased bone loss.
Changes in Pelvic Support: Pelvic floor weakness may contribute to pelvic organ prolapse or urinary incontinence.

Clinical Implications

Changes in hormone levels can affect sexual function, comfort, and reproductive health.
Vaginal dryness or fragile tissues may cause discomfort during hygiene and personal care.
Prostate enlargement can contribute to urinary hesitancy, weak stream, and retention.
Pelvic floor weakness may affect bladder control.
Older adults may remain sexually active and require appropriate privacy, dignity, and health education.

Important: Sexual activity and interest do not necessarily disappear with aging. Pain, unexplained bleeding, severe urinary symptoms, or sudden changes in reproductive health should not be dismissed as normal aging.
See Effects of Aging - Systems & Clinical Implications.
Common Diseases & Disorders

































































ConditionDescriptionCommon Causes / Risk FactorsCNA ConsiderationsBenign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH)Noncancerous enlargement of the prostate that may obstruct urine flowIncreasing age, hormonal changes, family historyObserve weak urine stream, hesitancy, nocturia, or urinary retention; report changesPelvic Organ ProlapseDescent of pelvic organs, such as the uterus or bladder, due to weakened supporting tissuesChildbirth, aging, menopause, obesity, chronic strainingObserve reported pelvic pressure, bulging, discomfort, or urinary difficulties; provide respectful assistanceVaginitisInflammation or irritation of the vagina, sometimes causing itching, discomfort, or abnormal dischargeYeast infection, bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, irritants, reduced estrogenReport unusual discharge, odor, irritation, or discomfort; provide gentle hygiene according to the care planAtrophic Vaginitis / Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause (GSM)Estrogen-related changes causing vaginal dryness, irritation, discomfort, and sometimes urinary symptomsReduced estrogen after menopause or certain medical treatmentsProvide gentle perineal care; report pain, bleeding, irritation, or urinary changesUterine FibroidsNoncancerous growths of uterine muscle tissue that may cause heavy bleeding or pelvic pressureReproductive hormones, family history, age, genetic factorsReport abnormal bleeding, pelvic discomfort, or changes in daily functioningEndometriosisCondition in which tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus, causing inflammation and painGenetic, immune, and hormonal factors; exact cause unknownObserve and report significant pelvic pain, painful menstruation, or functional limitationsProstatitisInflammation of the prostate that may cause pelvic pain and urinary symptomsBacterial infection in some cases; other inflammatory or pain-related mechanismsReport pelvic discomfort, painful urination, fever, or difficulty voidingSexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)Infections transmitted primarily through sexual contact, including chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, and genital herpesSexual exposure to an infected person; inconsistent barrier protectionReport symptoms objectively, follow infection-control guidance, and maintain confidentialityReproductive CancersCancers affecting organs such as the prostate, cervix, uterus, ovaries, or testesRisk factors vary by cancer; may include age, genetics, HPV infection, and family historyReport unusual bleeding, persistent pain, unexplained masses, or changes from baseline
Important Distinctions

BPH vs. Prostate Cancer: BPH is noncancerous prostate enlargement; prostate cancer involves malignant cell growth. Both may affect urinary function.
Cystocele vs. Uterine Prolapse: A cystocele involves the bladder bulging into the vaginal wall; uterine prolapse involves descent of the uterus.
Vaginitis vs. Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause: Vaginitis describes vaginal inflammation from several possible causes; GSM describes changes primarily related to low estrogen.
Menopause vs. Reproductive Disease: Menopause is a normal biological transition, not an illness.
STI vs. Vaginitis: STIs are transmitted through sexual contact; vaginitis can have infectious or noninfectious causes and is not always sexually transmitted.

Important: CNAs observe and report reproductive abnormalities rather than independently diagnosing conditions or choosing treatments.
When to Report

New genital pain, irritation, swelling, or unusual discharge.
Abnormal vaginal bleeding, especially bleeding after menopause.
New difficulty urinating or suspected urinary retention.
New pelvic pain, pressure, or discomfort.
Genital sores, lesions, or unexplained skin changes.
New lumps or swelling in the breast, testicles, or genital area.
Fever associated with pelvic or genital symptoms.
Any concerning change from the resident’s usual baseline.

Emergency signs: Sudden severe testicular or pelvic pain, heavy bleeding with signs of shock, or acute inability to urinate with severe pain requires urgent or emergency evaluation.
Study Notes

Endocrine System
Urinary System
Effects of Aging - Systems & Clinical Implications

Clinical Connections

Perineal Care: Proper hygiene supports comfort, skin integrity, and dignity.
Incontinence Care: Urinary changes may be associated with prostate enlargement or pelvic floor dysfunction.
Elimination Care: Reproductive and urinary anatomy are closely related.
Skin Integrity & Breakdown Prevention: Genital irritation and moisture exposure may contribute to skin problems.
Therapeutic Communication: Reproductive and sexual health concerns require respectful, private communication.
Patient Rights: Residents retain rights to privacy, dignity, bodily autonomy, and consensual intimacy, subject to applicable safeguards.
Abuse, Neglect & Rights Violations: Recognize and report suspected sexual abuse according to mandatory reporting and facility procedures.

Questions

What is the pathway sperm follow from the testes to the outside of the body?
What are the functions of the seminal vesicles, prostate, and bulbourethral glands?
What are the functions of the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, and vagina?
What is the difference between the vagina and vulva?
How do FSH and LH regulate reproduction?
What are the major phases of the menstrual cycle?
What happens during ovulation and fertilization?
How do prolactin and oxytocin differ?
What reproductive changes are common with aging?
What is the difference between perimenopause and menopause?
How can BPH affect urination?
What distinguishes cystocele from uterine prolapse?
What reproductive symptoms should a CNA report?

anatomy-and-physiology/respiratory-syste.title: Respiratory System
anatomy-and-physiology/respiratory-syste.content:
Overview
The respiratory system moves air into and out of the lungs and supports gas exchange, supplying oxygen to the blood and removing carbon dioxide.
It works closely with the cardiovascular system to deliver oxygen to tissues and remove waste gases.
The respiratory system also helps regulate blood pH, enables speech, and protects the body from inhaled particles and pathogens.
Major Structures
Upper Respiratory Tract

Nose and Nasal Cavity: Filter, warm, and humidify inhaled air.
Pharynx (Throat): Passageway shared by air and food.
Larynx (Voice Box): Contains the vocal cords and helps protect the lower airway during swallowing.
Epiglottis: Flap of cartilage that helps prevent food and liquids from entering the airway during swallowing.

Lower Respiratory Tract

Trachea (Windpipe): Conducts air toward the lungs; supported by cartilage rings.
Bronchi: Two main branches of the trachea that carry air into the lungs.
Bronchioles: Smaller branching airways that distribute air to the alveoli.
Alveoli: Tiny air sacs where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it.
Lungs: Organs containing branching airways and alveoli, where gas exchange occurs.
Pulmonary Capillaries: Tiny blood vessels surrounding the alveoli, allowing oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange.

Supporting Structures

Diaphragm: Primary muscle responsible for inhalation; contracts and moves downward, increasing chest cavity volume.
Intercostal Muscles: Muscles between the ribs that assist with breathing.
Pleura: Thin membranes covering the lungs and lining the chest cavity, allowing smooth movement during breathing.
Cilia: Microscopic hairlike structures lining much of the respiratory tract that move mucus and trapped particles toward the throat.

Key Processes

Ventilation: Movement of air into and out of the lungs.

Inhalation (Inspiration): The diaphragm contracts and moves downward, expanding the chest cavity and drawing air into the lungs.
Exhalation (Expiration): The diaphragm relaxes, and elastic recoil helps move air out. Forced exhalation also uses additional muscles.


Gas Exchange: Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into pulmonary capillaries, while carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli.
Oxygen Transport: Hemoglobin in red blood cells carries most oxygen from the lungs to body tissues.
Carbon Dioxide Removal: Carbon dioxide produced by cells is transported to the lungs and exhaled.
Respiratory Regulation: The brainstem adjusts breathing based on chemical signals, especially carbon dioxide levels and blood pH.
Airway Protection: Mucus, cilia, and coughing help remove inhaled particles and pathogens.
Acid-Base Regulation: Breathing helps regulate blood pH by controlling carbon dioxide removal.

Effects of Aging

Reduced Respiratory Muscle Strength: The diaphragm and other breathing muscles may become less effective.
Reduced Chest Wall Flexibility: Changes in the ribs, spine, and connective tissues can restrict chest expansion.
Reduced Lung Elasticity: Lung tissue loses some elastic recoil, potentially increasing air trapping.
Reduced Respiratory Reserve: The lungs may be less able to compensate during physical exertion or illness.
Less Effective Airway Clearance: Changes in cough reflexes and mucus clearance can make secretions harder to remove.

Clinical Implications

Respiratory infections, such as pneumonia, may be harder to tolerate.
Physical activity may cause fatigue or breathlessness more readily.
Immobility can increase the risk of secretion buildup and respiratory complications.
Observe respiratory rate, breathing effort, cough, and changes from baseline.
Encourage permitted mobility and positioning according to the care plan.

Important: Significant shortness of breath, low oxygen levels, or new respiratory distress should not be dismissed as normal aging.
Common Diseases & Disorders









































ConditionDescriptionCommon Causes / Risk FactorsCNA ConsiderationsChronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)Chronic airflow limitation, commonly involving emphysema and chronic bronchitis. Emphysema damages alveolar walls; chronic bronchitis causes airway inflammation and excess mucus.Smoking, long-term exposure to air pollutants, occupational dust or fumes, rarely genetic conditionsObserve dyspnea, wheezing, chronic cough, sputum production, fatigue, and changes in respiratory effort. Follow prescribed positioning, activity, and oxygen-safety instructions.AsthmaChronic airway inflammation with episodes of airway narrowing, often causing wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breathAllergens, smoke, respiratory infections, exercise, cold air, strong fragrances; genetic susceptibilityRecognize and report breathing difficulty, wheezing, coughing, or worsening symptoms. Assist with prescribed care within CNA scope.Tuberculosis (TB)Bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, usually affecting the lungs. Active pulmonary TB can cause prolonged cough, fever, night sweats, and weight loss.Airborne exposure to a person with infectious TB; increased risk with weakened immunity and certain congregate settingsReport suspected symptoms or exposure promptly; follow airborne precautions and facility protocols, including a negative-pressure room.PneumoniaInfection of lung tissue that causes inflammation and may fill alveoli with fluid or inflammatory material, impairing gas exchangeBacterial, viral, or fungal infection; aspiration, older age, impaired immunity, immobilityObserve cough, fever, increased respiratory effort, fatigue, and new confusion or functional decline. Report changes promptly.Acute BronchitisInflammation of the bronchi, commonly causing cough and sometimes mucus productionUsually respiratory viruses; smoke and other airway irritantsObserve cough, sputum, fever, and breathing changes. Report worsening symptoms.
Important: CNAs observe and report respiratory abnormalities rather than independently diagnosing conditions, prescribing oxygen, or selecting treatments.
Important Distinctions

Emphysema vs. Chronic Bronchitis: Emphysema involves destruction of alveolar walls and loss of elastic recoil. Chronic bronchitis involves chronic productive cough associated with airway inflammation and mucus production. Both may contribute to COPD.
Asthma vs. COPD: Asthma commonly involves variable airway narrowing and inflammation, often with substantial reversibility. COPD causes persistent airflow limitation, although symptoms and treatment responses can vary. Some patients have features of both.
Ventilation vs. Gas Exchange: Ventilation moves air into and out of the lungs. Gas exchange transfers oxygen and carbon dioxide between the alveoli and pulmonary capillaries.
Hypoxemia vs. Hypoxia: Hypoxemia means reduced oxygen in arterial blood. Hypoxia means inadequate oxygen availability or use at the tissue level. They are related but not identical.

When to Report

New or worsening shortness of breath.
Increased respiratory rate, effort, or unusual breathing patterns.
Persistent or worsening cough.
New or increased sputum production or changes in its appearance.
Fever or symptoms suggesting a respiratory infection.
New confusion, unusual fatigue, or reduced activity tolerance.
Oxygen saturation outside the resident’s prescribed parameters, when monitoring is part of the care plan.

Emergency signs: Severe difficulty breathing, inability to speak because of breathlessness, blue or gray lips or skin, sudden unresponsiveness, or signs of complete airway obstruction require immediate emergency response.
Study Notes

Vital Signs
Effects of Aging - Systems & Clinical Implications

Clinical Connections

Recognizing Patient Distress: Changes in breathing may indicate respiratory compromise or acute illness.
Choking & Airway Obstruction: Obstruction prevents adequate airflow and requires prompt recognition.
Cardiac Arrest & CPR Response: Inadequate breathing or circulation can require immediate emergency intervention.
Patient Positions: Upright positioning, when appropriate, can improve comfort and ease breathing.
Transmission-Based Precautions: Respiratory infections require appropriate transmission-based precautions.

Questions

What is the role of the alveoli and pulmonary capillaries?
What happens to the diaphragm during inhalation and exhalation?
What is the difference between ventilation and gas exchange?
How do mucus and cilia protect the respiratory tract?
How does aging affect respiratory reserve and airway clearance?
What distinguishes emphysema from chronic bronchitis?
How do asthma and COPD differ?
How is active pulmonary tuberculosis transmitted?
Why can pneumonia impair oxygen exchange?

anatomy-and-physiology/sensory-organs.title: Sensory Organs
anatomy-and-physiology/sensory-organs.content:
Overview
The sensory organs detect changes inside and outside the body and send information to the nervous system for interpretation.
The five traditionally recognized senses are:

Sight (Vision): Detection of light, color, and visual detail.
Hearing (Audition): Detection of sound.
Taste (Gustation): Detection of chemicals dissolved in saliva.
Smell (Olfaction): Detection of airborne chemicals.
Touch (Somatosensation): Detection of pressure, vibration, temperature, pain, and other sensations.

The sensory organs work closely with the Nervous System. Sensory receptors convert stimuli into electrical signals that travel through nerves to the brain or spinal cord.
The vestibular system of the inner ear also supports balance and spatial orientation.
Major Structures
Sight — Eyes
The eyes detect light and convert it into signals that the brain interprets as vision.

Sclera: Tough, white outer layer that protects the eye and maintains its shape.
Cornea: Transparent front surface that bends (refracts) incoming light.
Iris: Colored muscular structure that controls pupil size.
Pupil: Opening in the center of the iris through which light enters.
Lens: Focuses light onto the retina and changes shape to help focus at different distances.
Retina: Light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye containing photoreceptors.

Rods: Support vision in dim light; do not distinguish colors.
Cones: Support color vision and sharp visual detail, especially in brighter light.


Macula: Central region of the retina responsible for detailed central vision.
Optic Nerve: Transmits visual information from the retina to the brain.
Retinal Blood Vessels: Supply and drain blood from retinal tissue, including through the central retinal artery and vein.

Basic Pathway: Light → Cornea → Pupil → Lens → Retina → Optic Nerve → Brain.
Hearing & Balance — Ears
The ear has three major regions.
Outer Ear

Pinna (Auricle): Visible external ear that helps collect sound.
External Auditory Canal: Carries sound toward the eardrum.

Middle Ear

Tympanic Membrane (Eardrum): Vibrates in response to sound.
Ossicles: Three small bones that transmit and amplify vibrations.

Malleus (Hammer)
Incus (Anvil)
Stapes (Stirrup)


Eustachian (Auditory) Tube: Connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx and helps equalize pressure.

Inner Ear

Cochlea: Fluid-filled structure that converts vibrations into nerve signals for hearing.
Vestibular System: Includes the semicircular canals and otolith organs, which detect head movement and position.
Vestibulocochlear Nerve (CN VIII): Carries hearing and balance information to the brain.

Basic Hearing Pathway: Sound → Pinna → Ear Canal → Eardrum → Ossicles → Cochlea → Auditory Nerve → Brain.
Taste — Tongue & Taste Buds

Taste Buds: Collections of sensory cells primarily located on the tongue, with some elsewhere in the mouth and throat.
Taste Receptors: Detect dissolved chemicals associated with sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami tastes.
Sensory Nerves: Carry taste signals toward the brain through several cranial nerves.

Important: Flavor depends on both taste and smell.
Smell — Nose

Nasal Cavity: Allows inhaled air and odor molecules to reach olfactory receptors.
Olfactory Epithelium: Specialized tissue high in the nasal cavity containing smell receptors.
Olfactory Nerve (CN I): Transmits smell-related information toward the brain.
Olfactory Bulb: Processes initial smell signals before sending information to other brain regions.

Touch — Skin & Sensory Receptors

Mechanoreceptors: Detect touch, pressure, stretching, and vibration.
Thermoreceptors: Detect temperature changes.
Nociceptors: Detect potentially tissue-damaging stimuli associated with pain.
Peripheral Sensory Nerves: Carry information from receptors toward the CNS.

Touch and body sensation also depend on receptors in muscles, tendons, and joints.
Key Processes

Sensory Transduction: Sensory receptors convert physical or chemical stimuli into electrical signals.
Sensory Transmission: Peripheral nerves carry signals to the CNS.
Sensory Perception: The brain interprets signals as sights, sounds, smells, tastes, or physical sensations.
Visual Accommodation: The lens changes shape to focus on objects at different distances.
Sound Transduction: Inner-ear hair cells convert mechanical vibrations into neural signals.
Balance Regulation: Vestibular organs detect head movement and position; the brain integrates this with visual and proprioceptive information.
Protective Sensation: Pain and temperature sensation help the body recognize potentially harmful conditions.

Effects of Aging

Reduced Near Vision (Presbyopia): The lens becomes less flexible, making nearby objects harder to focus on.
Reduced Light Adaptation: Eyes may require more time to adjust to changes in lighting.
Increased Cataract Risk: Lens proteins can become cloudy with age.
Age-Related Hearing Loss (Presbycusis): Hearing often becomes less sensitive, particularly to high-frequency sounds.
Reduced Smell Sensitivity: Some odors may become harder to detect.
Reduced Taste Sensitivity: Taste perception may change, though medications, oral health, and impaired smell also contribute.
Changes in Touch & Vibration Sensation: Some sensations may become less sensitive.
Changes in Balance: Age-related vestibular and sensory changes can affect stability.

Clinical Implications

Vision changes can increase fall risk and difficulty with ADLs.
Hearing loss can make communication and instructions harder to understand.
Reduced smell can make smoke, spoiled food, and other environmental hazards harder to detect.
Changes in taste and smell may affect appetite and nutritional intake.
Reduced protective sensation can increase the risk of unnoticed injury.
Multiple sensory impairments can contribute to social withdrawal or reduced independence.

Important: Sudden vision or hearing loss, sudden severe vertigo, and abrupt neurological changes are not normal aging changes and require prompt evaluation.
Common Diseases & Disorders







































































ConditionDescriptionCommon Causes / Risk FactorsCNA ConsiderationsCataractsClouding of the eye’s lens, often causing blurry vision and glareAging, diabetes, smoking, corticosteroid use, ultraviolet exposureSupport adequate lighting, safe navigation, and use of prescribed visual aidsGlaucomaGroup of diseases that damage the optic nerve and can cause vision lossElevated eye pressure in many cases, aging, family history, certain medical conditionsObserve difficulty navigating or changes in vision; sudden painful eye symptoms require emergency evaluationAge-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD)Disease affecting the macula, impairing central visionAging, smoking, genetics, family history, cardiovascular risk factorsAssist with reading and detailed tasks; encourage prescribed visual aids and report changesPresbyopiaAge-related difficulty focusing on nearby objectsReduced flexibility of the eye’s lens with agingEnsure reading glasses and adequate lighting are available when neededHearing LossReduced ability to detect or understand sounds; may be conductive, sensorineural, or mixedAging, noise exposure, earwax blockage, infections, medicationsFace the resident, reduce background noise, and check that hearing aids are available and functioningTinnitusPerception of ringing, buzzing, or other sounds without an external sourceHearing loss, noise exposure, medications, ear disordersReport new or worsening symptoms, especially if accompanied by sudden hearing lossVertigoSensation of spinning or motion when no such movement is occurringInner-ear disorders such as BPPV, vestibular inflammation, migraine; sometimes neurological conditionsAssist with mobility, follow fall precautions, and promptly report new symptomsLoss of Smell (Anosmia)Partial or complete loss of the ability to smellRespiratory infections, nasal obstruction, aging, head injury, certain neurological diseasesObserve appetite and safety concerns; report new or unexplained changesReduced Taste (Hypogeusia)Decreased ability to perceive tastesAging, medications, oral conditions, infections, impaired smellObserve changes in appetite and food intake; report concernsPeripheral Sensory LossReduced ability to feel touch, vibration, temperature, or painDiabetes, peripheral neuropathy, nerve injury, vitamin deficienciesHelp protect areas with reduced sensation and report injuries or sensory changes
Important Distinctions

Cataracts: Clouding of the lens.
Glaucoma: Damage to the optic nerve.
Macular Degeneration: Damage affecting central retinal vision.
Presbyopia: Reduced ability to focus on nearby objects.
Conductive Hearing Loss: Sound transmission is impaired in the outer or middle ear.
Sensorineural Hearing Loss: Inner-ear or auditory nerve structures are affected.
Vertigo vs. dizziness: Vertigo involves a sensation of motion or spinning; dizziness is a broader description.

Important: CNAs observe and report changes in sensory function rather than diagnosing eye, ear, or neurological diseases.
When to Report

New or worsening difficulty seeing or hearing.
Sudden vision loss, flashes, or a new curtain-like shadow over vision.
Sudden hearing loss.
New severe eye pain.
New vertigo, severe dizziness, or difficulty walking.
New loss of smell or taste.
New numbness, reduced sensation, or unexplained injuries.
Increasing difficulty with communication, eating, or ADLs due to sensory changes.

Emergency signs: Sudden vision loss, severe eye pain with headache or nausea, or sensory changes accompanied by facial drooping, weakness, or speech difficulty require immediate emergency response.
Study Notes

Nervous System
Integumentary System

Clinical Connections

Fall Risk: Impaired vision, sensation, or balance can increase the chance of falls.
Therapeutic Communication: Hearing and vision impairments may require different communication approaches.
Dementia Care: Sensory limitations can affect orientation and communication.
Assisting with Feeding: Taste, smell, vision, and oral sensation may affect eating.
Standard Precautions: Eye and ear infections may require appropriate precautions.
Neurological Observations: Sudden changes in vision, sensation, or balance can indicate neurological problems.

anatomy-and-physiology/urinary-system.title: Urinary System
anatomy-and-physiology/urinary-system.content:
Overview
The urinary system (renal system) filters blood, removes waste products and excess water, regulates fluid and electrolyte balance, and produces urine.
It consists of the kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, and urethra.
The kidneys also help:

Regulate Blood Pressure: Adjust blood volume and release renin, which participates in blood pressure regulation.
Stimulate Red Blood Cell Production: The kidneys release erythropoietin (EPO), which signals the bone marrow to produce red blood cells.
Support Calcium Absorption: Activate vitamin D, helping the intestines absorb calcium.
Maintain Acid-Base Balance: Remove excess acid and regulate bicarbonate levels.

The bladder stores urine until signals from the nervous system coordinate urination.
Major Structures
Upper Urinary Tract

Kidneys: Two bean-shaped organs located toward the back of the abdomen, on either side of the spine, below the rib cage.

Renal Cortex: Outer region containing parts of the structures that filter blood.
Renal Medulla: Inner region containing structures involved in concentrating urine.
Nephrons: Functional units of the kidneys that filter blood and form urine.

Glomerulus: Network of capillaries that filters fluid and small substances from blood.
Renal Tubules: Reabsorb needed substances and secrete additional wastes into the forming urine.


Renal Pelvis: Collects urine and channels it into the ureter.


Ureters: Two muscular tubes that transport urine from the kidneys to the bladder through peristalsis.

Lower Urinary Tract

Urinary Bladder: Hollow, muscular organ in the pelvis that stores urine.

Detrusor Muscle: Smooth muscle in the bladder wall that contracts during urination.
Stretch Receptors: Detect bladder filling and send signals to the nervous system.


Urethra: Tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body.
Internal Urethral Sphincter: Involuntary smooth muscle at the bladder neck that helps prevent urine leakage.
External Urethral Sphincter: Skeletal muscle under voluntary control that helps maintain continence.

Supporting Structures

Pelvic Floor Muscles: Help support the bladder and maintain urinary continence.
Renal Arteries: Supply blood to the kidneys for filtration.
Renal Veins: Return blood from the kidneys to circulation.

Urine Pathway: Kidneys → Ureters → Bladder → Urethra → Outside the body.
Key Processes
Urine Formation
Urine is produced through three primary processes:

Glomerular Filtration: Water and small dissolved substances move from blood into the nephron.
Tubular Reabsorption: Needed water, glucose, electrolytes, and other substances return to the bloodstream.
Tubular Secretion: Additional wastes, medications, and excess ions move from the blood into the renal tubules.

Remaining fluid and dissolved waste products become urine.
Urination (Micturition)
Urination requires coordination between the bladder, sphincters, spinal cord, and brain.

The kidneys continuously produce urine.
Urine travels through the ureters and collects in the bladder.
As the bladder fills, stretch receptors send signals to the nervous system.
The person becomes aware of the need to urinate.
During normal voluntary urination, the detrusor muscle contracts and urethral sphincters relax.
Urine flows through the urethra and exits the body.

Continence: Ability to control when and where urination occurs.
Incontinence: Involuntary urine leakage caused by impaired bladder storage, sphincter function, neurological control, or other factors.
Fluid & Electrolyte Regulation

Water Balance: Kidneys adjust the amount of water excreted in urine.
Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH): Increases water reabsorption, helping conserve body fluids.
Aldosterone: Promotes sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion.
Electrolyte Balance: Kidneys regulate sodium, potassium, calcium, and other electrolytes.
Acid-Base Balance: Kidneys help maintain blood pH by excreting acid and regulating bicarbonate.

Blood Pressure & Hormone Regulation

Renin: Released by the kidneys and activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), which helps regulate blood pressure.
Erythropoietin (EPO): Stimulates bone marrow to produce red blood cells.
Vitamin D Activation: Kidneys convert vitamin D into its active hormonal form, calcitriol, which supports calcium absorption.

Effects of Aging

Reduced Kidney Reserve: Kidney blood flow and filtration capacity may decline, reducing the ability to handle physiological stress.
Altered Medication Clearance: Reduced kidney function can cause certain medications to accumulate.
Reduced Urine-Concentrating Ability: Kidneys may become less effective at conserving water during dehydration.
Reduced Bladder Capacity: Some older adults experience decreased functional bladder capacity and more frequent urination.
Bladder Emptying Changes: Incomplete emptying may become more common, increasing the risk of urinary retention and infection.
Pelvic Floor Changes: Reduced muscle support may contribute to urinary leakage.
Changes in Prostate Size: Prostate enlargement in some older men can obstruct urine flow.

Clinical Implications

Increased vulnerability to dehydration and electrolyte disturbances.
Changes in urinary frequency, urgency, or nighttime urination.
Increased risk of urinary retention and urinary tract infections in some residents.
Greater sensitivity to medications cleared through the kidneys.
Increased need for appropriate toileting assistance and observation of urinary patterns.

Important: Urinary incontinence, kidney failure, and urinary tract infections are not inevitable consequences of aging.
See Effects of Aging - Systems & Clinical Implications.
Common Diseases & Disorders

follow prescribed restrictionsUrinary Tract Infection (UTI)Infection affecting any part of the urinary tract, commonly the bladderBacterial entry into urinary tract, urinary retention, catheter use, urinary obstructionReport painful urination, urgency, frequency, fever, or new urinary symptoms; Types of Urinary Incontinence



































TypeDescriptionCommon CausesStress IncontinenceUrine leaks during coughing, laughing, sneezing, or liftingWeak pelvic floor or urethral supportUrge IncontinenceSudden intense urge to urinate followed by involuntary leakageOveractive bladder, detrusor overactivity, neurological conditionsOverflow IncontinenceLeakage associated with a bladder that does not empty adequatelyUrinary retention, obstruction, weak bladder contractionFunctional IncontinencePerson cannot reach or use the toilet in time despite potentially intact urinary functionMobility limitations, cognitive impairment, environmental barriersMixed IncontinenceCombination of two or more incontinence types, commonly stress and urgeMultiple contributing mechanisms
Important Distinctions

AKI vs. CKD: Acute kidney injury develops suddenly; chronic kidney disease develops or persists over months or years.
Urinary Retention vs. Incontinence: Retention is inadequate bladder emptying; incontinence is involuntary leakage. Both can occur together.
Stress vs. Urge Incontinence: Stress leakage occurs with increased abdominal pressure; urge leakage follows a sudden compelling need to urinate.
UTI vs. Kidney Infection: A bladder infection affects the lower urinary tract; pyelonephritis affects the kidney and may cause more serious illness.
Oliguria vs. Anuria: Oliguria means abnormally low urine output; anuria means nearly absent urine output.

Important: Cloudy or foul-smelling urine alone does not establish a UTI, and a positive urine culture does not always mean a symptomatic infection. CNAs report objective findings rather than diagnosing infection.
CNAs do not independently diagnose urinary conditions, prescribe fluid restrictions, or perform urinary catheter procedures unless specifically authorized within their role and training.
When to Report

New burning, pain, urgency, or difficulty with urination.
New or worsening urinary incontinence.
Inability to urinate or suspected urinary retention.
Markedly decreased urine output or significant change from baseline.
Blood in the urine.
Fever, chills, flank pain, or suspected infection.
New lower abdominal pain or distention.
Unexpected changes in intake and output.
New swelling, dizziness, or signs of dehydration.
Sudden confusion or functional decline, particularly when accompanied by other signs of illness.

Emergency signs: Inability to urinate with severe pain or distention, severe flank pain with fever, sudden unresponsiveness, or signs of severe infection require urgent or emergency evaluation according to facility protocol.
Study Notes

Fluid Balance
Effects of Aging - Systems & Clinical Implications
Endocrine System

Clinical Connections

Elimination Care: Proper toileting support and observation help maintain comfort and dignity.
Incontinence Care: Prompt hygiene reduces moisture exposure and skin breakdown.
Fluid Balance: Kidneys regulate water and electrolyte levels.
Dehydration: Reduced fluid intake or excessive fluid loss can affect kidney function.
Skin Integrity & Breakdown Prevention: Urinary incontinence can contribute to moisture-associated skin damage.
Vital Signs: Fever, blood pressure changes, and pulse changes may accompany urinary illness.
Standard Precautions: Urinary infections and catheter care require appropriate infection-prevention practices.
Recognizing Patient Distress: Acute urinary retention or severe infection may require urgent attention.

assessments-and-clinical-reasoning/neuro.title: Neurological Observations
assessments-and-clinical-reasoning/neuro.content:
What Am I Assessing?
Observe a resident’s neurological functioning and recognize changes that may indicate illness, injury, or an emergency.
Key Principle: Compare observations with the resident’s usual baseline.
What Should I Look For?
Level of Consciousness

Alertness and responsiveness.
Unusual drowsiness or difficulty waking.
Unresponsiveness.

Orientation & Cognition

New confusion or disorientation.
Difficulty recognizing familiar people or surroundings.
Sudden changes in attention or behavior.

Speech & Communication

Slurred or unclear speech.
Difficulty finding words.
Difficulty understanding instructions.
New inability to communicate.

Movement & Strength

New weakness, especially on one side.
Changes in walking or coordination.
New facial drooping or asymmetry.
Unusual movements or seizures.

Sensation & Vision

New numbness or tingling.
Sudden vision changes.
New dizziness or loss of balance.

Additional Warning Signs

Sudden severe headache.
Vomiting associated with an acute neurological change.
Sudden changes following a fall or head injury.

What Could It Mean?
Possible causes include:

Stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA).
Head injury.
Seizure activity.
Infection or delirium.
Medication effects.
Abnormal blood glucose or other metabolic disturbances.
Important: These observations do not establish a diagnosis.

What Should I Do?
Routine Observations

Observe the resident during regular care.
Compare behavior, movement, speech, and responsiveness with their baseline.
Ask simple questions appropriate to the resident’s abilities.
Report new or worsening changes promptly.
Document objective observations according to facility policy.

Suspected Stroke — BE FAST

B — Balance: Sudden loss of balance or coordination.
E — Eyes: Sudden vision changes.
F — Face: Uneven smile or facial drooping.
A — Arms: New arm weakness or drifting.
S — Speech: Slurred speech or difficulty speaking.
T — Time: Activate emergency response immediately; note symptom onset or last-known-well time.

Emergency Response

Activate the facility emergency response system for sudden neurological changes.
Stay with the resident when safe.
Observe breathing and responsiveness.
Follow directions from the nurse or emergency team.
Do not give food or drink to a resident with altered consciousness or suspected swallowing impairment.

Important Considerations

Sudden confusion is not automatically dementia.
A resident with chronic neurological impairment may have an established baseline different from other residents.
Sudden changes require prompt evaluation even if symptoms improve.
CNAs observe and report; formal neurological examination and diagnosis belong to qualified clinicians.

Related

Recognizing Patient Distress
Seizure Response
Aphasia
Dementia Care
Fall Risk
Vital Signs

Sources

CNA Module 12 — Emergency Procedures
CDC — Signs and Symptoms of Stroke
Facility neurological observation and emergency response procedures

Flashcards
What does BE FAST stand for?01-foundations / assessmentAnswerBalance, Eyes, Face, Arms, Speech, Time.
What is the response to sudden facial droop and new slurred speech?03-application / assessmentAnswerActivate emergency response for possible stroke.

assessments-and-clinical-reasoning/pain-.title: Pain Assessment
assessments-and-clinical-reasoning/pain-.content:
What Am I Assessing?
Recognize and report pain that may affect a resident’s comfort, mobility, sleep, and daily activities.
Pain is subjective: The resident’s self-report is the primary source of information when they can communicate reliably.
Types of Pain:

Acute: Recent onset, often associated with injury or illness.
Chronic: Persistent or recurring pain, commonly lasting longer than 3 months.

What Should I Look For?
Resident-Reported Pain
Ask questions appropriate to the resident’s communication abilities:

Location: Where does it hurt?
Intensity: How much does it hurt?
Quality: Is it sharp, dull, aching, burning, or throbbing?
Timing: When did it start? Is it constant or intermittent?
Triggers: What makes it better or worse?
Impact: Does it interfere with moving, sleeping, or eating?

Pain Scale
Numeric Rating Scale (0–10):

0: No pain.
10: Worst pain imaginable.
Ask the resident to choose the number that best describes their pain.
Use the communication method or pain scale specified in the care plan.

Nonverbal Signs

Facial grimacing or frowning.
Guarding or protecting an area.
Crying, moaning, or restlessness.
Withdrawal from activities.
Changes in movement or appetite.
New agitation or resistance during care.
Important: Behavioral signs can indicate discomfort but do not establish its cause. Absence of visible distress does not mean absence of pain.

What Could It Mean?
Pain may be associated with:

Injury or illness.
Pressure injuries or skin breakdown.
Immobility or poor positioning.
Infection or inflammation.
Other underlying conditions.
New, severe, or worsening pain may require urgent nursing evaluation.

What Should I Do?

Ask about pain before activities that may worsen discomfort.
Observe verbal and nonverbal responses during care.
Stop or modify activities that cause unexpected pain when safe.
Help with approved comfort measures, such as repositioning.
Report new, worsening, or uncontrolled pain to the nurse promptly.
Document observations and the resident’s statements according to facility policy.
Observe and report the response to prescribed comfort measures.
Urgent Reporting:


Sudden severe pain.
Chest pain or pressure.
Severe abdominal pain.
Pain accompanied by breathing difficulty, fainting, or sudden neurological changes.

Related

Recognizing Patient Distress
Pressure Injuries
Repositioning in Bed
Therapeutic Communication
Dementia Care

Sources

CNA clinical observations and reporting principles
MedlinePlus — Pain
Facility pain-assessment and reporting procedures

Flashcards
Whose report is the primary source for pain intensity when communication is reliable?03-application / assessmentAnswerThe resident's own report.
What does 0 mean on the numeric pain scale?01-foundations / assessmentAnswerNo pain.
Name three nonverbal pain cues.01-foundations / assessmentAnswerGrimacing, guarding, and moaning or restlessness.

assessments-and-clinical-reasoning/recog.filePath: Assessments and Clinical Reasoning/Recognizing Patient Distress.md
assessments-and-clinical-reasoning/recog.title: Recognizing Patient Distress
assessments-and-clinical-reasoning/recog.content:
What Am I Assessing?
Recognize sudden or concerning changes that may indicate a medical emergency.
ABCs:

Airway: Is the airway open?
Breathing: Is the patient breathing normally?
Circulation: Are there signs of severe bleeding or inadequate circulation?

What Should I Look For?
Signs (Objective):

Excessive bleeding.
Abnormally fast or slow breathing.
Abnormal heart rate or blood pressure.
Unresponsiveness.
Sudden changes in mental status.
Symptoms (Subjective):
Chest pain or pressure.
Difficulty breathing or throat tightness.
Numbness or tingling.
Nausea.
Sudden visual disturbances.

Stroke Recognition — BE FAST
Use BE FAST to recognize common warning signs of stroke:

B — Balance: Sudden loss of balance or coordination.
E — Eyes: Sudden vision loss or visual disturbance.
F — Face: Facial drooping or asymmetry.
A — Arms: Sudden arm weakness, especially on one side.
S — Speech: Slurred speech or difficulty speaking or understanding language.
T — Time: Activate emergency response immediately and note when symptoms began or when the person was last known to be well.

Important: Stroke-like symptoms remain an emergency even if they disappear. Do not wait to see whether they improve.
What Could It Mean?

Airway obstruction or respiratory distress.
Cardiac or circulatory emergency.
Neurological emergency.
Shock or significant blood loss.
Other acute medical deterioration.

What Should I Do?

Ensure scene safety.
Recognize potentially life-threatening changes.
Activate the emergency response system when indicated.
Notify the nurse immediately.
Provide emergency assistance within training and authorization.
Remain with the patient when safe and communicate observations.

Related

Cardiac Arrest & CPR Response
Choking & Airway Obstruction
Bleeding, Shock & Injury Response
Emergency Preparedness & Response

Sources

CNA Module 12 — Emergency Procedures
American Heart Association — 2025 Adult Basic Life Support Guidelines
CDC — Signs and Symptoms of Stroke
Facility rapid-response and emergency-activation procedures (verify at clinical site)

Flashcards
What are the ABCs of emergency observation?03-application / assessmentAnswerAirway, breathing, circulation.
What should a CNA do when a resident has sudden life-threatening symptoms?03-application / assessmentAnswerActivate emergency response, notify the nurse, assist within training.
What does BE FAST stand for in stroke recognition?01-foundations / assessmentAnswerBalance, Eyes, Face, Arms, Speech, Time.
What should a CNA do when a resident develops sudden stroke-like symptoms?03-application / assessmentAnswerActivate emergency response immediately, even if symptoms resolve.

assessments-and-clinical-reasoning/vital.title: Vital Signs
assessments-and-clinical-reasoning/vital.content:
What Am I Assessing?
Vital signs provide measurements of essential physiological functions.
Common Vital Signs:

Temperature: Body temperature and thermoregulation.
Pulse: Heart rate and rhythm.
Respirations: Breathing rate, rhythm, and effort.
Blood Pressure: Arterial pressure during circulation.
Oxygen Saturation (SpO₂): Estimate of blood oxygen saturation.
Pain: Often assessed alongside vital signs.
Key Principle: Compare measurements with the resident’s usual baseline, current condition, and care plan.

What Should I Look For?
Temperature

Elevated or abnormally low temperature.
Chills, sweating, or unusual warmth.
Changes from the resident’s normal temperature.
Measurement site and method.

Pulse

Rate: Fast, slow, or within expected range.
Rhythm: Regular or irregular.
Strength: Strong, weak, or difficult to detect.
Changes from baseline.

Respirations

Rate: Breaths per minute.
Rhythm: Regular or irregular.
Depth: Shallow or deep.
Effort: Relaxed or labored.
Associated coughing, wheezing, or visible distress.

Blood Pressure

Systolic and diastolic measurements.
Unexpectedly high or low readings.
Dizziness or weakness associated with position changes.
Changes from baseline.

Oxygen Saturation

SpO₂ reading and whether it is consistent with the resident’s condition.
Poor signal quality or movement affecting measurements.
Signs of breathing difficulty despite a seemingly acceptable reading.

Pain

Resident-reported pain score when appropriate.
Location, severity, and changes.
Nonverbal indicators of discomfort.

What Could It Mean?









































ObservationPossible ConcernElevated temperatureInfection, inflammation, or other illnessLow temperatureHypothermia or impaired temperature regulationRapid pulsePain, fever, dehydration, or physiological stressSlow pulseMedication effect, normal variation, or cardiac conduction changesRapid or labored breathingRespiratory distress or other acute illnessLow blood pressureDehydration, blood loss, medication effects, or circulatory problemsElevated blood pressureStress, pain, or hypertensionLow SpO₂Possible impaired oxygenation or measurement error
Important: These are possible explanations, not diagnoses.
What Should I Do?

Review the care plan and required measurement schedule.
Explain the procedure and prepare equipment.
Obtain measurements using trained methods.
Record the values, units, time, and relevant measurement details.
Compare with the resident’s baseline and reporting parameters.
Notify the nurse about unexpected or concerning results.
Follow directions for repeat measurements and ongoing observation.

Urgent Findings
Activate the appropriate emergency response for:

Severe breathing difficulty.
Unresponsiveness or sudden significant mental-status changes.
Chest pain with concerning symptoms.
Signs of stroke or shock.
Other critical findings identified by the facility’s emergency protocol.

Important Considerations

Vital signs must be interpreted in context.
A change from baseline may be important even when the reading falls within a typical adult range.
Pain, activity, medications, positioning, and illness can affect readings.
Report symptoms alongside numeric measurements.
CNAs observe, measure, document, and report; licensed clinicians perform clinical interpretation and treatment planning.

Related

Vital Sign Ranges
Measuring Blood Pressure
Blood Pressure
Recognizing Patient Distress
Pain Assessment
Neurological Observations
Orthostatic Hypotension

Sources

MedlinePlus — Vital Signs
CNA clinical skills training and facility reporting parameters

Flashcards
Which features of respiration should be observed beyond rate?01-foundations / assessmentAnswerRhythm, depth, effort, and signs of distress.
Why is baseline more useful than a normal-range table alone?02-mechanisms / assessmentAnswerA meaningful change may occur within a typical reference range.
What should accompany an abnormal vital-sign report?03-application / assessmentAnswerSymptoms, context, and relevant changes from baseline.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/documentation.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Documentation and Charting.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/documentation.title: Documentation and Charting
clinical-skills-and-how-to/documentation.content:
When & Why?
Documentation creates an accurate record of resident care, observations, and changes in condition.
Clinical records support:

Communication between healthcare workers.
Continuity of care.
Monitoring resident progress.
Accountability and legal requirements.

Documentation must be accurate, complete, confidential, and organized.
Before You Start

Confirm the correct resident and chart.
Review the care provided and observations made.
Check that measurements and times are accurate.
Use authorized paper or electronic documentation systems.
Follow facility charting procedures.
Protect resident confidentiality.

Steps
Routine Documentation

Confirm the correct resident record.
Document the care actually provided.
Record the date and time accurately.
Use factual, specific, and objective language.
Include relevant measurements with units.
Record resident statements accurately, using quotation marks when helpful.
Include the resident’s response or relevant changes.
Record care refusals and incomplete care accurately.
Authenticate the entry according to facility procedure.
Report significant findings to the nurse without waiting for documentation.

Timing: Chart promptly after care or observations, following facility procedure. Avoid relying on memory at the end of a long shift.
Commonly Charted Information









































CategoryExamplesNutritionPercentage of meals eaten, fluid intakeEliminationBowel movements, urine measurementsMobilityAmbulation distance, transfers, assistance levelRestorative careRange-of-motion exercises, assigned activitiesADLsBathing, dressing, toileting, hygieneBehaviorSpecific observed actions and resident statementsRefusalsCare offered, resident response, nurse notificationChangesNew symptoms, measurements, or unusual observations
Good vs. Poor Charting





























AvoidPreferResident was difficultResident declined bathing and stated, “I don’t want a shower today”Ate poorlyAte approximately 25% of lunchWalked wellAmbulated 40 feet with walker and assigned assistanceWas aggressiveResident struck the bedside table twice with an open handSeemed sickResident reported nausea and vomited once
Paper Charting

Use approved writing instruments and formats.
Follow facility rules for ink color.
Write legibly.
Do not erase, obscure, or overwrite an incorrect entry.
Follow the approved correction procedure, which may require a single line through an error, initials, and a corrected entry.
Never chart for another person’s work as though it were your own.

Electronic Health Records (EHR)

Use your own authorized credentials.
Select the correct resident record.
Verify entries before submission.
Use the system’s approved correction or addendum process.
Do not share passwords or leave an unlocked record accessible to unauthorized persons.
Follow facility policy for documenting late entries.
Never attempt to bypass an audit trail.

Incident Reports
Incident reports document unexpected events or events with potential for injury or harm.
Examples:

Resident falls or injuries.
Suspected abuse or neglect.
Employee injuries.
Blood or body-fluid exposure.
Injuries involving visitors.
Other events identified by facility policy.

CNA Responsibilities

Ensure immediate resident or personal safety.
Notify the nurse or supervisor promptly.
Follow emergency procedures when needed.
Record relevant resident observations and care in the clinical record.
Complete or contribute to the incident report as required by your role and facility policy.
Provide accurate, factual information without speculation.

Important: An incident report does not replace resident charting. Follow the facility’s rules about the documentation of incident reporting and investigations.
Suspected abuse or neglect also requires following applicable mandatory-reporting procedures.
Safety & Precautions

Do not chart care before performing it.
Do not chart care that was not provided.
Do not document another staff member’s care as your own.
Do not falsify dates or times.
Never silently alter a completed entry.
Avoid judgmental or speculative language.
Protect confidential resident information.
Use only approved abbreviations.
Notify the nurse promptly of urgent findings.

What Should I Remember?
Good documentation is:

Accurate.
Factual.
Timely.
Complete.
Legible or clearly entered.
Properly attributed.
Confidential.

Important distinction:

Reporting communicates information requiring attention.
Charting creates a lasting record.

Both may be required for the same event.
Related

Observation & Reporting
Medical Terminology & Abbreviations
Measuring Intake & Output
Patient Refusal of Care
Abuse, Neglect & Rights Violations
Vital Signs

Practice

 Studied
 Observed
 Practiced
 Passed checkoff

Sources

CNA Module 15 — Written Documentation
42 CFR §483.70 — Medical Records
The Joint Commission — Information Management Standards
Facility charting, incident-reporting, privacy, and correction policies

Flashcards
What are the core qualities of good charting?01-foundations / clinical-skillsAnswerAccurate, factual, timely, complete, and confidential.
Should documentation be delayed until the end of every shift?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNo. Chart promptly according to facility policy.
May a CNA document care before performing it?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNo. Chart only care actually provided.
What should a CNA do after making a paper charting error?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerFollow the approved correction procedure; never erase or conceal the entry.
How are EHR errors corrected?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerThrough the authorized correction or addendum process.
Does an incident report replace clinical documentation?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNo. Relevant resident care must still be charted.
Should a CNA write personal judgments in the resident's chart?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNo. Record observable facts and relevant direct statements.
What should a CNA document when a resident refuses care?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerCare offered, resident's response, and actions taken.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/emergency-res.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Emergency Response/Bleeding, Shock and Injury Response.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/emergency-res.title: Bleeding, Shock and Injury Response
clinical-skills-and-how-to/emergency-res.content:
Quick Reference
Hemorrhage (Severe Bleeding)
External Bleeding:

Arterial bleeding may be bright red and pulsatile.
Venous bleeding may flow steadily and appear darker.
Color alone does not reliably determine severity.
Internal Bleeding — Possible Signs:
Unexplained bruising or swelling.
Abdominal pain or distention.
Blood in urine or stool.
Black, tarry stool.
Weakness, dizziness, or signs of shock.
Response:
Ensure scene safety and activate emergency response.
Wear appropriate PPE.
Apply firm direct pressure to external bleeding.
Use a tourniquet or wound packing when indicated and trained.
Monitor the patient until help arrives.

Syncope (Fainting)
Temporary loss of consciousness caused by reduced blood flow to the brain.
Possible Causes:

Orthostatic hypotension.
Dehydration or blood loss.
Heart rhythm abnormalities.
Vasovagal reactions, including straining.
Response:
Assist the resident to a safe position.
Call for help and notify the nurse promptly.
Check breathing and responsiveness.
Do not immediately stand the resident back up.

Shock
Life-threatening failure of adequate tissue perfusion.





















TypeMechanismCardiogenicHeart cannot pump effectivelyHypovolemicReduced circulating blood or fluid volumeAnaphylacticSevere allergic reaction causing distributive shock
Possible Signs:

Rapid pulse and breathing.
Cool, clammy skin, depending on shock type.
Low blood pressure.
Altered mental status.
Anxiety, weakness, or nausea.
Response:
Activate emergency response immediately.
Keep the resident safely positioned, usually lying down if tolerated.
Maintain warmth and monitor breathing.
Follow directions from the nurse or emergency team.

Burns





















TypeDescriptionSuperficialEpidermis affected; redness and painPartial ThicknessEpidermis and part of dermis affected; may blisterFull ThicknessEntire dermis destroyed; may appear leathery and be less painful
Response:

Remove the resident from danger if safe.
Stop the burning process.
Cool minor thermal burns with cool running water when appropriate.
Cover with a clean, nonadherent dressing.
Obtain emergency assistance for serious burns.

Poisoning
Possible Signs:

Nausea or vomiting.
Unusual chemical odor.
Burns around the mouth.
Altered consciousness or breathing.
Response:
Protect yourself from exposure.
Activate appropriate emergency assistance.
Identify the suspected substance if safe.
Do not induce vomiting.
Follow Poison Control or emergency responder directions.

Important Considerations

Never delay emergency assistance while collecting detailed information.
Do not give food or drink to a person with altered consciousness.
Do not routinely elevate the legs of every person in shock; positioning depends on injuries and breathing.
Do not remove clothing stuck to burns.
Nosebleeds: lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose continuously; report persistent or severe bleeding.
Follow facility protocols and authorized first-aid training.

Related

Recognizing Patient Distress
Orthostatic Hypotension
Fall Risk
Emergency Preparedness & Response

Sources

CNA Module 12 — Emergency Procedures
Red Cross — Life-Threatening Bleeding
Poison Control

Flashcards
What is the immediate basic response to severe external bleeding?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerCall for help and apply firm direct pressure, with PPE.
Why is shock dangerous?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerTissues receive inadequate perfusion.
What should you never do after suspected poisoning without direction?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerInduce vomiting.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/emergency-res.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Emergency Response/Cardiac Arrest and CPR Response.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/emergency-res.title: Cardiac Arrest and CPR Response
clinical-skills-and-how-to/emergency-res.content:
When & Why?
Cardiac arrest occurs when the heart stops effectively pumping blood.
Immediate CPR and early defibrillation can improve survival.
Possible causes:

Heart attack or dangerous arrhythmia.
Respiratory failure or choking.
Drowning, trauma, or overdose.

Before You Start

Know the facility’s emergency response and Code Blue procedures.
Know how resident resuscitation status and DNR/POLST orders are communicated to direct-care staff.
Review applicable resuscitation orders as part of routine care preparation, before an emergency occurs.
Ensure you know how to summon assistance and locate an AED.
Maintain current CPR/BLS training as required by your facility.

Important: Resuscitation preferences should be established and accessible before an emergency. Do not delay indicated emergency care to independently search through medical records.
Steps

Ensure scene safety.
Check responsiveness and breathing according to current BLS training.
Immediately activate the facility’s emergency response system and request an AED.
If cardiac arrest is suspected and there is no known, applicable, valid order prohibiting CPR, begin CPR promptly according to current training.
If a valid DNR/POLST order prohibiting CPR is already known and applicable, do not initiate CPR. Summon nursing assistance immediately and provide appropriate comfort and supportive care.
If resuscitation status is uncertain, follow the facility’s emergency protocol without delaying indicated care.
If CPR is initiated, apply and follow AED instructions as soon as available.
Continue according to current BLS guidance and authorized team direction.

Important: Do not independently interpret ambiguous medical orders. Escalate uncertainty immediately to licensed nursing staff while following the emergency protocol.
Safety & Observations

Gasping is not normal breathing.
Minimize interruptions to chest compressions.
Follow current certification training for compression technique and ventilation.
AEDs should be used as trained.
Follow applicable DNR/POLST orders and facility policy.

What Should I Remember?

Recognize → Call → CPR → AED.
Cardiac arrest is not the same as a heart attack.
Early intervention matters.
CPR competency requires hands-on training.

Related

Recognizing Patient Distress
Choking & Airway Obstruction
End-of-Life Care
Emergency Preparedness & Response

Practice

 Studied
 Observed
 Practiced
 Passed checkoff

Sources

CNA Module 12 — Cardiac Arrest
AHA — Adult Basic Life Support
California POLST — Quick Reference Guide for Emergency Departments
National POLST — Patient POLST Form Guide
Facility resuscitation-status communication, DNR/POLST, and emergency-response policies (verify at clinical site)

Flashcards
Does gasping count as normal breathing?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNo; agonal gasps are abnormal breathing.

What is the initial response to unresponsiveness and absent normal breathing?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerActivate emergency response, begin trained CPR, obtain an AED.
Should a CNA delay indicated CPR to search for a resident's POLST form?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNo. Follow the emergency protocol and promptly involve licensed staff.
What should a CNA do when a known, valid, applicable DNR order prohibits CPR?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerDo not initiate CPR; summon help and provide appropriate supportive care.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/emergency-res.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Emergency Response/Choking and Airway Obstruction.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/emergency-res.title: Choking and Airway Obstruction
clinical-skills-and-how-to/emergency-res.content:
When & Why?
Respond to foreign-body airway obstruction before it causes respiratory or cardiac arrest.
Mild Obstruction:

Patient can cough effectively and move air.
Encourage coughing and monitor closely.
Severe Obstruction:
Weak or absent cough.
Unable to speak or breathe effectively.
Little or no airflow.
May become cyanotic or unresponsive.

Before You Start

Ensure scene safety.
Determine whether the patient can cough or speak.
Summon assistance and activate emergency response for severe obstruction.
Follow the patient’s emergency orders and facility protocol.

Steps
Responsive Adult — Severe Airway Obstruction

Activate the emergency response system and summon assistance.
Deliver 5 back blows using the trained technique.
Deliver 5 abdominal thrusts.
Repeat alternating cycles until the object is expelled or the person becomes unresponsive.
If the obstruction clears, continue monitoring until appropriate medical personnel arrive.

Special Circumstances: For adults in late pregnancy or when the rescuer cannot encircle the abdomen, use 5 chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts, alternating with 5 back blows.
If the Resident Becomes Unresponsive

Activate emergency response if not already done.
Begin CPR, starting with chest compressions, according to current BLS training.
When opening the airway to provide breaths, look for a visible foreign object.
Remove the object only if clearly visible and safely reachable.
Never perform blind finger sweeps.
Continue CPR according to current training until advanced care takes over or the resident recovers.

Follow the resident’s documented emergency care orders and facility protocol.
Safety & Observations

Do not interfere with effective coughing.
Never perform blind finger sweeps.
Do not give food or drink to clear an obstruction.
Monitor breathing and responsiveness.
Follow the patient’s documented emergency care orders.

What Should I Remember?

Mild: Encourage coughing.
Severe: Activate help and intervene.
Unresponsive: Start CPR.
Practice using current BLS/first-aid training.

Related

Cardiac Arrest & CPR Response
Recognizing Patient Distress
Emergency Preparedness & Response

Practice

 Studied
