 Practiced
 Passed checkoff

Sources

CNA Module 12 — Airway Obstruction
AHA — Adult Basic Life Support
AHA — 2025 Adult Foreign-Body Airway Obstruction Algorithm

Flashcards
What indicates severe rather than mild choking?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerInability to cough effectively, speak, or breathe.

What should you do if a choking person can cough effectively?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerEncourage coughing and monitor.

What must not be done for airway obstruction?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerBlind finger sweeps.
What should you do if a severely choking adult becomes unresponsive?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerBegin CPR with chest compressions; check for a visible object before breaths.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/emergency-res.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Emergency Response/Fire Safety and Response (RACE, PASS).md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/emergency-res.title: Fire Safety and Response (RACE, PASS)
clinical-skills-and-how-to/emergency-res.content:
When & Why?
Prevent fires, protect residents and staff, and respond safely when a fire occurs.
Before You Start

Know alarm locations, exits, and evacuation routes.
Identify fire doors, extinguishers, and evacuation equipment.
Understand the facility’s fire response procedures.

Steps
RACE — Fire Response

R — Rescue: Remove people from immediate danger if safe.
A — Alarm: Activate the fire alarm and notify emergency responders.
C — Contain: Close doors to limit fire and smoke spread.
E — Extinguish/Evacuate: Use an extinguisher only if trained and safe; otherwise evacuate according to the plan.

PASS — Fire Extinguisher

P — Pull the pin.
A — Aim at the base of the fire.
S — Squeeze the handle.
S — Sweep side to side.

Safety & Observations

Never use elevators during a fire unless specifically directed under an approved evacuation procedure.
Keep fire doors and exits unobstructed.
Avoid smoke-filled areas.
Do not attempt to fight large or spreading fires.
Use extinguishers only when trained, with a safe escape route.

What Should I Remember?

RACE = Response.
PASS = Extinguisher.
Report frayed cords, damaged outlets, and fire hazards.
Keep electrical equipment away from water and heat.
Follow the facility’s evacuation plan.

Related

Emergency Preparedness & Response
Facility & Environmental Safety

Practice

 Studied
 Observed
 Practiced
 Passed checkoff

Sources

CNA Module 4 — Fire Safety
Facility fire response and evacuation policy
OSHA — Emergency Action Plans

Flashcards
What does RACE stand for?01-foundations / clinical-skillsAnswerRescue, Alarm, Contain, Extinguish or Evacuate.
What does PASS stand for?01-foundations / clinical-skillsAnswerPull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep.
When should a CNA attempt to use a fire extinguisher?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerOnly when trained, safe, and with a clear escape route.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/emergency-res.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Emergency Response/Seizure Response.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/emergency-res.title: Seizure Response
clinical-skills-and-how-to/emergency-res.content:
When & Why?
Seizures result from abnormal electrical activity in the brain.
The priority is preventing injury, protecting breathing, and obtaining help when needed.
Common presentations:

Brief staring or impaired awareness.
Repetitive movements.
Loss of consciousness and convulsions.
Confusion or fatigue after the seizure.
Status Epilepticus: A prolonged seizure or recurrent seizures without recovery; a convulsive seizure lasting five minutes or longer is an emergency.

Before You Start

Recognize seizure activity.
Ensure personal and resident safety.
Call for assistance and note when the seizure begins.
Follow any prescribed seizure action plan.

Steps
During a Seizure

Stay calm and time the seizure.
Protect the resident from nearby hazards.
Cushion the head when appropriate.
Do not restrain movements.
Do not place anything in the mouth.
Turn the resident gently onto their side when safe and appropriate.
Activate emergency response for prolonged seizures or other emergency indicators.

After a Seizure

Observe breathing and responsiveness.
Maintain a safe position and provide reassurance.
Allow recovery in a quiet environment.
Report duration, movements, responsiveness, and injuries.
Follow nurse directions for vital signs, hygiene, and ongoing observation.

Safety & Observations
Emergency assistance is needed for:

Seizure lasting five minutes or longer.
Repeated seizures without recovery.
Breathing difficulty or failure to regain consciousness.
Significant injury or a first-known seizure.
Other emergency criteria in the facility’s seizure protocol.

What Should I Remember?

Time → Protect → Do Not Restrain → Report.
Never place objects or fingers in the mouth.
Never offer oral food, fluids, or medication until the resident is fully alert and safe to swallow.
Follow individualized seizure response instructions.

Related

Recognizing Patient Distress
Emergency Preparedness & Response
Neurological Observations

Practice

 Studied
 Observed
 Practiced
 Passed checkoff

Sources

CNA Module 12 — Seizures
CDC — Seizure First Aid

Flashcards
What two actions must you never do during a seizure?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerRestrain movements or place objects in the mouth.
What seizure duration is an emergency threshold in the note?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerFive minutes or longer for a convulsive seizure.
What should be documented after a seizure?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerDuration, movements, responsiveness, and injuries.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Hygiene and Personal Care/Assisting with Feeding.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.title: Assisting with Feeding
clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.content:
When & Why?
Assist residents who require help eating while supporting safe swallowing, adequate nutrition, independence, comfort, and dignity.
Before You Start

Verify the resident’s identity and prescribed meal tray.
Confirm food texture, liquid consistency, allergies, diet restrictions, and assistance level.
Review swallowing and positioning precautions.
Check for required adaptive utensils or equipment.
Offer toileting assistance when appropriate.
Perform hand hygiene and assist the resident with hand hygiene.
Position the resident upright as directed by the care plan.
Explain the meal and ask about food preferences.
Confirm that food and drinks are at safe serving temperatures.

Steps

Explain the procedure and obtain permission.
Provide privacy, comfort, and a pleasant eating environment.
Verify that the meal and drinks match the resident’s prescribed diet.
Help the resident sit in the approved eating position.
Place a clothing protector if requested.
Sit near the resident at an appropriate height.
Describe food placement for residents with visual impairment.
Ask which food the resident would like first.
Offer manageable bites at a comfortable pace.
Allow sufficient time for chewing and swallowing before offering more.
Offer permitted drinks according to the care plan and swallowing instructions.
Observe swallowing, comfort, fatigue, and interest throughout the meal.
Encourage independence and allow appropriate choices.
When finished, provide mouth and hand hygiene assistance as needed.
Ensure the resident is safely positioned and has access to the call light.
Record meal intake according to facility policy and report concerns.

Safety & Observations
Aspiration Precautions

Follow prescribed texture and liquid-consistency requirements.
Do not automatically offer a sip after every bite.
Use straws, spout cups, and other adaptive drinking equipment only when permitted.
Do not rush, force-feed, or feed a resident who cannot safely participate.
Stop feeding and request help for new coughing, choking, wet or gurgling voice, breathing changes, or difficulty swallowing.
Activate emergency response for severe airway obstruction or respiratory distress.
Keep the resident in the prescribed position after eating for the required period.

Mealtime Safety

Check food temperature before offering food.
Do not touch ready-to-eat foods with bare hands.
Use a napkin rather than the spoon to clean the resident’s mouth.
Respect refusal of food and communicate concerns without coercion.
Observe for fatigue or decreased alertness.

What Should I Remember?

Correct resident → Correct diet → Safe position → Slow pace → Observe → Report.
The resident sets the pace whenever possible.
Never assume that straws, thin liquids, or alternating bites and sips are safe for everyone.
Eating assistance should preserve independence and dignity.

Flashcards
What must be verified before assisting with a meal?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerResident, diet, allergies, texture, liquids, and feeding precautions.
Why should the CNA allow time between bites?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerTo permit safe chewing and swallowing.
Are straws appropriate for every resident with dysphagia?01-foundations / clinical-skillsAnswerNo. Follow the individualized swallowing plan.
What should a CNA do if a resident begins coughing during feeding?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerStop feeding, observe safety, and obtain nursing help.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.title: Dressing and Clothing Assistance
clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.content:
When & Why?
Help residents dress comfortably while preserving independence, dignity, and personal preferences.
Before You Start

Review the care plan and mobility restrictions.
Offer clothing choices.
Ensure clothing is clean, appropriate, and comfortable.
Explain the procedure and provide privacy.
Check for painful or weakened limbs and medical devices.

Steps

Encourage the resident to dress independently where possible.
Position the resident safely.
Assist with undergarments and other clothing as needed.
Support affected or painful limbs without pulling.
Ensure clothing is properly positioned and comfortable.
Help with footwear and grooming as appropriate.

One-Sided Weakness
Dressing: Affected or weaker arm goes into the sleeve first.
Undressing: Unaffected or stronger arm comes out first.
Safety & Observations

Avoid pulling on weak or injured limbs.
Protect IV lines, catheters, and other medical devices.
Use adaptive clothing or dressing aids as directed.
Watch for skin irritation, pain, and restricted movement.

What Should I Remember?

Dress the weak side first; undress the strong side first.
Allow the resident to choose their appearance.
Encourage independence rather than completing every task for them.

Daily Personal Care & ADLs

Limited Mobility

Which side is dressed first when a resident has one-sided weakness?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerThe weak or affected side.
Which side is undressed first when a resident has one-sided weakness?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerThe strong or unaffected side.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.title: Eyeglasses and Hearing Aid Care
clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.content:
When & Why?
Maintain sensory aids so residents can communicate, participate in care, and navigate safely.
Before You Start

Review the care plan and resident preferences.
Perform hand hygiene.
Prepare approved cleaning supplies.
Handle personal devices carefully.

Steps
Eyeglasses

Check for damage and proper fit.
Clean lenses with approved solution or water and a soft cloth.
Inspect nose pads and temples.
Check for irritation on the nose and behind the ears.
Return glasses to the resident or store safely.

Hearing Aids

Identify the correct hearing aid for each ear.
Inspect for visible damage and soiling.
Clean using manufacturer-approved tools.
Check power or battery status as appropriate.
Help the resident insert or remove the aid as trained.
Confirm comfort and ability to hear.
Store safely according to device instructions.

Safety & Observations

Avoid exposing hearing aids to water or unapproved cleaning solutions.
Do not routinely use alcohol wipes on hearing aids unless manufacturer-approved.
Never force hearing aids into the ear.
Report redness, pain, malfunction, or missing devices.

What Should I Remember?

Clean → Check → Fit → Confirm.
Sensory aids support independence and reduce communication barriers.
Different hearing aids have different charging and storage requirements.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Hygiene and Personal Care/Hair, Nail, Foot and Shaving Care.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.title: Hair, Nail, Foot and Shaving Care
clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.content:
When & Why?
Maintain hygiene, comfort, appearance, and skin integrity while respecting resident preferences.
Before You Start

Review the care plan and permitted grooming procedures.
Ask about personal preferences.
Gather clean supplies and appropriate PPE.
Check for pain, skin injury, or relevant precautions.

Steps
Hair Care

Brush or comb gently and assist with preferred styling.
Shampoo using an approved shower, bedside, or rinseless method.
Protect the eyes and keep the resident warm.
Dry and style hair according to preference.

Nail Care

Inspect nails and surrounding skin.
Wash and dry hands.
Clean beneath nails gently using approved tools.
File or trim nails only when permitted by training, policy, and the care plan.
Report abnormal nails or skin.

Foot Care

Inspect feet, heels, and between toes.
Wash using comfortably warm water.
Rinse and dry carefully, especially between toes.
Apply approved moisturizer to appropriate areas, avoiding between toes.
Help with clean socks and suitable footwear.

Shaving

Confirm the resident’s preferred shaving method.
Use a suitable clean razor and shaving product.
Support and protect the skin.
Shave using the manufacturer’s recommended technique.
Clean and dry the skin and equipment afterward.

Safety & Observations

Avoid unapproved nail cutting, particularly with diabetes, poor circulation, neuropathy, or high injury risk.
Follow facility policy for toenail care.
Use additional precautions for residents taking anticoagulants; an electric razor may be preferred.
Never use damaged, dull, or shared disposable blades.
Inspect for redness, cracks, blisters, wounds, or fungal changes.
Report skin injuries, thickened nails, and unexpected bleeding.

What Should I Remember?

Inspect → Clean → Protect → Report.
Keep feet dry between the toes.
Respect grooming choices, including hair loss accommodations, wigs, scarves, and facial hair.
Personal appearance is an important part of dignity.

Related

Daily Personal Care & ADLs
Skin Integrity & Breakdown Prevention
Culturally Responsive Care

 Observed
 Practiced

Why are nail trimming and foot care restricted for some residents?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerDiabetes, poor circulation, or neuropathy can increase injury risk.
Where should moisturizer generally not be left on the feet?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerBetween the toes.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Hygiene and Personal Care/Making an Occupied and Unoccupied Bed.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.title: Making an Occupied and Unoccupied Bed
clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.content:
When & Why?
Clean, properly fitted linens help maintain hygiene, comfort, skin integrity, and a safe resident environment.
Unoccupied bed: Made while the resident is out of bed.
Occupied bed: Changed while the resident remains in bed.
Before You Start
Supplies

Fitted or bottom sheet.
Draw or lift sheet when used.
Incontinence pad if indicated.
Top sheet and blanket.
Pillowcase.
Bath blanket when appropriate.
Gloves and linen bag.

Preparation

Perform hand hygiene.
Explain the procedure and provide privacy.
Gather linens and prepare a clean surface.
Position the bed at a safe working height.
Lock the bed wheels.
Follow the care plan for assistance, positioning, and rails.

Steps
Unoccupied Bed

Remove used linens without shaking them.
Place soiled linens in the appropriate receptacle.
Perform hand hygiene and change gloves as indicated.
Apply the clean bottom sheet.
Add the draw sheet and protective pad if indicated.
Smooth wrinkles from the mattress surface.
Add the top sheet and blanket.
Make appropriate folds, including a toe pleat if required.
Replace the pillowcase.
Lower the bed and complete the safety check.

Occupied Bed

Explain the procedure and assess the resident’s ability to assist.
Provide privacy and cover the resident appropriately.
Position the resident safely on one side, using assistance as required.
Loosen soiled linens on the exposed side.
Roll the soiled linens inward toward the resident.
Place clean bottom linens on the exposed mattress, rolling excess fabric toward the resident.
Assist the resident across to the clean side using safe repositioning techniques.
Remove remaining soiled linens.
Unroll and secure the clean bottom linens.
Smooth wrinkles and position the resident comfortably.
Replace upper bedding and pillowcase.
Return the bed to the appropriate low position.
Ensure the call light and required items are accessible.
Perform hand hygiene and document as indicated.

Safety & Observations
Infection Prevention

Keep clean linens separate from used linens.
Do not shake or snap soiled linens.
Keep linens away from your uniform.
Do not place linens on the floor.
Follow PPE and hand-hygiene requirements.

Body Mechanics

Adjust bed height before working.
Avoid excessive bending, twisting, and reaching.
Ask for assistance when repositioning exceeds safe handling limits.
Use appropriate repositioning equipment.

Skin & Comfort

Remove wrinkles beneath the resident.
Check for moisture and soiling.
Observe pressure areas and report skin changes.
Respect pain, mobility restrictions, and positioning instructions.
Follow the individualized care plan regarding support surfaces and pads.

What Should I Remember?
Prepare → Protect resident → Remove soiled linens → Apply clean linens → Reposition → Safety check.
Instructor Terms:

Closed Bed: A fully made bed with top linens pulled up, prepared when the bed is not currently in use.
Open Bed: A bed with the top linens folded down to make it easier for the resident to enter.
Mitered Corner: A neat, angled fold that secures bedding around the mattress corner.
Toe Pleat: A small fold or loosened area in the top bedding that provides space for the resident’s feet and reduces pressure on the toes.
Draw Sheet: A sheet placed across the middle portion of the bed, sometimes used with appropriate assistance and technique for repositioning.
Bath Blanket: A lightweight blanket used to maintain warmth and privacy during personal care or linen changes.

Related

Repositioning in Bed
Log Rolling a Resident
Body Mechanics & Injury Prevention
Skin Integrity & Breakdown Prevention
Hand Hygiene
Standard Precautions

clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Hygiene and Personal Care/Oral Care and Denture Care.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.title: Oral Care and Denture Care
clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.content:
When & Why?
Maintain oral health, comfort, nutrition, and dignity.
Poor oral hygiene may contribute to:

Tooth decay and gum disease.
Pain and difficulty eating.
Bad breath and decreased self-esteem.
Increased oral bacterial burden.

Before You Start

Check the care plan, swallowing precautions, and level of assistance.
Explain the procedure and provide privacy.
Perform hand hygiene and use appropriate PPE.
Gather toothbrush, toothpaste, water, towels, and denture supplies as needed.
Position the resident upright when possible.

Steps
Natural Teeth

Help the resident brush at least twice daily, as appropriate.
Use a soft toothbrush and suitable toothpaste.
Clean outer, inner, and chewing surfaces.
Gently clean the tongue and oral tissues as appropriate.
Assist with rinsing and spitting if safe.
Clean and store supplies.

Dentures

Ask the resident to remove dentures; assist if necessary.
Place a towel or protective barrier in the sink to prevent breakage.
Clean dentures using an appropriate denture brush and cleaner.
Rinse thoroughly according to product instructions.
Clean the resident’s gums, tongue, and mouth.
Replace dentures or store them in a labeled container with the recommended solution.

Residents With Swallowing Difficulties or Aspiration Precautions

Review the care plan for swallowing restrictions, permitted positioning, oral-care products, and required assistance.
Position the resident upright or side-lying as directed by the care plan.
Use approved oral-care supplies appropriate to the resident’s swallowing ability.
Avoid offering water or mouthwash for rinsing when the resident cannot safely swallow or spit.
Use only the prescribed amount of oral-care product and avoid excess fluid.
Request trained nursing assistance when suction-assisted oral care is required and outside your assigned competency.
Stop care and obtain help if the resident develops coughing, choking, breathing difficulty, or other signs of distress.
Report and document concerns according to facility policy.

Important: NPO status does not eliminate the need for oral hygiene. Follow the individualized oral-care plan and do not provide oral fluids or rinses contrary to swallowing restrictions.
Safety & Observations

Follow aspiration precautions and modified oral-care procedures for residents with swallowing difficulties.
Avoid forcing the mouth open.
Never use hot water on dentures.
Use denture-specific cleaning products unless directed otherwise.
Check for loose dentures and damaged teeth.
Stop and report significant pain or bleeding.
Do not assume a resident can safely rinse, spit, or swallow because they are awake.
Never give oral rinse water contrary to NPO orders or swallowing precautions.
Do not independently perform suctioning unless trained, authorized, and assigned under facility procedures.
Oral hygiene remains important for residents receiving tube feeding or restricted oral intake.

What Should I Remember?

Natural teeth and dentures both require regular cleaning.
Denture removal and insertion must be gentle.
Label and store dentures safely.
Residents who cannot rinse or spit need an individualized oral-care approach.

Related

Daily Personal Care & ADLs
Standard Precautions
Communication Accommodations

 Practiced
 Passed checkoff

CDC — Oral Health in Healthcare Settings to Prevent Pneumonia Toolkit

Facility dysphagia, NPO, oral hygiene, and suctioning procedures (verify at clinical site)

Flashcards
Why is oral care important for dependent residents?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerIt supports comfort, oral health, and infection prevention.
What is important when caring for removable dentures?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerHandle gently, clean as directed, and store safely in a labeled container.
Should oral hygiene be omitted when a resident is NPO?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNo. Follow the individualized oral-care plan without violating intake restrictions.
What should a CNA do if a resident cannot safely rinse or spit?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerAvoid oral rinsing and follow the prescribed aspiration-safe oral-care procedure.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Hygiene and Personal Care/Perineal Care.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.title: Perineal Care
clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.content:
When & Why?
Perineal care (peri-care) involves cleaning the genital and anal areas to:

Maintain hygiene and comfort.
Prevent infection and skin breakdown.
Remove urine, feces, and other contaminants.
Preserve resident dignity.
When: During routine bathing, after episodes of incontinence, and as needed.

Before You Start
Supplies:

At least 6 washcloths — 2 sets of 3:

Front: 1 soapy, 1 rinsing, 1 drying.
Back: 1 soapy, 1 rinsing, 1 drying.


Basin with comfortably warm water.
Soap or approved cleanser.
Gloves and other appropriate PPE.
Towels and waterproof underpad.
Clean incontinence product and barrier cream if indicated.
Linen bag or designated soiled-linen container.
Preparation:


Explain the procedure and obtain permission.
Perform hand hygiene and gather supplies.
Provide privacy and adjust the bed to a safe working height.
Check water temperature and resident comfort.
Position the resident on their back and expose only the area being cleaned.
Place a waterproof pad beneath the resident as needed.
Apply gloves before providing care.

Steps
General Principles

Always clean from clean to dirty.
Use a fresh section of washcloth for each stroke.
Use separate cloths for front and back.
Wash, rinse, then pat dry.
Avoid exposing more of the resident than necessary.

Front — Resident with Female Genitalia

Gently separate the labia with your nondominant hand.
With the front soapy cloth, clean from front to back:

Far labial fold.
Near labial fold.
Center, over the urethral opening.


Use a clean section of cloth for each stroke.
Repeat with the front rinsing cloth.
Gently pat dry with the front drying cloth.

Front — Resident with Male Genitalia

If uncircumcised, gently retract the foreskin only if it moves easily.
With the front soapy cloth, clean the tip of the penis, moving outward from the urinary opening.
Continue cleaning down the shaft and around the scrotum.
Use a clean section of cloth for each stroke.
Repeat with the front rinsing cloth.
Pat dry with the front drying cloth.
Return the foreskin to its normal position immediately after cleaning.

Back — Buttocks & Anal Area

Assist the resident onto their side using appropriate positioning techniques.
Expose only the buttocks and anal area.
With the back soapy cloth, clean the buttocks and anal area, working from cleaner areas toward the anus and avoiding transfer of fecal contamination.
Use a clean section of cloth for each stroke.
Repeat with the back rinsing cloth.
Pat dry with the back drying cloth, especially within skin folds.

After Care

Inspect the skin for redness, irritation, moisture damage, or breakdown.
Apply prescribed barrier cream if indicated.
Replace soiled underpads or incontinence products.
Reposition the resident comfortably.
Remove gloves and perform hand hygiene.
Dispose of or place used supplies in designated containers.
Lower the bed, ensure safety, and place the call light within reach.
Document care and relevant elimination observations according to facility policy.

Safety & Observations

Clean to dirty: Never wipe from the anus toward the urethra.
Separate cloths: Do not reuse front washcloths for the back.
Fresh surfaces: Use a clean section of cloth for every stroke.
Foreskin: Never force retraction; always replace it after cleaning.
Skin protection: Avoid vigorous scrubbing or rubbing fragile skin.
Infection control: Change gloves and perform hand hygiene whenever required to avoid cross-contamination.
Privacy: Keep the resident covered as much as possible.
Resident preference: Explain each step and adapt to comfort, anatomy, mobility, and care-plan needs.
Report:
Redness, excoriation, rash, or open skin.
Unusual discharge, odor, or bleeding.
Pain or discomfort.
Inability to retract a foreskin when cleaning is indicated; never force it.
Swelling or a foreskin that cannot be returned to its normal position (urgent).

What Should I Remember?

6 cloths minimum: 3 front + 3 back.
Each set: Soap → Rinse → Dry.
Female: Front to back, outer folds before center.
Male: Tip outward → Shaft → Scrotum → Replace foreskin.
Back: Buttocks → Anal area.
Use a clean section for every stroke.
Protect privacy and inspect skin throughout.

Related

Routine Bathing
Incontinence Care
Skin Integrity & Breakdown Prevention
Daily Personal Care & ADLs
Standard Precautions

Practice

 Studied
 Observed
 Practiced
 Passed checkoff

Sources

CNA Module 8 — Perineal Care
Female Perineal Care Skills Video
Facility perineal care skills checklist

Flashcards
In which direction should cleansing generally proceed for female perineal care?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerFront to back to reduce contamination.
What should be done if new irritation or bleeding is noticed?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerReport to the nurse.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Hygiene and Personal Care/Routine Bathing.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.title: Routine Bathing
clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.content:
When & Why?
Maintain hygiene, skin integrity, comfort, and dignity.
Bathing frequency and method should reflect the resident’s assessed needs, preferences, and individualized care plan.

Offer full or partial bathing as scheduled and when additional hygiene is needed.
Provide prompt cleansing when a resident becomes soiled.
Respect preferences regarding bathing time and method.
Report persistent hygiene needs, barriers to care, or changes requiring care-plan reassessment.

Important: There is no single bathing frequency appropriate for every resident. Do not substitute a facility’s typical bathing schedule for an individualized care plan.
Before You Start

Check care plan, mobility, assistance needs, and precautions.
Gather supplies and verify safe water temperature with patient.
Explain care, obtain consent, and provide privacy.
Perform hand hygiene and use appropriate PPE.

Steps

Prepare the environment and assist with safe positioning or transfer.
Encourage independence; wash from cleanest to dirtiest, leaving perineal care until last.
Rinse and dry thoroughly, especially skin folds.
Assist with dressing, grooming, and comfort.
Ensure safety, clean equipment, perform hand hygiene, and document/report as required.

Additional Bathing Considerations
Partial Bed Bath:

Face and eyes.
Hands and underarms.
Under breasts and skin folds.
Perineal area as indicated.
Complete Bed Bath — General Sequence:


Face and neck.
Arms and hands.
Chest and abdomen.
Underarms and back.
Legs and feet.
Perineal area last.
Distressed Bathing:


Identify pain, fatigue, cold, embarrassment, or fear.
Maintain warmth, coverage, and privacy.
Offer choices, breaks, or alternative bathing methods.
Stop if the resident becomes significantly distressed.
Respect refusal and report concerns.
Skin Observations:
Redness or discoloration.
Open or excoriated areas.
Moisture-related irritation.
Pressure areas and skin folds.

Safety & Observations
Watch for:

Redness, open skin, excoriation, or pressure injuries.
Skin folds, perineal area, and pressure points.
Pain, fatigue, dizziness, or distress.

If bathing causes distress:

Pause, ask what’s wrong, and adjust the pace.
Maintain warmth, privacy, and dignity.
Stop if necessary; report concerns and offer appropriate alternatives.

Alternatives:

Bed bath.
Washing hair separately.
No-rinse products, if appropriate.

What Should I Remember?

Promote independence whenever possible.


Keep the resident covered and warm.
Never force bathing.
Offer lotion or gentle back care when appropriate; avoid massaging reddened pressure areas.
Report new or concerning skin changes.

Related

Perineal Care
Skin Integrity & Breakdown Prevention
Fall Risk
Hair, Nail, Foot & Shaving Care

Practice

 Passed checkoff

Flashcards
What part of routine bathing is usually performed last?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerPerineal cleansing.
Why inspect skin folds during bathing?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerMoisture and friction can cause irritation or breakdown.
What should you do if a resident declines bathing?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerRespect refusal, explore needs, and report as appropriate.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Hygiene and Personal Care/Wound Dressings and Bandage Care.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.title: Wound Dressings and Bandage Care
clinical-skills-and-how-to/hygiene-and-p.content:
When & Why?
Dressings protect wounds, absorb drainage, and support wound healing.
CNAs may assist with certain dressing-related activities when authorized by the care plan, facility policy, and applicable scope-of-practice rules.
CNA Responsibilities:

Observe the skin and condition of existing dressings.
Follow the resident’s care plan and nursing instructions.
Assist with specifically authorized nonsterile tasks.
Report new redness, open areas, drainage, bleeding, odor, or pain.
Ask the nurse for clarification when instructions or permissions are uncertain.

Important: Do not independently select wound dressings, treat open wounds, perform debridement, or apply medicated ointments.
Common Types of Dressings








































DressingPurposeImportant ConsiderationsGauze sponges (2×2, 4×4)Cover wounds and absorb some drainageMay adhere to wounds; sometimes used with gauze rolls or tapeNon-adherent padsProtect wounds while minimizing adherenceMay require additional absorbent layersFoam dressingsAbsorb moderate to heavy drainage and provide cushioningCommonly used for certain pressure injuriesCalcium alginatesAbsorb moderate to heavy drainageForm a gel when exposed to wound fluid; generally unsuitable for dry woundsHydrogelsAdd moisture to relatively dry woundsGenerally have limited absorption capacityTransparent filmsProvide a thin protective coveringAppropriate for selected superficial, minimally draining wounds; limited absorbency
Wet-to-Dry Dressings
Wet-to-dry dressings involve applying moistened gauze that dries and is subsequently removed.
The removal process may pull away wound tissue, making it a form of mechanical debridement.
Important:

Debridement is not an independent CNA responsibility.
Wet-to-dry dressings can damage healthy tissue and are not appropriate for every wound.
Follow the nurse’s instructions and wound-care plan.

Before You Start

Review the assigned task and resident’s care plan.
Confirm with the nurse that the activity is permitted within your role and training.
Identify any precautions related to the wound, dressing, or resident.
Explain the activity and obtain permission.
Perform hand hygiene and use appropriate PPE.
Gather only the supplies required for the authorized task.
Provide privacy and position the resident comfortably.

Steps
Observation & Authorized Assistance

Identify the resident and explain the care being provided.
Perform hand hygiene and follow Standard Precautions.
Observe the existing dressing for:

Looseness or displacement.
Wetness or saturation.
Visible drainage or bleeding.
Unusual odor.
Resident-reported pain or discomfort.


Observe surrounding skin during authorized care for redness, irritation, swelling, or breakdown.
Assist with permitted activities according to the nurse’s instructions and facility procedure.
Do not remove or replace a wound dressing unless the specific task is authorized and within your scope.
Ensure the resident is comfortable and safely positioned.
Dispose of used supplies according to infection-prevention procedures.
Remove PPE and perform hand hygiene.
Report and document observations according to facility policy.

Safety & Observations
Signs of Possible Wound Complications

Increased redness, warmth, or swelling.
New or worsening pain.
Increased or unusual drainage.
Thick, cloudy, or pus-like drainage.
New unpleasant odor.
Bleeding.
Skin breakdown or wound enlargement.
New dark or discolored tissue.

Urgent Concerns:

Significant or uncontrolled bleeding.
Rapidly spreading redness with systemic symptoms.
Sudden severe pain or rapid deterioration.
Other signs of acute illness or instability.

Promptly notify the nurse and activate emergency response when indicated.
Scope & Safety

Do not independently determine which dressing a wound needs.
Do not perform wound debridement.
Do not probe, pack, or manipulate an open wound.
Do not apply topical medications or ointments without appropriate authorization.
Do not remove or alter surgical dressings outside assigned and permitted duties.
Do not perform sterile wound procedures as routine CNA care.
Follow the resident’s care plan and facility infection-control procedures.

What Should I Remember?

Observe, protect, report.
Dressing choice depends on wound characteristics and the treatment plan.
Highly absorbent dressings are generally intended for more heavily draining wounds.
Hydrogels add moisture; alginates absorb moisture.
Wet-to-dry dressing removal may debride tissue.
A change in drainage, pain, odor, or surrounding skin may indicate a complication.
Knowing a dressing’s purpose does not authorize independently using it.

Flashcards
What is the primary purpose of a wound dressing?01-foundations / clinical-skillsAnswerProtect the wound, manage drainage, and support healing.
What type of dressing is commonly used for moderate to heavy drainage?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerFoam or calcium alginate, depending on the wound.
What is the main purpose of a hydrogel dressing?01-foundations / clinical-skillsAnswerAdd moisture to relatively dry wounds.
What happens when calcium alginate contacts wound drainage?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerIt absorbs fluid and forms a gel.
What type of wound is a transparent film generally suited for?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerA superficial wound with little drainage.
What is wet-to-dry dressing removal?01-foundations / clinical-skillsAnswerA form of mechanical debridement.
May a CNA independently perform wound debridement?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNo. It requires appropriately authorized clinical personnel.
Should a CNA independently choose a wound dressing?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNo. Follow the prescribed wound-care plan.
What wound changes should a CNA report?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNew pain, redness, swelling, bleeding, unusual drainage, or odor.
Can a CNA independently apply an over-the-counter ointment to an open wound?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNo. Appropriate authorization and care-plan instructions are required.
A wound is relatively dry and needs moisture added. Which dressing?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerHydrogel dressing.
A wound produces moderate to heavy drainage and needs cushioning. Which dressing?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerFoam dressing.
A wound produces heavy drainage and needs highly absorbent material. Which dressing?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerCalcium alginate dressing.
A superficial wound has minimal drainage and needs a protective covering that can be checked on. Which dressing?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerTransparent film dressing.
A wound has delicate new tissue, and the dressing must not stick. Which dressing?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNon-adherent pad.
A wound needs basic coverage and absorption of light drainage. Which dressing?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerGauze sponge.
A wound has nonviable tissue, and mechanical debridement has been specifically ordered. Which traditional dressing method?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerWet-to-dry gauze dressing.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/infection-con.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Infection Control/Donning and Doffing PPE.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/infection-con.title: Donning and Doffing PPE
clinical-skills-and-how-to/infection-con.content:
When & Why?
Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) protects healthcare workers and residents from exposure to infectious materials.

Donning: Putting on PPE before exposure.
Doffing: Removing PPE while minimizing self-contamination.
PPE selection depends on anticipated exposure and required precautions.

Before You Start

Check required precautions and isolation signage.
Select appropriate PPE and correct sizes.
Inspect equipment for damage.
Perform hand hygiene.
Know the designated location for PPE removal.

Steps
Donning (Putting On)
Common sequence:

Gown: Cover torso and arms; secure according to the gown design.
Mask/Respirator: Position securely over nose and mouth. Perform a user seal check for a tight-fitting respirator.
Goggles/Face Shield: Position securely to protect eyes and face.
Gloves: Extend gloves over gown cuffs.
Remember: Gown → Mask/Respirator → Eye Protection → Gloves.

Doffing (Removing)
Example sequence:

Gloves: Remove without contaminating bare hands.
Eye Protection: Remove using straps or earpieces.
Gown: Release ties and pull away, turning contaminated surfaces inward.
Mask/Respirator: Remove using straps without touching the front.
Hand Hygiene: Clean hands after PPE removal.
Important: Approved doffing sequences vary. Some protocols remove gown and gloves together, and respiratory protection may be removed in a different location.

Safety & Observations

PPE exteriors may be contaminated after use.
Avoid touching your face with contaminated gloves.
Perform hand hygiene whenever hands become contaminated during removal.
Change gloves between contaminated and clean tasks as required.
Never touch the contaminated front of a mask or face shield.
Respirators for airborne precautions are generally removed after leaving the isolation room and closing the door.
Follow facility-specific instructions for reusable eye protection.
Follow the procedure taught during your competency assessment.

What Should I Remember?

Donning: Gloves usually go on last.
Doffing: Avoid contaminating yourself.
PPE must match the anticipated exposure.
Gloves never replace hand hygiene.
Incorrect doffing can cause self-contamination.

Related

Hand Hygiene
Standard Precautions
Transmission-Based Precautions
Enhanced Barrier Precautions

 Studied
 Observed
 Practiced
 Passed checkoff

Why is the removal sequence for PPE important?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerContaminated surfaces can transfer organisms to skin or clothing.
What must be performed after PPE removal?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerHand hygiene.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/infection-con.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Infection Control/Hand Hygiene.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/infection-con.title: Hand Hygiene
clinical-skills-and-how-to/infection-con.content:
When & Why?
Hand hygiene prevents the transmission of microorganisms between patients, healthcare workers, and the environment.
Perform hand hygiene:

Before and after patient contact.
Before clean or aseptic procedures.
After contact with bodily fluids or contaminated surfaces.
After removing gloves.
When moving from contaminated to clean tasks.

Before You Start
Choose the appropriate method:

















MethodWhen to UseAlcohol-based hand rubPreferred for most patient care when hands are not visibly soiledSoap & waterVisibly dirty hands, after restroom use, before eating, and during certain infectious diarrhea outbreaks
Steps
Soap & Water

Turn on sink,
Wet hands under clean, running water.
Apply soap.
Scrub all surfaces for at least 20 seconds, including between fingers, thumbs, fingertips, and under nails. Also, up to two inches up wrist.
Rinse thoroughly under running water.
Dry with a disposable towel.
Use a different towel to turn off the faucet.

Alcohol-Based Hand Rub

Apply the manufacturer’s recommended amount.
Rub all hand surfaces, including fingertips, thumbs, and between fingers.
Continue rubbing until completely dry (approximately 20 seconds).

Safety & Observations

Gloves never replace hand hygiene.
Avoid touching contaminated surfaces after cleaning.
Change gloves and perform hand hygiene between contaminated and clean tasks as appropriate.
During C. difficile or norovirus outbreaks, follow facility guidance for soap-and-water washing.
Keep nails short and clean; follow facility restrictions on artificial nails and jewelry.

What Should I Remember?

Before touching, after touching, after gloves.
Clean thumbs, fingertips, and between fingers — commonly missed areas.
Never rinse or wipe off alcohol-based sanitizer before it dries.
Maintain healthy skin; report cracks or irritation that interfere with hand hygiene.

Related

Standard Precautions
Transmission-Based Precautions
Donning & Doffing PPE
Chain of Infection

Practice

 Studied
 Observed
 Practiced
 Passed checkoff

Sources

CDC — Hand Hygiene for Healthcare Workers

Flashcards
When is hand hygiene required during routine resident care?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerBefore and after contact, before clean procedures, after bodily-fluid exposure, after gloves, and between dirty and clean tasks.
Which method is generally preferred when hands are not visibly soiled?01-foundations / clinical-skillsAnswerAlcohol-based hand rub.
When should soap and water be used instead of alcohol-based hand rub?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerWhen hands are visibly dirty, after restroom use, before eating, and when required by infection-control protocols.
What is the minimum soap-and-water scrubbing time?01-foundations / clinical-skillsAnswerAt least 20 seconds.
Which areas are commonly missed during hand hygiene?01-foundations / clinical-skillsAnswerThumbs, fingertips, between fingers, and around nails.
Why must you perform hand hygiene after removing gloves?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerGloves can become contaminated, and hands may be contaminated during removal.
flashcards/03-application/clinical-skills What is the correct sequence for washing hands with soap and water?
?

Wet hands.
Apply soap.
Scrub all surfaces for at least 20 seconds.
Rinse thoroughly.
Dry with a disposable towel.
Turn off the faucet using a clean towel.

How should alcohol-based hand rub be applied?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerUse the recommended amount, cover all hand surfaces, and rub until dry.
Should alcohol-based hand rub be rinsed or wiped off?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNo. Allow it to dry completely.
What should you do during a C. difficile or norovirus outbreak?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerFollow facility-specific hand hygiene requirements, including when soap and water is indicated.
Does wearing gloves eliminate the need for hand hygiene?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNo. Gloves never replace hand hygiene.
What should you do if your hands develop cracks or irritation that interfere with hand hygiene?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerReport the issue and follow approved skin-care or occupational-health guidance.
When is alcohol-based hand rub generally preferred?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerMost routine care when hands are not visibly soiled.
How long should hands be scrubbed with soap and water?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerAt least 20 seconds.
Do gloves replace hand hygiene?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNo; clean hands at indicated times including after glove removal.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/infection-con.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Infection Control/Occupational Exposure and Response.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/infection-con.title: Occupational Exposure and Response
clinical-skills-and-how-to/infection-con.content:
When & Why?
Prevent and respond to exposure to infectious materials, sharps, and hazardous chemicals.
Before You Start

Follow Standard Precautions.
Select appropriate PPE.
Know sharps disposal procedures.
Locate eyewash stations, spill supplies, and Safety Data Sheets (SDS).
Know how to contact the supervisor and occupational health.

Steps
Blood or Body Fluid Exposure

Wash needlestick injuries or contaminated skin with soap and water.
Flush exposed mouth or nose with water; irrigate eyes with clean water or saline.
Report the exposure immediately.
Obtain prompt medical evaluation for testing and possible post-exposure treatment.
Complete required incident documentation.

Chemical Exposure

Stop exposure and move away from the hazard if safe.
Alert the nurse or supervisor immediately.
Follow the chemical’s SDS and facility emergency procedures.
Use the designated eyewash or shower when indicated; obtain emergency assistance as necessary.
Obtain medical evaluation and complete required reporting.

Safety & Observations

Never recap used needles or handle sharps unnecessarily.
Dispose of sharps in approved containers.
Bloodborne pathogens include HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C.
Not all bodily fluids have identical bloodborne pathogen risks.
Never mix cleaning chemicals.
Do not touch or enter a contaminated area without appropriate protection.

What Should I Remember?

Exposure → First Aid → Report → Medical Evaluation.
Post-exposure treatment can be time-sensitive.
Follow the SDS for chemical-specific first aid.
Hepatitis B vaccination is an important occupational protection.

Related

Standard Precautions
Donning & Doffing PPE
Hand Hygiene
Employee Rights

 Studied

 Practiced

Flashcards
What is the first action after a contaminated needlestick or splash?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerImmediately perform appropriate first aid and report the exposure.
Why is prompt reporting of blood exposure important?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerTime-sensitive medical assessment and post-exposure measures may be needed.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/measurements-.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Measurements and Monitoring/Measuring Blood Pressure.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/measurements-.title: Measuring Blood Pressure
clinical-skills-and-how-to/measurements-.content:
When & Why?
Measure the force of circulating blood against arterial walls to monitor cardiovascular status and identify changes.
Blood Pressure Components:

Systolic: Pressure during ventricular contraction (top number).
Diastolic: Pressure during ventricular relaxation (bottom number).
Units: Millimeters of mercury (mmHg).

Before You Start
Equipment:

Correctly sized blood pressure cuff.
Manual sphygmomanometer and stethoscope, or validated automatic monitor.
Documentation equipment.
Preparation:


Perform hand hygiene.
Explain the procedure and obtain permission.
Review the care plan and measurement restrictions.
Select an appropriate arm and cuff size.
Allow the resident to rest quietly for approximately 5 minutes when feasible.
Position the resident with back supported, feet flat, palms facing upward, and legs uncrossed when possible.
Support the bare upper arm at heart level.
Ask the resident not to talk or move during measurement.

Steps
Manual Blood Pressure — Auscultatory Method (One Step)

Locate the brachial artery on the inner upper arm.

Check the side closer to pinky, and slightly on or closer to the heart than the elbow fold.


Wrap the cuff snugly around the bare upper arm, with the lower edge approximately 2–3 cm above the elbow crease.
Position the cuff’s artery marker over the brachial artery.

Make sure it’s ~1 finger worth of space.


Estimate systolic pressure by palpation according to the trained procedure, to avoid missing an auscultatory gap.

Pump to ~160 mmHg, confirming you do not hear the heartrate. If you do, up by 10 mmHg.


Place the stethoscope over the brachial artery without positioning it beneath the cuff.

Use two fingers to place. Like -0-


Inflate the cuff approximately 20–30 mmHg above the estimated systolic pressure.
Deflate slowly, approximately 2–3 mmHg per second.
Listen for Korotkoff sounds:

First clear tapping sound: Systolic pressure.
Disappearance of sounds: Diastolic pressure in most adults.


Deflate the cuff fully and remove it.
Record the measurement and report concerning results.

Automatic Blood Pressure

Select the correct cuff size and site.
Position the resident and arm appropriately.
Apply the cuff according to manufacturer instructions.
Start the measurement.
Ensure the resident remains still and quiet.
Read and document the result.
Repeat or confirm unexpected readings according to facility policy.

Safety & Observations

Avoid measuring over clothing.
Use the correct cuff size; a poorly sized cuff can produce inaccurate readings.
Follow restrictions for arms with vascular access, injuries, or other contraindications.
Do not allow the arm to hang unsupported.
Avoid talking or moving during measurement.
Follow instructions for residents who cannot tolerate standard seated positioning.
Report unexpectedly high or low readings, especially with concerning symptoms.
Notify the nurse if readings are difficult to obtain or appear inconsistent.
Don’t take BP from same side as a masectomy. It can cause painful lymphedema (swelling in that arm)

What Should I Remember?

Rest → Position → Cuff → Measure → Document.
First Korotkoff sound = systolic.
Disappearance of sounds = diastolic.
Correct cuff size and arm positioning matter.
A single abnormal reading does not establish a diagnosis.
Use the exact sequence required by your CNA skills checklist.

Related

Blood Pressure
Vital Signs
Vital Sign Ranges
Hypertension
Hypotension
Orthostatic Hypotension

 Passed checkoff

Flashcards
What does the first Korotkoff sound indicate?01-foundations / clinical-skillsAnswerSystolic pressure.
What does disappearance of Korotkoff sounds usually indicate in adults?01-foundations / clinical-skillsAnswerDiastolic pressure.
Why should the arm be supported at heart level?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerIncorrect positioning can distort the reading.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/measurements-.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Measurements and Monitoring/Measuring Height and Weight.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/measurements-.title: Measuring Height and Weight
clinical-skills-and-how-to/measurements-.content:
When & Why?
Measure height and weight to monitor health, nutritional status, fluid changes, and treatment progress.
Before You Start

Review the care plan for measurement frequency and required equipment.
Select a standing, wheelchair, bed, or lift scale as appropriate.
Verify scale condition and zero or tare it correctly.
Explain the procedure and obtain permission.
Follow mobility restrictions and required assistance levels.

Steps
Measuring Weight

Prepare the scale and verify the units.
Zero or tare the scale, accounting for wheelchair or equipment weight.
Assist the resident onto the scale using the prescribed method.
Ensure the resident is stable and correctly positioned.
Read and record the measurement.
Help the resident safely off the scale.
Document weight, units, and relevant measurement conditions.

Measuring Height

Select a stadiometer, height rod, or approved alternative.
Position the resident correctly according to the method.
Obtain the measurement.
Record height and units accurately.

Common Equipment

Standing Scale: For residents who can stand safely.
Wheelchair Scale: Weighs the resident and wheelchair; subtracts or tares equipment weight.
Bed Scale: For residents who cannot safely leave bed.
Lift Scale: Measures weight using compatible mechanical lift equipment.
Stadiometer: Measures standing height.

Safety & Observations

Never use a standing scale if the resident cannot stand safely.
Confirm scale and equipment weight capacities.
Use appropriate transfer assistance and fall precautions.
Ensure wheelchair or lift accessories are accounted for when required.
Report unexpected or significant weight changes.
Avoid estimating measurements when accurate methods are available.

What Should I Remember?

Zero → Position → Measure → Document.
1 kg ≈ 2.2 lb.
Always record units.
Use consistent measurement conditions when possible.
Follow the care plan for measurement frequency.

Related

Healthcare Measurement Conversions
Limited Mobility
Vital Signs
Elimination Care

Practice

 Studied
 Observed
 Practiced
 Passed checkoff

Sources

CNA Module 7 — Weights and Measures

Facility height and weight measurement procedure

Why use the same measurement method when tracking weight trends?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerConsistency helps distinguish real change from measurement variation.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/measurements-.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Measurements and Monitoring/Measuring Intake and Output.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/measurements-.title: Measuring Intake and Output
clinical-skills-and-how-to/measurements-.content:
When & Why?
Intake and output (I&O) monitoring measures fluids entering and leaving the body.
It helps the healthcare team evaluate hydration and fluid balance.
Before You Start

Review the I&O order and care plan.
Identify what needs to be measured and how frequently.
Assemble graduated containers and documentation supplies.
Explain the procedure to the resident.
Perform hand hygiene and wear appropriate PPE when handling bodily fluids.

Steps
Measuring Intake

Record the volume of drinks consumed.
Include other items counted as fluids under the facility’s protocol.
Measure fluids actually consumed, not just fluids served.
Include enteral or IV intake only according to the assigned documentation process.
Record measurements in milliliters (mL).
Examples of oral intake:


Water.
Juice.
Milk.
Soup or broth.
Gelatin or frozen desserts when counted as fluids by facility policy.

Measuring Output

Use the appropriate collection device.
Avoid contamination with toilet paper.
Transfer fluid into a graduated container if necessary.
Read the volume at eye level on a stable surface.
Record output in milliliters.
Clean and store measuring equipment as directed.
Report unusual volume, appearance, or symptoms.

Calculating Totals
Total Intake: Sum of all counted fluid intake.
Total Output: Sum of all measured fluid output.
Net Fluid Balance = Intake − Output
Example:

Intake = 1,500 mL.
Output = 1,200 mL.
Net = +300 mL.
Important: Measured net balance does not capture every source of fluid loss, including unmeasured perspiration and breathing losses.

Safety & Observations

Document values accurately and promptly.
Don’t estimate when a measurement can be obtained.
Follow procedures for incontinent residents.
Report unexpectedly low urine output.
Observe for signs of dehydration or fluid overload.
Don’t independently change fluid restrictions or intake goals.

Unexpectedly Low or Absent Urine Output
Possible concerning observations include:

Urine output substantially below the resident’s usual pattern or prescribed reporting parameters.
No recorded urine output during an interval when output would normally be expected.
A resident reporting an inability to urinate despite feeling the need.
Lower abdominal discomfort or distention accompanying inability to urinate.
Decreased urine output accompanied by weakness, confusion, swelling, or breathing difficulty.

CNA Response:

Verify that the recorded output is accurate and that no collection or documentation was missed.
For a resident with a urinary catheter, observe for visible kinks, tension, or obvious drainage-system problems without disconnecting or manipulating the catheter.
Notify the nurse promptly about unexpectedly low or absent output.
Escalate immediately for sudden inability to urinate with significant pain or distention, or for severe accompanying symptoms.
Report the time of the last known output, measured amounts, symptoms, and relevant changes from baseline.
Follow instructions for continued observations and documentation.

Important: Do not independently diagnose urinary retention, alter prescribed fluid intake, irrigate a catheter, or initiate treatment.
Urine-output thresholds and monitoring intervals depend on the resident’s condition and care plan. Do not assume a single cutoff applies to every resident.
What Should I Remember?

1 liter = 1,000 mL.
1 US fluid ounce ≈ 30 mL for common bedside calculations.
The total is only as reliable as the individual measurements.

Related

Fluid Balance
Dehydration
Elimination Care
Urinary Catheter Care
Healthcare Measurement Conversions
Vital Signs

Practice

 Studied
 Observed
 Practiced
 Passed checkoff

Sources

CNA Module 9C — Intake and Output
Facility I&O documentation procedures
NIDDK — Urinary Retention: Definition & Facts
MedlinePlus — Urination: Difficulty With Flow

Flashcards
What is the net fluid balance formula?01-foundations / clinical-skillsAnswerMeasured intake minus measured output.
What is the approximate mL equivalent of one US fluid ounce?01-foundations / clinical-skillsAnswer30 mL.
Does measured output include every route of fluid loss?01-foundations / clinical-skillsAnswerNo; breathing and sweating may be unmeasured.
What is urinary retention?01-foundations / clinical-skillsAnswerInability to empty the bladder completely or at all.
What should a CNA do when urine output is unexpectedly low or absent?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerCheck recording accuracy, observe for problems, and promptly report to the nurse.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/measurements-.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Measurements and Monitoring/Measuring Oxygen Saturation.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/measurements-.title: Measuring Oxygen Saturation
clinical-skills-and-how-to/measurements-.content:
When & Why?
Use pulse oximetry to estimate arterial oxygen saturation (SpO₂) and recognize changes that may require reporting.
SpO₂: Estimated percentage of hemoglobin carrying oxygen.
Pulse oximetry does not directly measure ventilation, carbon dioxide, or the underlying cause of respiratory distress.
Before You Start

Review the care plan and prescribed reporting thresholds.
Explain the procedure and obtain permission.
Perform hand hygiene.
Select an appropriate pulse oximeter and sensor.
Ensure the sensor is clean and functioning.
Check for factors that may interfere with the reading.

Steps

Position the resident comfortably.
Select an appropriate measurement site, usually a finger.
Apply the sensor according to manufacturer instructions.
Ask the resident to remain still when possible.
Allow the reading to stabilize.
Observe the SpO₂ value and displayed pulse rate.
Check the signal quality or other reliability indicators provided by the device.
Record the reading, time, and relevant details according to facility policy.
Report abnormal values or concerning symptoms promptly.
Clean and disinfect reusable equipment as required.

Safety & Observations
Factors Affecting Accuracy:

Poor peripheral circulation.
Cold extremities.
Movement.
Nail polish or artificial nails.
Incorrect sensor placement.
Skin pigmentation and differences in device performance.

Important: A pulse oximeter can produce an inaccurate reading. Do not rely on SpO₂ alone to determine whether a resident is experiencing respiratory distress.
Reporting & Escalation

Report readings outside prescribed parameters.
Report unexpected changes from baseline.
A reading below 90% generally warrants urgent clinical attention, but follow the resident’s individualized targets and facility escalation policy.
Activate emergency response for severe breathing difficulty, cyanosis, sudden deterioration, or other critical symptoms, regardless of the displayed number.
Do not independently change oxygen flow rates or prescribed treatment.

What Should I Remember?

A commonly taught adult SpO₂ reference range is 95–100% at sea level.
Some residents have individualized oxygen saturation targets.
A normal-appearing reading does not exclude respiratory distress.
Poor signal quality can make measurements unreliable.
Follow the care plan and report symptoms alongside measurements.

Related

Vital Signs
Vital Sign Ranges
Recognizing Patient Distress
Care of Residents With Medical Tubing

Practice

 Studied
 Observed
 Practiced
 Passed checkoff

Sources

CNA Module 10 — Pulse Oximetry
FDA — Pulse Oximeters
FDA — Pulse Oximeter Basics
Facility pulse-oximetry and oxygen-therapy procedures

Flashcards
What does SpO₂ estimate?01-foundations / clinical-skillsAnswerThe percentage of hemoglobin saturated with oxygen.
Does normal SpO₂ rule out respiratory distress?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNo. Symptoms and clinical condition must also be considered.
What factors can affect pulse oximeter accuracy?02-mechanisms / clinical-skillsAnswerMovement, poor circulation, sensor placement, nail polish, and skin pigmentation.
May a CNA independently increase oxygen flow because SpO₂ is low?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNo. Report the finding and follow authorized emergency procedures.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/measurements-.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Measurements and Monitoring/Measuring Pulse and Respirations.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/measurements-.title: Measuring Pulse and Respirations
clinical-skills-and-how-to/measurements-.content:
When & Why?
Measure the resident’s pulse and respiratory rate to recognize changes in circulation and breathing.
Pulse: Arterial pulsations produced by the heartbeat.
Respiratory Rate: Number of complete breathing cycles per minute.
Before You Start

Review the care plan and required measurements.
Explain the procedure and provide privacy.
Perform hand hygiene.
Ensure the resident is comfortably positioned and resting when appropriate.
Prepare a watch or timer with a seconds display.
Identify any individual reporting parameters.

Steps
Radial Pulse

Position the resident’s arm comfortably with the wrist supported.
Locate the radial artery on the thumb side of the wrist.
Use the pads of the index and middle fingers.
Avoid using your thumb to feel the pulse.
Apply gentle pressure until the pulsations are felt.
Count the beats for 60 seconds, or follow the approved skills procedure.
Observe rhythm and pulse strength as trained.
Document the pulse rate and report irregularities or concerning findings.

Respirations

Keep the resident comfortably positioned.
Observe the movement of the chest or abdomen.
Count one complete rise and fall as one breath.
Count respirations for 60 seconds when required by the skills checklist or when breathing is irregular.
Observe rhythm, depth, effort, and signs of distress.
Record the respiratory rate in breaths per minute.
Report concerning breathing patterns or changes.

Observation Tip: Respirations may change when someone deliberately controls their breathing. When appropriate, observe discreetly after measuring the radial pulse without misleading the resident about the care being provided. Can do this by faking checking pulse.
Safety & Observations

Use two fingers rather than the thumb when palpating the radial pulse.
Avoid excessive pressure that makes the pulse difficult to detect.
Report a newly irregular, unusually weak, or difficult-to-detect pulse.
Do not assess respirations by rate alone; observe depth, rhythm, and effort.
Severe respiratory distress requires immediate escalation, regardless of the counted respiratory rate.
Never delay emergency assistance to complete a full-minute count.

What Should I Remember?

Pulse: Rate, rhythm, strength.
Respirations: Rate, rhythm, depth, effort.
One complete chest rise and fall equals one breath.
Commonly taught adult reference ranges:

Pulse: 60–100 beats/min.
Respirations: 12–20 breaths/min.


Always consider symptoms, baseline, and the care plan.

Related

Vital Signs
Vital Sign Ranges
Measuring Blood Pressure
Recognizing Patient Distress

Practice

 Studied
 Observed
 Practiced
 Passed checkoff

Sources

CNA Module 10 — Pulse and Respiration
MedlinePlus — Vital Signs
Facility pulse and respiratory-rate skills checklist

Flashcards
Where is the radial pulse palpated?01-foundations / clinical-skillsAnswerOn the thumb side of the wrist.
Which fingers are used to check the radial pulse?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerIndex and middle fingers.
What counts as one respiration?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerOne complete rise and fall of the chest or abdomen.
What should be observed in respirations beyond rate?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerRhythm, depth, effort, and distress.
Why should respirations be observed discreetly?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerConscious attention can change breathing patterns.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/measurements-.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Measurements and Monitoring/Measuring Temperature.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/measurements-.title: Measuring Temperature
clinical-skills-and-how-to/measurements-.content:
When & Why?
Measure body temperature to monitor health and recognize changes that may indicate illness or other clinical concerns.
Temperature varies with measurement route, activity, environment, age, and time of day.
Before You Start

Review the care plan and approved measurement route.
Explain the procedure and provide privacy.
Perform hand hygiene.
Select an appropriate thermometer and probe cover.
Confirm that the device is clean and functioning.
Check for conditions that may affect measurement accuracy.

Methods








































RouteMethodImportant ConsiderationsOralProbe positioned beneath the tongueRecent food, drinks, or smoking may affect readingsAxillaryProbe placed against skin in the armpitMay be less accurate for estimating core temperatureTympanicInfrared probe measures temperature in the earPlacement and earwax can affect readingsTemporalScanner measures temperature near the foreheadFollow device-specific positioning instructionsRectalProbe measures rectal temperatureInvasive; requires specific authorization and precautionsNon-contactInfrared device measures without skin contactDistance, environment, and positioning can affect results
Steps

Confirm the resident and prescribed measurement method.
Explain the procedure and obtain permission.
Perform hand hygiene and prepare the thermometer.
Apply the appropriate disposable probe cover when required.
Position the resident and thermometer according to the device instructions.
Obtain the temperature reading.
Remove the device and dispose of the probe cover appropriately.
Clean and disinfect reusable equipment according to policy.
Document the temperature, units, time, and measurement route.
Report concerning findings according to facility parameters.

Safety & Observations

Wait the appropriate period after oral intake, smoking, or activities that affect temperature according to the device and training instructions.
Do not use an oral thermometer when the resident cannot safely cooperate with the procedure.
Do not assume axillary measurement is appropriate for every resident with dementia.
Do not perform rectal temperature measurement without the required authorization, training, and precautions.
Do not compare readings from different routes as though they were identical.
Report unexpectedly high or low readings, especially with concerning symptoms.
Do not delay urgent escalation for a resident who appears seriously ill.

What Should I Remember?

Record the route, not just the temperature.
Use the approved method for the individual resident.
Temperature readings require clinical context.
Follow the exact procedure required by your CNA skills checklist.

Vital Signs
Vital Sign Ranges
Recognizing Patient Distress
Standard Precautions

Why must the temperature measurement route be recorded?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerExpected readings and accuracy differ by route.
What can temporarily affect an oral temperature reading?02-mechanisms / clinical-skillsAnswerRecent eating, drinking, smoking, or exercise.
Why should temperature readings from different routes not be treated as identical?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerDifferent routes may produce different values.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Mobility and Transfers/Assisting with Ambulation.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.title: Assisting with Ambulation
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.content:
When & Why?
Support safe walking, maintain mobility, encourage independence, and reduce fall risk.
Before You Start

Review mobility level, weight-bearing restrictions, and care plan.
Check footwear and assistive devices.
Clear the walking path.
Obtain required assistance.
Assess readiness to stand and walk.

Levels of Assistance

























LevelDescriptionIndependentResident walks without physical assistanceStandby AssistCaregiver remains nearby for safetyOne-Person AssistOne caregiver provides prescribed physical assistanceTwo-Person AssistTwo caregivers provide prescribed assistance
Important Considerations:

Follow the care plan for assistance level and equipment.
Use a gait belt when indicated and safe.
Report increased or decreased assistance needs.
Never attempt unsafe manual lifting.
Stop for dizziness, weakness, pain, or significant fatigue.

Steps

Explain the activity and prepare the environment.
Assist the resident to a safe standing position.
Apply the prescribed gait belt or assistive device.
Walk alongside the resident using the trained guarding technique.
Match the resident’s pace and monitor tolerance.
Assist the resident safely to a seated or resting position.
Report changes in mobility or assistance needs.

Safety & Observations

Watch for dizziness, weakness, fatigue, or shortness of breath.
Do not pull on the resident’s arms.
Stop and seek help if the resident cannot safely continue.
Use the fall-response technique taught by your facility.

What Should I Remember?

Safety before distance.
Encourage independence when appropriate.
Never exceed the assistance level permitted by the care plan.
Report increased assistance requirements.

Dangling at Bedside
Fall Risk
Safe Patient Transfers

clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Mobility and Transfers/Bed-to-Stretcher Transfer.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.title: Bed-to-Stretcher Transfer
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.content:
When & Why?
Move a resident between a bed and stretcher when they cannot safely transfer independently.
Before You Start

Verify care plan, transfer restrictions, and required staff.
Select approved transfer equipment.
Position bed and stretcher as directed.
Lock applicable brakes and clear obstacles.
Check IV lines, catheters, and other attached equipment.
Assign roles and identify who will coordinate movement.

Steps

Prepare the resident and receiving surface.
Position the approved transfer device or sheet.
Arrange staff according to the transfer plan.
Coordinate movement using a shared count.
Transfer the resident while maintaining body alignment.
Secure the resident and reassess equipment, lines, and comfort.

Safety & Observations

Use the approved lateral transfer device and technique.
Avoid unnecessary manual lifting and shearing.
Protect the head, limbs, lines, and attached devices.
Obtain specialized assistance for spinal precautions or complex transfers.

What Should I Remember?

Prepare all equipment before moving.
Communication and coordination prevent injury.
The number of assistants depends on the procedure and transfer equipment.

Safe Patient Transfers
Using a Mechanical Lift

clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Mobility and Transfers/Dangling at Bedside.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.title: Dangling at Bedside
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.content:
When & Why?
Dangling involves assisting a resident to sit at the edge of the bed with their legs hanging over the side.

Helps the resident adjust to an upright position.
Allows observation of sitting balance and activity tolerance.
Prepares the resident for standing, transfers, or ambulation.

Before You Start

Review the care plan, mobility restrictions, and required assistance.
Explain the procedure and obtain permission.
Lock the bed and adjust its height.
Ensure appropriate footwear and transfer equipment are available.
Check for pain, weakness, or existing dizziness.

Steps

Assist the resident toward the side of the bed using the approved technique.
Support the resident while moving from lying to sitting.
Guide the legs over the bedside while supporting the upper body.
Ensure the resident is stable and appropriately supported.
Allow time to adjust while observing balance and symptoms.
Assist with footwear when the resident is safely seated.
Proceed with standing or transfer only when the resident is ready and the care plan permits.

Safety & Observations
Watch for orthostatic intolerance:

Dizziness or lightheadedness.
Weakness or faintness.
Blurred vision.
Pallor, nausea, or sweating.
Check readiness to stand:
Can maintain sitting balance with the planned assistance.
Is alert and able to participate as expected.
Is not experiencing concerning dizziness or weakness.
Has appropriate footwear and support available.
If symptoms occur:


Stop the activity immediately. Do not attempt standing or transferring.
Maintain physical support and call for assistance.
If dizziness, faintness, or loss of postural control occurs, assist the resident back to a safe supported lying position using the approved technique and necessary staff or equipment.
Notify the nurse promptly and report the symptoms, circumstances, and changes from baseline.
If the resident becomes unresponsive, develops severe breathing difficulty, or shows other signs of an emergency, activate the facility’s emergency response protocol.
Do not resume standing or ambulation until the resident has been evaluated and cleared according to the care plan or nursing direction.

Important: Do not leave a faint or unstable resident sitting at the edge of the bed. Never attempt an unsafe manual lift or repositioning maneuver.
What Should I Remember?

Sit → Observe → Stabilize → Stand.
Dangling helps evaluate tolerance; it does not guarantee blood pressure will normalize.
Never leave an unsteady resident unsupported at the bedside.
Report new or worsening dizziness.
Dangling allows observation of tolerance to sitting, but it does not diagnose or exclude orthostatic hypotension. Formal orthostatic vital-sign measurements are performed according to the ordered assessment procedure.

Using a Gait Belt
Fall Risk

What should a CNA do if a resident becomes faint while dangling?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerStop, maintain support, assist to a safe lying position, and summon nursing help.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Mobility and Transfers/Log Rolling a Resident.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.title: Log Rolling a Resident
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.content:
When & Why?
Turn a resident while maintaining alignment of the head, neck, spine, and trunk.
May be used when spinal movement must be restricted or when ordered for other clinical needs.
Before You Start

Check the care plan, spinal precautions, and required staffing.
Obtain trained assistance.
Explain the procedure and prepare positioning supports.
Confirm who will direct and coordinate movement.

Steps

Position staff according to the approved procedure.
Establish appropriate head, neck, trunk, and limb support.
Explain the movement and coordinate using a shared count.
Roll the resident as a coordinated unit without twisting the spine.
Place prescribed positioning supports.
Check alignment, comfort, and safety.

Safety & Observations

Avoid independent movement of the head, trunk, or pelvis.
Do not perform suspected spinal injury transfers without trained direction.
Watch for pain, neurological changes, or distress.
Maintain alignment throughout the procedure.

What Should I Remember?

Move the body as one unit.
Clear team communication is essential.
Staffing and technique depend on the resident’s condition and facility procedure.
