clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Mobility and Transfers/Range-of-Motion Exercises.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.title: Range-of-Motion Exercises
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.content:
When & Why?
Range-of-motion (ROM) exercises move joints through their available range to maintain flexibility and function.

Maintain joint mobility.
Help prevent stiffness and contractures.
Support functional independence.

Types

Active ROM (AROM): Resident moves the joint independently.
Active-Assisted ROM (AAROM): Resident participates with additional assistance.
Passive ROM (PROM): Caregiver moves the joint without active movement from the resident.

Before You Start

Review the care plan for prescribed movements and restrictions.
Check for pain, recent injury, surgery, or joint limitations.
Explain the exercises and obtain permission.
Position the resident comfortably.
Provide adequate support for the joint and limb.

Steps

Explain which joint will be moved.
Position and support the limb appropriately.
Encourage active participation when possible.
Move the joint slowly and smoothly through the prescribed range.
Avoid forcing movement beyond resistance or comfort.
Repeat according to the care plan.
Return the limb to a comfortable, supported position.
Report pain, stiffness, or changes in movement.

Safety & Observations

Never force a joint beyond its available range.
Stop if the resident experiences pain.
Support the joint and limb throughout movement.
Follow fracture, surgical, neurological, and weight-bearing precautions.
Watch for swelling, muscle spasms, or unusual resistance.
Do not perform unapproved exercises.

What Should I Remember?

Slow, supported, and pain-free.
Encourage active movement whenever appropriate.
ROM should be individualized, not forced.
Report changes in mobility or tolerance.

Related

Joint Movements & Terminology
Restorative & Rehabilitative Care
Limited Mobility
Assisting with Ambulation

 Observed

What should you never do during range-of-motion movement?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerForce a joint past resistance or cause pain.
Why is joint alignment important during ROM?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerTo avoid injury while supporting mobility.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Mobility and Transfers/Repositioning in Bed.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.title: Repositioning in Bed
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.content:
When & Why?
Reposition residents to maintain comfort, support body alignment, and reduce prolonged pressure.

Helps prevent pressure injuries.
Reduces discomfort and stiffness.
Supports mobility and circulation.
Helps maintain skin integrity.

Before You Start

Review the care plan for positioning restrictions and frequency.
Assess mobility, pain, skin condition, and required assistance.
Explain the procedure and obtain permission.
Gather pillows, slide sheets, or appropriate repositioning equipment.
Lock the bed and adjust its working height.
Check attached tubing, drains, and medical devices.

Steps

Explain the intended position and encourage resident participation.
Prepare the bed and required positioning aids.
Position caregivers and equipment according to the approved technique.
Coordinate movement using clear instructions and a shared count.
Reposition using appropriate assistance and friction-reducing equipment.
Support the head, limbs, and body with pillows as indicated.
Check alignment, comfort, skin pressure, and tubing.
Restore the bed to a safe position and place the call light within reach.

Safety & Observations
Prevent friction and shear:

Avoid dragging the resident across linens.
Use approved slide sheets or repositioning devices.
Coordinate movement with assisting staff.
Minimize unnecessary sliding down the bed.
Protect pressure areas:
Inspect bony prominences and device contact points.
Offload heels when indicated.
Use appropriate support between knees and ankles.
Avoid prolonged direct pressure on vulnerable skin.
Resident participation:
Encourage appropriate pushing, turning, or use of mobility aids.
Do not expect residents to assist beyond their abilities.
Follow restrictions on rails, trapeze bars, and other equipment.

What Should I Remember?

Lift or glide with appropriate equipment; never drag.
Encourage independence when safe.
Follow individualized repositioning schedules.
Your CNA course teaches approximately every 2 hours in bed, but the care plan determines actual frequency.
Recheck skin, comfort, and body alignment after repositioning.

Related

Pressure Injuries

clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Mobility and Transfers/Safe Patient Transfers.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.title: Safe Patient Transfers
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.content:
When & Why?
Assist residents in moving between surfaces while maintaining safety, independence, and comfort.
Before You Start

Review care plan, weight-bearing status, and required assistance.
Assess resident participation, balance, strength, and tolerance.
Select appropriate equipment and request help as needed.
Ensure proper footwear and a clear transfer path.
Position equipment and lock brakes.
Explain the transfer and agree on communication cues.

Steps

Prepare the destination and required equipment.
Position the resident safely, following mobility restrictions.
Apply approved transfer equipment as indicated.
Coordinate movement using clear instructions and a shared count.
Assist the resident to the destination using the trained technique.
Confirm safe positioning, comfort, and access to the call light.

Safety & Observations

Watch for dizziness, weakness, pain, or poor balance.
Never pull a resident by the arms or shoulders.
Do not manually lift a resident who requires mechanical assistance.
Stop if the resident cannot safely participate as expected.
Follow the care plan for one-person versus two-person assistance.

What Should I Remember?

Plan → Prepare → Communicate → Transfer → Reassess.
Lock brakes before transferring.
Encourage independence without compromising safety.
Report changes in the assistance required.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Mobility and Transfers/Using a Gait Belt.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.title: Using a Gait Belt
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.content:
When & Why?
A gait belt provides a secure handhold when assisting appropriate residents with transfers and ambulation.

Improves caregiver control and support.
Reduces the need to pull on the resident’s arms or shoulders.
Helps support residents with impaired balance or mobility.

Before You Start

Review care plan, weight-bearing restrictions, and required assistance.
Confirm the resident can participate in the planned movement.
Inspect the belt for damage and verify proper fit.
Explain the procedure and obtain permission.
Ensure appropriate footwear and a clear transfer path.

Steps

Position the belt around the resident’s waist, over clothing.
Secure the buckle and remove slack.
Check that the belt is snug but comfortable, usually allowing approximately two fingers underneath.
Position the buckle away from sensitive areas.
Use the approved grip and guarding technique.
Communicate before assisting the resident to stand, transfer, or walk.
Remove the belt after the activity when the resident is safely positioned.

Safety & Observations

Never use a gait belt to lift a resident’s full body weight.
Never pull the resident by the arms, shoulders, or clothing.
Check for abdominal wounds, recent surgery, feeding tubes, ostomies, or other restrictions affecting belt placement.
Use an alternative method when the belt is contraindicated or the resident requires mechanical assistance.
Watch for dizziness, weakness, pain, or loss of balance.

What Should I Remember?

Snug, not tight. Two fingers.
Follow the care plan for assistance level and equipment.
Maintain a stable stance and avoid twisting.
A gait belt provides assistance, not full-body lifting.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Mobility and Transfers/Using a Mechanical Lift.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.title: Using a Mechanical Lift
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.content:
When & Why?
A full-body mechanical lift transfers residents who cannot safely complete transfers using less supportive methods.

Supports residents with significant weakness or limited weight-bearing ability.
Reduces physical strain on caregivers.
May be appropriate for residents requiring specialized or bariatric transfer equipment.

Before You Start

Check the care plan for lift type, sling, and required staffing.
Verify resident weight and equipment capacity.
Inspect the lift, sling, straps, and attachment points.
Confirm sling compatibility with the lift.
Prepare the destination and clear the transfer path.
Explain the procedure and obtain required assistance.

Steps

Prepare the lift and correct sling according to manufacturer instructions.
Position the resident and apply the sling using the approved technique.
Attach sling loops or clips to the appropriate lift points.
Verify all connections and sling positioning.
Raise the resident only enough to confirm secure support and clearance.
Recheck attachments and resident comfort.
Complete the transfer slowly, following equipment instructions.
Lower the resident into a stable, supported position.
Remove or leave the sling according to the care plan and manufacturer guidance.
Reassess comfort, alignment, and safety.

Safety & Observations

Never exceed the rated capacity of the lift or sling.
Use only compatible, approved lift and sling combinations.
Follow manufacturer-specific attachment configurations; loop lengths are not universal.
Never leave a resident unattended while suspended.
Monitor for pain, anxiety, slipping, skin injury, or equipment malfunction.
Follow required staffing and emergency lowering procedures.
Do not use a damaged lift or sling.

What Should I Remember?

Correct lift → Correct sling → Check attachments → Transfer.
Verify weight capacity before use.
Recheck the resident’s position before raising fully.
Use mechanical assistance instead of unsafe manual lifting.
Full-body and sit-to-stand lifts serve different mobility needs.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Mobility and Transfers/Using a Sit-to-Stand Lift.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.title: Using a Sit-to-Stand Lift
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.content:
When & Why?
Assist eligible residents from sitting to standing or between seated surfaces using mechanical support.
Typically used when residents can participate and bear the amount of weight required by the device.
Before You Start

Confirm the care plan permits sit-to-stand transfers.
Check resident weight-bearing ability and cooperation.
Verify device capacity, sling compatibility, and condition.
Obtain required staff assistance.
Explain the procedure and provide appropriate footwear.

Steps

Prepare and position the resident according to the care plan and the manufacturer’s instructions.
Position the lift and align the resident with its footplate.
Secure feet and lower legs according to device instructions.
Apply the approved sling or support.
Verify straps, attachments, and connections.
Raise the resident gradually while monitoring comfort.
Move toward the destination using the trained procedure.
Confirm they feel the seat with their body.
Lower the resident slowly into a safe seated position.
Remove equipment as appropriate and reassess comfort.

Safety & Observations

Never use with residents who cannot meet the device’s participation or weight-bearing requirements.
Verify sling and lift compatibility.
Follow manufacturer-specific sling placement and attachment instructions.
Watch for pain, anxiety, slipping, or inability to maintain position.
Never leave a resident unattended while supported by the lift.

What Should I Remember?

Confirm weight-bearing ability before starting.
Check every attachment before raising.
Communicate throughout the transfer.
Sit-to-stand and full-body lifts are not interchangeable.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Mobility and Transfers/Wheelchair Transport and Positioning.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.title: Wheelchair Transport and Positioning
clinical-skills-and-how-to/mobility-and-.content:
When & Why?
Safely transport and position residents using wheelchairs while maintaining comfort and independence.
Before You Start

Check care plan and mobility restrictions.
Inspect wheelchair condition, brakes, and footrests.
Verify proper wheelchair fit.
Explain the movement and destination.

Steps

Position the resident with hips supported toward the chair back.
Align the trunk and support arms and legs as required.
Position feet on footrests or the floor as appropriate.
Check required positioning devices.
Release brakes before moving.
Move smoothly and communicate before starting, stopping, or turning.
At the destination, secure the wheelchair and check comfort and safety.

Safety & Observations

Keep arms and elbows clear of doorways and obstacles.
Watch for slipping, discomfort, and pressure points.
Use appropriate techniques for ramps, thresholds, and slopes.
Never use positioning devices as restraints unless legally authorized and indicated.
Follow the care plan for footrests and self-propulsion.

What Should I Remember?

Lock brakes during stationary transfers.
Check feet and arm placement before moving.
Communicate before movement.
Ensure access to the call light when leaving a resident.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/other-care-pr.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Other Care Procedures/Anti-Embolism Stockings.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/other-care-pr.title: Anti-Embolism Stockings
clinical-skills-and-how-to/other-care-pr.content:
When & Why?
Anti-embolism stockings, sometimes called TED hose, provide graduated compression to support venous return and help reduce venous thromboembolism risk in appropriately selected patients.
Before You Start

Confirm the order, care plan, and prescribed wearing schedule.
Verify that the stockings are the correct type and professionally determined size.
Confirm that the resident has been assessed for contraindications by the appropriate clinician.
Inspect the legs and feet for redness, wounds, swelling, discoloration, or other skin changes.
Ask about pain, numbness, tingling, or discomfort.
Explain the procedure and position the resident comfortably.

When to seek nursing guidance before applying:

Suspected or known peripheral arterial disease or impaired circulation.
Peripheral neuropathy or reduced sensation.
Fragile, injured, or irritated skin.
Significant leg swelling or a recent change in leg size.
A device that appears too tight, damaged, or incorrectly sized.

CNAs observe and report concerning findings. They do not independently determine whether compression therapy is medically appropriate.
Steps

Remove stockings when directed and inspect the skin.
Ensure skin is clean and dry.
Gather the stocking and position it over the foot and heel.
Gradually extend it over the leg without excessive pulling.
Smooth wrinkles and check heel alignment.
Ensure the upper edge is not rolled or folded.
Check comfort, skin color, and circulation.

Safety & Observations

Stockings must fit correctly; folds or rolled edges can create concentrated pressure.
Never roll down the top edge to form a constricting band.
Follow the prescribed schedule for wearing, removal, hygiene, and skin inspections.
Remove stockings for routine skin inspection according to the care plan and facility procedure.
Pay particular attention to heels, ankles, toes, and other areas vulnerable to pressure.
If pain, blistering, significant skin marking, discoloration, or other concerning changes occur, stop application or remove the stocking when appropriate, and notify the nurse promptly.
Do not independently choose a different size, compression level, or wearing schedule.
Do not apply stockings when contraindications are suspected or unresolved; seek nursing guidance.
Follow manufacturer instructions and facility policy.

What Should I Remember?

Correct size, smooth fit, no wrinkles.
Follow the prescribed wearing and removal schedule.
Check skin and comfort during routine care.
Follow manufacturer instructions for laundering.

Related

Limited Mobility
Skin Integrity & Breakdown Prevention
Daily Personal Care & ADLs

Flashcards
Why avoid wrinkles or folds in anti-embolism stockings?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerThey can create pressure or impair proper fit.
Who determines whether and how long stockings are used?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerThe prescribed care plan and clinical orders.
Why might anti-embolism stockings be unsafe for a resident with peripheral arterial disease?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerCompression may worsen impaired circulation.
What should a CNA do if anti-embolism stockings cause pain or skin discoloration?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerStop application or remove as appropriate and notify the nurse promptly.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/other-care-pr.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Other Care Procedures/Assisting with a Bedpan.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/other-care-pr.title: Assisting with a Bedpan
clinical-skills-and-how-to/other-care-pr.content:
When & Why?
Assist a resident who cannot safely use the bathroom or bedside commode with urination or bowel elimination.
Common devices:

Standard bedpan.
Fracture bedpan for residents needing a lower-profile pan.

Before You Start

Review the care plan and positioning restrictions.
Explain the procedure and provide privacy.
Gather bedpan, gloves, wipes, linens, and other supplies.
Offer assistance with clothing and positioning.

Steps

Perform hand hygiene and apply appropriate gloves.
Position the resident safely according to the care plan.
Place the bedpan using the trained technique.
Check comfort, alignment, and stability.
Raise the head of the bed as appropriate and permitted.
Provide privacy while remaining available for assistance.
Remove the bedpan safely when finished.
Observe urine or stool before disposal.
Provide perineal care and ensure the resident is dry and comfortable.
Measure and document output when required.
Clean and disinfect equipment according to policy.

Safety & Observations

Never leave an unsafe or high-fall-risk resident unattended.
Avoid dragging the bedpan against the skin.
Protect pressure areas during prolonged use.
Report blood, unusual output, pain, or difficulty eliminating.
Follow infection-control and specimen collection requirements.

What Should I Remember?

Privacy → Position → Assist → Observe → Clean.
Encourage independence when possible.
Do not leave a resident on a bedpan longer than necessary.
Report changes in elimination patterns.

Related

Elimination Care
Perineal Care
Incontinence
Limited Mobility

Practice

 Studied
 Observed
 Practiced
 Passed checkoff

Sources

CNA Module 8 — Elimination Needs

Flashcards
What safety and dignity measures matter during bedpan assistance?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerPrivacy, safe positioning, call light access, prompt hygiene.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/other-care-pr.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Other Care Procedures/Hot and Cold Therapy.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/other-care-pr.title: Hot and Cold Therapy
clinical-skills-and-how-to/other-care-pr.content:
When & Why?
Hot and cold therapies may help relieve pain, swelling, and muscle discomfort.
Heat:

Promotes local blood flow.
May help relax muscles and reduce stiffness.
Cold:
Reduces local blood flow and swelling.
May decrease pain and inflammation.

Before You Start

Review the care plan and confirm the therapy is authorized.
Check application site, skin integrity, sensation, and circulation.
Gather the approved equipment and protective covering.
Explain the procedure and obtain permission.

Steps

Confirm the correct treatment, location, and duration.
Prepare the approved hot or cold application.
Place a protective barrier between the device and skin.
Apply according to the care plan.
Monitor comfort and skin condition during treatment.
Remove after the prescribed duration.
Reassess skin and comfort, and report concerns.

Safety & Observations

Never apply extreme temperatures directly to skin.
Heat may cause burns; cold may cause tissue injury.
Use additional caution with impaired sensation, circulation, fragile skin, or difficulty communicating discomfort.
Do not independently apply treatment to an area with contraindications.
Stop immediately for pain, unusual discoloration, numbness, or skin injury.

What Should I Remember?

Correct temperature → Protect skin → Monitor → Remove.
Module 14 mentions 10–15 minutes, but actual duration depends on the treatment order and facility policy.
Do not leave residents unattended with potentially hazardous temperature applications.
Report unexpected skin changes or discomfort.

Related

Restorative & Rehabilitative Care
Skin Integrity & Breakdown Prevention
Pain Assessment

Practice

 Studied
 Observed
 Practiced
 Passed checkoff

Sources

CNA Module 14 — Hot & Cold Therapies
Facility hot and cold application procedure

Flashcards
What should a CNA monitor during ordered hot or cold therapy?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerSkin changes, discomfort, and time or temperature limits in the care plan.
Why should hot or cold therapy not be applied without authorization?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerTemperature injury or contraindications may occur.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/other-care-pr.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Other Care Procedures/Post-Mortem Care.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/other-care-pr.title: Post-Mortem Care
clinical-skills-and-how-to/other-care-pr.content:
When & Why?
Post-mortem care is the respectful preparation and care of a person’s body after death.
Its purposes include:

Preserving dignity and privacy.
Supporting loved ones and cultural practices.
Preparing the body for authorized transfer.
Following infection-prevention and identification requirements.

Important: The CNA does not independently pronounce death or decide when post-mortem care may begin.
Before You Start

Confirm that death has been pronounced or otherwise verified by authorized personnel under applicable policy.
Obtain nursing direction and authorization to begin.
Confirm any restrictions involving medical examiner review, organ or tissue donation, autopsy, or medical equipment.
Review cultural, religious, and personal preferences.
Confirm whether loved ones want time with the deceased or wish to participate in permitted rituals.
Gather approved supplies and required PPE.
Arrange sufficient assistance for safe handling and repositioning.
Provide privacy and explain the care being performed when loved ones are present.

Steps
Preparation

Perform hand hygiene and apply appropriate PPE.
Maintain a respectful, private environment.
Follow the nurse’s instructions about positioning, personal belongings, identification, and equipment.
Explain the procedure to anyone remaining in the room as appropriate.

Body Care

Gently cleanse and dry the body according to facility procedure.
Change soiled clothing or linens as authorized.
Provide clean clothing or a gown according to the care plan and family preferences.
Position the body as instructed, often supine with the head slightly elevated.
Gently close the eyes when appropriate and permitted.
Position the hands comfortably according to instructions and cultural preferences.
Assist with dentures, glasses, and meaningful personal objects only as authorized.
Do not remove tubes, lines, drains, dressings, or devices unless specifically instructed and permitted.

Completion

Follow identification and personal-belongings procedures.
Prepare the body for transfer using the approved method.
Assist authorized transport personnel when directed.
Dispose of supplies and clean equipment according to facility policy.
Remove PPE and perform hand hygiene.
Complete assigned documentation and report completion to the nurse.

Safety & Observations
Legal and Procedural Requirements

Do not begin care before authorization.
Follow instructions regarding medical examiner or coroner cases.
Preserve medical equipment, personal effects, and potential evidence when required.
Do not independently remove invasive devices.
Follow the facility’s body identification and transfer procedures.

Infection Prevention

Use Standard Precautions and additional precautions when indicated.
Use appropriate protection against contact with blood and body fluids.
Handle and move the body using approved equipment and sufficient staff.
Follow facility requirements for cleaning, containment, and transportation.

Dignity & Family Support

Treat the deceased with the same respect afforded a living resident.
Protect privacy during preparation and transportation.
Do not assume family members must leave the room; follow their wishes when feasible and consistent with policy.
Respect cultural, religious, and personal preferences.
Handle dentures, glasses, jewelry, and other belongings according to the documented inventory and facility procedures.
Do not make unsupported statements about the cause of death.

What Should I Remember?

Authorization comes first.
Preserve identification and follow restrictions.
Do not independently remove medical equipment.
Use appropriate PPE and safe body-handling techniques.
Respect the deceased and their loved ones.
Follow facility and nursing instructions throughout the procedure.

Related

End-of-Life Care
Standard Precautions
Body Mechanics & Injury Prevention
Emotional & Family Support
Patient Rights

Practice

 Studied
 Observed
 Practiced
 Passed checkoff

Sources

CNA Module 16 — Post-Mortem Care
National Institute on Aging — Providing Care and Comfort at the End of Life
Facility post-mortem care, infection-prevention, body identification, and transfer procedures
Applicable local medical examiner, donation, and death-reporting requirements

Flashcards
What is the purpose of post-mortem care?01-foundations / clinical-skillsAnswerPreserve dignity, prepare the body, and support respectful transfer.
Who must authorize post-mortem care before a CNA begins?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerThe appropriate authorized staff member under facility policy.
May a CNA independently pronounce death?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNo.
May a CNA independently remove IV lines, drains, or other medical devices after death?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNo. Follow authorization and facility procedures.
Why might post-mortem care need to be delayed or modified?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerMedical examiner, donation, autopsy, or legal requirements.
Should family members always be required to leave during post-mortem care?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNo. Respect preferences and follow facility policy.
What precautions apply during post-mortem care?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerStandard Precautions and any additional required infection-control measures.
What should be verified before transferring the body?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerCorrect identification, required documentation, authorization, and transfer instructions.

clinical-skills-and-how-to/other-care-pr.filePath: Clinical Skills and How-To/Other Care Procedures/Specimen Collection.md
clinical-skills-and-how-to/other-care-pr.title: Specimen Collection
clinical-skills-and-how-to/other-care-pr.content:
When & Why?
Collecting clinical specimens helps the healthcare team investigate infections, organ function, bleeding, and other medical concerns.
Common specimens include:

Urine: Urinalysis, culture, and other testing.
Stool: Occult blood, infections, and digestive concerns.
Sputum: Respiratory infections and other lung conditions.
Kidney stones: Analysis of stone composition.

Before You Start

Verify the specimen order and collection instructions with the nurse.
Confirm the correct collection method, container, required quantity, and timing.
Identify the resident using approved identifiers.
Explain the procedure, provide privacy, and obtain permission.
Perform hand hygiene and use appropriate PPE.
Assemble supplies and check labeling requirements.
Follow facility and laboratory requirements for labeling, storage, and transport.
Important: Do not touch the inside of specimen containers or lids.

Steps
Urine — Midstream Clean-Catch
Use only when the ordered test requires this collection method.

Provide the resident with appropriate cleansing supplies and instructions.
Assist with cleansing as directed by the collection protocol.
Ask the resident to begin urinating into the toilet.
Collect the middle portion of the urine stream into the specimen container.
Avoid touching the container’s interior or contaminating the specimen.
Secure the lid and follow required labeling and transport procedures.
Assist with hygiene and leave the resident comfortable.
Remember: The instructor emphasizes three cleansing strokes, wiping from the urethral area toward the anus for applicable anatomy. Exact techniques vary by collection protocol and anatomy.

Stool Specimen

Prepare a clean, dry collection device such as a commode hat or bedpan.
Avoid mixing the specimen with urine, water, or toilet paper.
Using the appropriate collection utensil, transfer the amount required.
If directed, obtain material from more than one part of the stool.
Close the container securely.
Label and transport according to instructions.

Fecal Occult Blood Test
Used to detect blood that may not be visible in stool.

Follow the specific test kit instructions.
Some guaiac-based tests use a card and developer solution.
Other fecal blood tests use different collection devices and laboratory processing.
Never assume the same procedure applies to every kit.
Perform or assist with point-of-care testing only when authorized and trained.

Sputum Specimen
Before Collection

Verify the specimen order and collection instructions with the nurse.
Confirm whether the resident requires Transmission-Based Precautions.
Follow the facility’s infection-prevention requirements, including appropriate location and PPE.
Obtain the specified sterile collection container.
Explain the procedure and reinforce instructions provided by the nurse.
Collection Assistance
Explain that sputum comes from the lower respiratory tract rather than ordinary saliva.
Assist the resident with the prescribed collection procedure within your training and assigned responsibilities.
Avoid touching the interior of the container or lid.
Secure the container and follow bedside labeling requirements.
Transfer the specimen according to laboratory transport instructions.
Perform hand hygiene and dispose of contaminated supplies appropriately.
Airborne Infection Precautions


If pulmonary tuberculosis is suspected or confirmed, do not initiate routine sputum collection without first confirming the required airborne precautions and collection location.
Sputum collection for suspected TB requires an appropriate designated environment and respiratory protection according to facility infection-control procedures.
Do not independently perform sputum induction or other aerosol-generating procedures.
Seek nursing or infection-prevention guidance when isolation requirements are uncertain.

Important: A standard surgical mask does not replace a properly fitted respirator when respiratory protection is required for airborne TB exposure.
Straining Urine for Kidney Stones

Prepare the urine collection device and designated strainer.
Instruct the resident on how to use the collection device.
Pour collected urine through the strainer as directed.
Look for retained stone material.
Place any recovered material in the designated labeled container.
Notify the nurse.

Safety & Observations

Follow Standard Precautions.
Maintain privacy and dignity.
Avoid specimen contamination.
Never obtain invasive specimens outside your authorized role.
Report visible blood, significant discomfort, or unexpected specimen findings.
Transport specimens promptly using the appropriate biohazard precautions.
Do not assume all specimens should be refrigerated; follow test-specific instructions.
Respiratory specimens: Verify isolation precautions before assisting with sputum collection. Suspected airborne infections may require specialized collection environments and respiratory protection.

What Should I Remember?
Correct patient → Correct specimen → Correct container → Correct label → Correct transport.
Related

Elimination Care
Bloodborne Pathogens
Standard Precautions
Hand Hygiene
Occupational Exposure & Response

Practice

 Studied
 Observed
 Practiced
 Passed checkoff

Sources

CNA Module 9A — Collection of Specimens
Facility specimen collection and laboratory transport procedures
CDC — Clinical and Laboratory Diagnosis for Tuberculosis
CDC — Tuberculosis Infection Control
CDC — Guidelines for Preventing TB Transmission in Healthcare Settings
Facility respiratory-isolation, sputum collection, and specimen-handling policies (verify at clinical site)

Flashcards
What five checks prevent specimen collection errors?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerCorrect resident, specimen, container, label, and transport.
Can every specimen be refrigerated if processing is delayed?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNo; follow test-specific storage instructions.
What distinguishes sputum from saliva?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerSputum comes from the lower respiratory tract after coughing.
What must be verified before collecting sputum from a resident with suspected TB?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerAirborne precautions, approved collection location, and required respiratory protection.
Should a CNA independently perform sputum induction?03-application / clinical-skillsAnswerNo. It requires authorized personnel and appropriate infection-control procedures.

diseases-and-conditions/aphasia.title: Aphasia
diseases-and-conditions/aphasia.content:
What is it?
Aphasia is an acquired language disorder caused by damage to language-related areas of the brain.

Commonly occurs after a stroke.
May also result from traumatic brain injury, tumors, or neurological disease.
Can affect speaking, understanding, reading, and writing.
Aphasia does not mean a person has lost their intelligence.

Why does it matter?

Makes communicating needs and preferences more difficult.
May interfere with expressing pain or discomfort.
Can lead to frustration, isolation, and misunderstandings.
May make participation in care decisions more challenging.

Types of Aphasia

























TypeCharacteristicsExpressive (Broca’s)Difficulty producing fluent speech; understanding may be relatively preservedReceptive (Wernicke’s)Speech may be fluent but difficult to understand; comprehension is often impairedGlobalSevere impairment of both expression and comprehensionAnomicDifficulty recalling or naming words
Important: Aphasia does not always fit neatly into one category.
What should I look for?

Difficulty finding words.
Short, effortful speech.
Incorrect or substituted words.
Difficulty following spoken instructions.
Trouble reading or writing.
Frustration when attempting to communicate.
Responses that do not match the question.
Emergency Warning: Sudden new difficulty speaking or understanding language may indicate a stroke. Activate emergency response immediately.

What should I do?
Supporting Communication

Approach calmly and gain the resident’s attention.
Speak directly to the resident, not only to family or caregivers.
Use short, clear sentences and a natural adult tone.
Allow additional time for responses.
Ask one question at a time.
Use gestures, pictures, writing, or communication boards when helpful.
Verify understanding without repeatedly correcting the resident.
Reduce background distractions.

Expressive Difficulties

Give the resident time to find words.
Offer choices when appropriate.
Encourage alternative ways of communicating.
Avoid finishing sentences unless the resident welcomes help.

Receptive Difficulties

Give instructions one step at a time.
Use gestures or demonstrations.
Confirm understanding through appropriate methods.
Avoid assuming that a verbal “yes” always indicates comprehension.

What should I report?

Sudden or worsening language difficulties.
Inability to communicate essential needs.
New frustration, withdrawal, or distress.
Changes in previously effective communication methods.

Related

Communication Accommodations
Therapeutic Communication
Recognizing Patient Distress
Emotional & Family Support
Rehabilitation & Therapy Services

Sources

ASHA — Aphasia
ASHA — Communicating With Adults With Language Disorders

Flashcards
Does aphasia necessarily reduce intelligence?02-mechanisms / diseases-conditionsAnswerNo; it impairs language abilities.
What communication strategy helps residents with aphasia?03-application / diseases-conditionsAnswerShort clear speech, extra time, and appropriate communication aids.
What is urgent about sudden new aphasia?03-application / diseases-conditionsAnswerIt may be a sign of stroke requiring emergency response.

diseases-and-conditions/blood-loss.title: Blood Loss
diseases-and-conditions/blood-loss.content:
What is it?
Blood loss is a reduction in circulating blood volume caused by bleeding.

Acute blood loss: Occurs over a short period, such as after trauma or surgery.
Chronic blood loss: Develops gradually through repeated or ongoing bleeding.
Hemorrhage: The escape of blood from damaged blood vessels; can be external or internal.

Hemorrhage
Hemorrhage means bleeding due to blood escaping from the circulatory system.

External hemorrhage: Blood leaves the body through a wound or opening.
Internal hemorrhage: Blood accumulates within the body.
Acute hemorrhage: Bleeding occurs over a relatively short period.
Chronic blood loss: Smaller or repeated episodes of bleeding over time.
Clinical Connection: Severe hemorrhage can reduce circulating blood volume, decrease cardiac output, and cause hypovolemic shock.
For emergency response, see Bleeding, Shock & Injury Response.

How does it work?
Effects on Circulation

Blood is lost from the circulatory system.
Circulating blood volume decreases.
Venous return to the heart may decrease.
Reduced ventricular filling can decrease Cardiac Output.
Blood pressure may fall if compensatory mechanisms are insufficient.

Compensation
The body initially attempts to maintain circulation through:

Increasing heart rate.
Constricting blood vessels.
Redirecting blood flow toward vital organs.
Important: Blood pressure may remain near normal during early significant blood loss because the body compensates.

Severe Blood Loss

Can result in hypovolemic shock.
Reduces oxygen delivery to tissues.
May impair brain, kidney, and other organ function.

Why does it matter clinically?
Blood loss can cause:

Reduced tissue perfusion.
Dizziness, weakness, and fainting.
Rapid pulse and breathing.
Shock and organ damage when severe.
Anemia with chronic or repeated blood loss.

What should I look for?
External Bleeding:

Visible bleeding from wounds or injuries.
Blood-soaked dressings or linens.
Possible Internal Bleeding:
Unexplained bruising or swelling.
Abdominal pain or distention.
Black, tarry stool.
Blood in urine or stool.
Signs of Significant Blood Loss:
Rapid or weak pulse.
Pale, cool, or clammy skin.
Dizziness or fainting.
Unusual weakness.
Confusion or decreased responsiveness.
Low blood pressure, which may be a later finding.

What should I do?

Recognize and report unexpected bleeding promptly.
Activate emergency response for severe bleeding or signs of shock.
Follow trained first-aid procedures and facility emergency protocols.
Observe and communicate changes in pulse, breathing, consciousness, and skin appearance.
Use appropriate PPE when contact with blood is anticipated.
Document objective findings according to facility policy.
CNA Scope: Recognize, provide authorized emergency assistance, and report. Determining the cause and medical treatment of bleeding are responsibilities of qualified clinicians.

Related

Bleeding, Shock & Injury Response
Cardiac Output
Systemic Vascular Resistance
Blood Pressure
Hypotension
Orthostatic Hypotension
Dehydration
Recognizing Patient Distress

Sources

CNA Module 12 — Emergency Procedures
Cardiovascular physiology — circulating blood volume and perfusion

Flashcards
Why can blood pressure be near normal during early serious blood loss?02-mechanisms / diseases-conditionsAnswerCompensatory increased heart rate and vasoconstriction.
What is a possible late consequence of severe blood loss?02-mechanisms / diseases-conditionsAnswerHypovolemic shock from reduced circulating volume.

diseases-and-conditions/c.-difficile-inf.title: C. difficile Infection
diseases-and-conditions/c.-difficile-inf.content:
What is it?
Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) is a spore-forming bacterium that can cause inflammation of the colon and diarrhea.

Often associated with antibiotic use.
Spreads through the fecal-oral route.
Spores can survive on surfaces for prolonged periods.

Why does it matter?

May cause severe diarrhea and dehydration.
Can lead to serious colitis and complications.
Spores are difficult to eliminate with routine cleaning.
Healthcare facilities are important transmission settings.

What should I look for?

New frequent watery or loose stools.
Abdominal pain, cramping, or tenderness.
Fever or signs of dehydration.
Changes in bowel patterns following antibiotic use.

What should I do?

Follow required Contact Precautions.
Use gloves and gown as directed.
Perform hand hygiene according to facility policy.
During C. difficile outbreaks, use soap and water after patient care and glove removal.
Use approved sporicidal disinfectants according to facility procedures.
Report new or worsening diarrhea promptly.

Related

Transmission-Based Precautions
Hand Hygiene
Incontinence Care
Elimination Care
Chain of Infection

Sources

CNA Module 6 — C. difficile
CDC — Clinical Guidance for C. diff

Flashcards
What common symptoms may suggest C. difficile infection?01-foundations / diseases-conditionsAnswerNew watery diarrhea and abdominal discomfort.
What prevention measures matter for C. difficile?03-application / diseases-conditionsAnswerAppropriate contact precautions and facility hand-hygiene protocols.

diseases-and-conditions/cancer.title: Cancer
diseases-and-conditions/cancer.content:
Overview
Cancer is a group of diseases in which abnormal cells grow and divide uncontrollably, invade surrounding tissues, and may spread to other parts of the body.
Cancer develops when genetic changes disrupt the normal mechanisms controlling cell growth, division, and death.
Unlike normal cells, cancer cells may:

Divide when they should not.
Ignore signals to stop growing.
Avoid programmed cell death (apoptosis).
Invade nearby tissues.
Stimulate the formation of new blood vessels.
Spread to distant locations.

Cancer can develop in almost any organ or tissue.
Important: Cancer is not a single disease. Different cancers have different causes, behaviors, treatment options, and prognoses.
Benign vs. Malignant Tumors
A tumor (neoplasm) is an abnormal mass of tissue. Tumors can be benign or malignant.








































CharacteristicBenignMalignantCancerous?NoYesGrowthOften slower, though variableMay grow rapidly or slowlyInvades nearby tissue?Does not invadeCan invadeMetastasizes?NoMay spread to distant locationsCan cause serious problems?Yes, especially through pressure or obstructionYes, through invasion, organ damage, or metastasisExamplesLipoma, uterine fibroidLung carcinoma, osteosarcoma
Important: A benign tumor can still be dangerous depending on its size and location. Some malignant cancers, such as leukemia, do not typically form solid tumors.
Metastasis
Metastasis is the spread of cancer cells from the original (primary) site to distant tissues or organs.
How Metastasis Occurs

Cancer cells invade nearby tissues.
Some cells enter blood vessels or lymphatic vessels.
The cells travel through the bloodstream or lymphatic system.
Some leave the vessels and enter distant tissues.
They may multiply and form secondary tumors.

Common Sites of Metastasis

Bones: May cause pain or fractures.
Lungs: May cause coughing or difficulty breathing.
Liver: May affect liver function and sometimes cause jaundice.
Brain: May cause headaches, seizures, weakness, or neurological changes.

The sites affected depend on the primary cancer.
Important: Metastatic cancer retains the identity of the original cancer.
For example, breast cancer that spreads to the lungs is called metastatic breast cancer, not primary lung cancer.
Types of Cancer
Cancers can be classified according to the cells or tissues where they originate.













































TypeTissue of OriginExamplesCarcinomaEpithelial cells lining organs and body surfacesLung cancer, many breast cancers, colorectal cancer, prostate cancerSarcomaBone, muscle, fat, cartilage, and other connective tissuesOsteosarcoma, liposarcomaLeukemiaBlood-forming tissue, usually bone marrowAcute myeloid leukemia, chronic lymphocytic leukemiaLymphomaLymphocytes within lymphatic and other tissuesHodgkin lymphoma, non-Hodgkin lymphomaCentral Nervous System (CNS) CancersCells and tissues of the brain or spinal cordGlioblastoma, medulloblastomaMyelomaPlasma cells, a type of immune cellMultiple myelomaMelanomaMelanocytes, the cells that produce melaninCutaneous melanoma
Important Distinctions

Carcinoma: Cancer originating in epithelial tissue; the most common broad cancer category.
Sarcoma: Cancer of connective or supportive tissues.
Leukemia: Cancer typically involving blood-forming tissue and abnormal blood cells.
Lymphoma: Cancer originating in lymphocytes.
CNS Cancers: Cancers originating in the brain or spinal cord; not all brain tumors are malignant.
Melanoma: Cancer of pigment-producing cells; often occurs in the skin.

Common Cancers







































































CancerDescriptionCommon Causes / Risk FactorsPossible Signs & SymptomsLung CancerCancer arising in lung tissueSmoking, radon, secondhand smoke, asbestos, air pollutionPersistent cough, coughing blood, chest discomfort, shortness of breathBreast CancerCancer originating in breast tissueAge, inherited mutations such as BRCA1/2, family history, hormonal factorsBreast lump, skin or nipple changes, abnormal dischargeColorectal CancerCancer of the colon or rectumAge, family history, hereditary syndromes, smoking, obesity, alcoholBlood in stool, bowel habit changes, abdominal discomfort, anemiaProstate CancerCancer originating in the prostateAge, family history, inherited genetic factorsOften asymptomatic early; sometimes urinary symptoms or bone pain if advancedSkin CancerCancer involving skin cells, including basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanomaUV exposure, prior sunburns, skin characteristics, family history, immune suppressionChanging moles, new or nonhealing skin lesionsPancreatic CancerCancer originating in pancreatic tissueSmoking, age, chronic pancreatitis, obesity, family historyJaundice, abdominal or back pain, weight lossCervical CancerCancer originating in the cervixPersistent infection with high-risk HPV typesAbnormal vaginal bleeding, unusual discharge, pelvic painLiver CancerCancer originating in liver tissueChronic hepatitis B or C, cirrhosis, alcohol-related liver disease, metabolic dysfunction-associated liver diseaseAbdominal pain, weight loss, jaundiceLeukemiaCancer of blood-forming tissuesRisk factors vary; some genetic conditions, prior chemotherapy, radiation exposureFatigue, infections, easy bruising, bleedingLymphomaCancer originating in lymphocytesRisk varies by subtype; immune suppression, some infections, ageEnlarged lymph nodes, night sweats, fever, weight loss
Important: Many cancers cause few or no symptoms in their early stages. Symptoms alone do not establish a cancer diagnosis.
Causes & Risk Factors
Cancer arises from genetic changes affecting normal cell behavior.
These changes may result from:

Random errors during cell division.
Inherited genetic variants.
Environmental or occupational exposures.
Certain infections.
The accumulation of changes over time.

Major Risk Factors























































Risk FactorHow It ContributesExamplesTobacco UseExposure to chemicals that damage DNALung, bladder, pancreatic, head and neck cancersUltraviolet (UV) RadiationDamages DNA in skin cellsMelanoma, basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinomaAlcoholAlcohol and its metabolites contribute to cancer riskLiver, breast, colorectal, esophageal cancersObesity & Physical InactivityAssociated with hormonal, inflammatory, and metabolic changesColorectal, endometrial, and certain breast cancersInfectious AgentsCertain infections can cause chronic inflammation or directly promote cancer developmentHPV, hepatitis B and C, H. pyloriIonizing RadiationCan damage cellular DNALeukemia and certain solid tumorsInherited Genetic VariantsIncrease susceptibility to specific cancersBRCA1/2, Lynch syndromeAgeMore time for genetic changes to accumulateMany cancer types become more common with ageImmune SuppressionReduced immune surveillance can increase riskCertain lymphomas and infection-associated cancers
A risk factor increases the likelihood of developing cancer but does not guarantee that cancer will occur.
Carcinogens
A carcinogen is an agent capable of causing cancer.
Carcinogens may be chemical, physical, or biological.





















CategoryExamplesChemicalTobacco smoke, asbestos, benzenePhysicalUltraviolet radiation, ionizing radiationBiologicalHigh-risk HPV, hepatitis B and C viruses, Helicobacter pylori
Important: Carcinogen exposure does not guarantee cancer. Risk depends on the agent, exposure, duration, and individual susceptibility.
Cancer Prevention
Measures that can reduce the risk of certain cancers include:

Avoiding tobacco and secondhand smoke.
Limiting alcohol consumption.
Protecting skin from excessive UV exposure.
Maintaining regular physical activity.
Following a healthy dietary pattern.
Receiving recommended HPV and hepatitis B vaccinations.
Reducing avoidable occupational carcinogen exposure.
Participating in age- and risk-appropriate cancer screening.

Cancer cannot always be prevented, and having cancer does not imply that someone made unhealthy choices.
How Cancer Is Diagnosed
Cancer diagnosis often involves a combination of clinical evaluation, laboratory testing, imaging, and tissue examination.









































MethodPurposeMedical History & Physical ExaminationIdentify symptoms, findings, and risk factorsScreening TestsDetect possible cancer or precancerous changes before symptoms developBlood & Laboratory TestsIdentify abnormalities or measure selected biomarkersImaging (CT, MRI, Ultrasound, PET)Locate abnormalities and assess their extentEndoscopyExamine internal organs and potentially obtain tissue samplesBiopsyRemove cells or tissue for microscopic examinationPathologyIdentify cancer type, cellular features, and other characteristicsMolecular / Biomarker TestingIdentify tumor characteristics that may guide treatment
Biopsy
A biopsy removes a tissue or cell sample for examination.
A pathologist examines the sample to determine whether cancer is present and may identify the type and grade.
A biopsy is often needed for a definitive diagnosis, although some cancers can be diagnosed through specialized blood or bone marrow testing.
Screening vs. Diagnosis

Screening: Tests people without symptoms to look for possible disease.
Diagnostic Testing: Investigates symptoms or abnormal screening results to establish a diagnosis.

A positive screening result does not automatically mean cancer is present.
Staging Cancer
Cancer staging describes the extent of cancer within the body, including tumor size, involvement of nearby structures or lymph nodes, and distant spread.
Staging helps determine treatment options and estimate prognosis.
TNM Staging System
The TNM system is used for many solid tumors.

T — Tumor: Size or local extent of the primary tumor.
N — Nodes: Whether nearby regional lymph nodes contain cancer.
M — Metastasis: Whether cancer has spread to distant sites.

General Cancer Stages





























StageGeneral MeaningStage 0Carcinoma in situ: abnormal cells have not invaded nearby tissueStage IOften a relatively small or localized cancerStage IIMore extensive local disease, depending on cancer typeStage IIIMore advanced local or regional disease, often involving nearby nodesStage IVDistant metastatic spread for many solid cancers
Important: These descriptions are general. Staging differs by cancer type; leukemia, lymphoma, and many CNS tumors use other classification or staging approaches.
Stage vs. Grade

Stage: How far the cancer has spread.
Grade: How abnormal the cancer cells appear and, in some cancers, how aggressively they may behave.

Stage describes extent; grade describes cellular characteristics.
Treatment Options
Cancer treatment depends on cancer type, stage, molecular characteristics, overall health, and the patient’s goals.













































TreatmentHow It WorksSurgeryRemoves cancerous tissue; may also relieve symptomsChemotherapyUses drugs to kill or inhibit cancer cells, often affecting other rapidly dividing cellsRadiation TherapyUses high-energy radiation to damage or destroy cancer cellsImmunotherapyHelps the immune system recognize or attack cancerTargeted TherapyTargets specific molecules or pathways involved in cancer growthHormone TherapyReduces or blocks hormones that support certain cancersStem Cell TransplantRestores blood-forming cells after certain intensive treatmentsActive SurveillanceCarefully monitors selected cancers without immediate treatmentPalliative TreatmentsRelieve symptoms or complications, sometimes alongside cancer-directed treatment
Treatment may combine several approaches.
Treatment Goals

Curative: Attempt to eliminate the cancer.
Disease Control: Slow progression or maintain remission.
Palliative: Relieve symptoms and improve quality of life.

Not every cancer is curable, but even incurable cancers may be treatable.
Common Effects of Cancer & Treatment
Both cancer and its treatments can cause symptoms.





























































EffectPossible CausesFatigueCancer, anemia, treatment, sleep disruption, poor nutritionPainTumor pressure or invasion, procedures, treatment effectsNausea & VomitingChemotherapy, medications, cancer-related illnessLoss of Appetite / Weight LossCancer-related metabolic changes, nausea, taste changes, swallowing problemsHair Loss (Alopecia)Certain chemotherapy regimens and radiation to hair-bearing areasMucositis / Mouth SoresCertain chemotherapy and radiation treatmentsDiarrhea or ConstipationTreatments, medications, altered intake, diseasePeripheral NeuropathyCertain chemotherapy medications or tumor-related nerve injuryAnemiaCancer, bleeding, impaired bone marrow function, treatmentNeutropeniaReduced neutrophils, sometimes caused by chemotherapy, increasing infection riskThrombocytopeniaReduced platelets, increasing bruising and bleeding riskSkin ChangesRadiation, medications, surgery, underlying diseaseEmotional DistressUncertainty, symptoms, treatment burden, changes in independence
These effects vary considerably. Not every person with cancer experiences the same symptoms.
Palliative Care
Palliative care is specialized care focused on relieving symptoms, reducing suffering, and improving quality of life for people living with serious illness.
It can address:

Pain.
Fatigue.
Nausea and other physical symptoms.
Emotional distress.
Social and spiritual concerns.
Treatment decisions and goals of care.

Palliative care can begin at diagnosis and can be provided alongside treatments intended to cure or control cancer.
Palliative Care vs. Hospice

Palliative Care: Can be provided at any stage of serious illness, including during curative treatment.
Hospice Care: Focuses on comfort and quality of life when care goals have shifted away from curing the terminal illness.

See Caring for Residents with Cancer.
CNA Considerations

Observe and report new symptoms or changes from baseline.
Follow prescribed infection-prevention precautions.
Report fever or signs of infection promptly, especially in residents receiving chemotherapy.
Observe fatigue, pain, food and fluid intake, nausea, bowel changes, and skin integrity.
Support permitted activity and independence.
Follow individualized mobility, nutritional, and treatment-related precautions.
Protect confidentiality and respect the resident’s care preferences.
Do not independently diagnose cancer, interpret staging, or provide cancer-specific treatment.

When to Report

New or worsening pain.
Fever, chills, or signs of infection.
Unexpected bruising or bleeding.
Significant fatigue or weakness.
Persistent nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Poor intake, dehydration, or rapid weight loss.
New confusion or functional decline.
New difficulty breathing or swallowing.
Changes around surgical wounds or treatment sites.

Emergency signs: Severe breathing difficulty, uncontrolled bleeding, sudden neurological changes, or unresponsiveness require immediate emergency response.
A fever in a patient with known or suspected neutropenia may represent a medical emergency and requires immediate clinical assessment.
Study Notes

Clinical Connections

Caring for Residents with Cancer: Symptom support, person-centered care, and palliative care.
Standard Precautions: Some treatments weaken immune defenses.
Recognizing Patient Distress: Cancer and treatment complications may require urgent attention.
Skin Integrity & Breakdown Prevention: Immobility, malnutrition, and treatment effects can increase skin vulnerability.
Fluid Balance: Vomiting, diarrhea, or poor intake can disturb hydration.
Vital Signs: Fever and other abnormalities may indicate illness or complications.

diseases-and-conditions/dehydration.title: Dehydration
diseases-and-conditions/dehydration.content:
What is it?
Dehydration occurs when the body loses more water than it takes in, resulting in a deficit of body water.
It can result from:

Inadequate fluid intake.
Vomiting or diarrhea.
Fever and excessive sweating.
Increased urine production.
Illness or difficulty accessing fluids.

Older adults are at increased risk because they may experience reduced thirst, mobility limitations, or difficulty obtaining and drinking fluids.
How does it work?
Significant fluid loss can reduce circulating blood volume and venous return.
This may decrease Cardiac Output and Blood Pressure, reducing blood flow to organs.
Severe dehydration can contribute to circulatory instability, kidney dysfunction, and changes in mental status.
Why does it matter clinically?
Dehydration may increase the risk of:

Dizziness and falls.
Weakness and reduced activity tolerance.
Low blood pressure.
Reduced urine output.
Confusion or other changes in mental status.
Serious complications when fluid loss becomes severe.

Recognition and Assessment
Possible Warning Signs

Thirst or dry mouth.
Reduced fluid intake.
Darker or decreased urine output.
Dizziness, weakness, or unusual fatigue.
Increased heart rate.
Recent vomiting, diarrhea, or fever.

Important: Older adults may not experience pronounced thirst. No single symptom reliably establishes or excludes dehydration.
Urgent Warning Signs

New confusion or significant change in alertness.
Fainting or loss of consciousness.
Absent or markedly reduced urination.
Rapid breathing or heartbeat accompanied by concerning symptoms.
Severe weakness, collapse, or suspected shock.
Inability to drink safely or ongoing substantial fluid loss with clinical deterioration.

These findings require immediate nursing assessment or activation of the facility’s emergency response protocol, depending on severity.
Care Considerations
CNA Responsibilities:

Observe and accurately record fluid intake when assigned.
Assist with drinking and hydration according to the resident’s care plan.
Respect fluid restrictions and swallowing precautions.
Observe and report changes in urine output, alertness, mobility, and activity tolerance.
Report vomiting, diarrhea, fever, poor intake, or other factors contributing to fluid loss.
Promptly notify the nurse of suspected dehydration or significant changes.
Activate emergency response for severe symptoms according to facility policy.

Scope & Safety:

Do not independently diagnose dehydration.
Do not change ordered fluid goals or restrictions.
Do not offer oral fluids to residents who cannot safely swallow or have restrictions prohibiting intake.
Do not assume that all residents need increased fluids; some have conditions requiring fluid restriction.
Follow nursing direction for further monitoring and care.

diseases-and-conditions/dementia.title: Dementia
diseases-and-conditions/dementia.content:
What is it?
Dementia is an umbrella term for a decline in memory, thinking, language, or other cognitive abilities severe enough to interfere with daily activities.

Dementia is not a normal part of aging.
It is a syndrome rather than a single disease.
Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause.
Symptoms and progression depend on the underlying condition.

How does it work?
Dementia develops when damage or disease affects brain cells and the connections between them.
Different brain areas control memory, language, reasoning, behavior, and movement, so symptoms vary depending on the affected regions.
Common Types





























TypeCommon CharacteristicsAlzheimer’s DiseaseProgressive memory impairment, often followed by broader cognitive declineVascular DementiaCognitive difficulties associated with cerebrovascular diseaseLewy Body DementiaFluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, and movement symptomsFrontotemporal DementiaEarly changes in behavior, personality, or languageMixed DementiaMore than one disease process contributes to cognitive decline
Why does it matter?
Dementia can affect:

Memory and orientation.
Communication and comprehension.
Judgment and safety awareness.
Ability to complete activities of daily living.
Emotional regulation and behavior.
Mobility, swallowing, and nutrition as the condition progresses.

What should I look for?
Cognitive Changes

Forgetting familiar people or routines.
Confusion about time or place.
Difficulty following instructions.
Word-finding or communication difficulties.
Difficulty recognizing familiar objects.

Behavioral & Emotional Changes

Anxiety or fear.
Restlessness or agitation.
Withdrawal from activities.
Sleep disturbances.
Changes in personality or usual behavior.

Functional Changes

Increased assistance needed for dressing, bathing, or eating.
Difficulty navigating familiar environments.
Unsafe mobility or increased fall risk.
Difficulty expressing pain or discomfort.

Dementia vs. Delirium

























DementiaDeliriumUsually develops graduallyOften develops suddenlyOften progressiveMay fluctuate substantially over hoursAssociated with underlying brain diseaseOften triggered by acute illness, medication effects, or other medical causesChronic cognitive impairmentAcute disturbance in attention and awareness
Important: A resident with dementia can also develop delirium.
Sudden confusion or a major change from baseline must be reported promptly rather than assumed to be dementia.
What should I do?

Compare the resident’s current behavior and abilities with their usual baseline.
Speak calmly and use clear, simple instructions.
Allow adequate time for responses.
Maintain predictable routines when helpful.
Offer choices and encourage independence.
Check for possible unmet needs such as pain, hunger, toileting, fatigue, or discomfort.
Follow the individualized care plan.
Respect dignity, preferences, and resident rights.
Report new or worsening cognitive, behavioral, or functional changes.
CNA Scope: Observe changes, provide appropriate support, and report concerns. Diagnosis and treatment planning are responsibilities of qualified clinicians.

Related

Communication Accommodations
Therapeutic Communication
Fall Risk
Patient Rights

Flashcards
Is dementia a normal part of aging?01-foundations / diseases-conditionsAnswerNo.
How does delirium typically differ from dementia?02-mechanisms / diseases-conditionsAnswerDelirium is usually acute and fluctuating; dementia often develops gradually.
What should a CNA do about sudden confusion in a person with dementia?03-application / diseases-conditionsAnswerReport promptly; do not assume it is usual dementia.

diseases-and-conditions/hiv-and-aids.title: HIV and AIDS
diseases-and-conditions/hiv-and-aids.content:
Overview
Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) is a virus that attacks the immune system, especially CD4 T lymphocytes.
Without effective treatment, HIV can weaken immune defenses and eventually progress to Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS).

HIV: The virus and infection.
AIDS: The most advanced stage of HIV infection, defined by severe immune damage or certain AIDS-defining conditions.

Important: Having HIV does not mean someone has AIDS. With effective treatment, people with HIV can live long, healthy lives and may never develop AIDS.
HIV vs. AIDS



































FeatureHIVAIDSDefinitionInfection with human immunodeficiency virusMost advanced stage of HIV infectionImmune functionMay be relatively preserved or impairedSeverely compromisedSymptomsMay be absent, mild, or significantMay include serious opportunistic illnessesDiagnosisHIV-specific testingHIV plus AIDS-defining criteriaTreatmentAntiretroviral therapy (ART)ART plus treatment or prevention of complications
A person with HIV meets AIDS criteria when their CD4 count falls below 200 cells/mm³ or they develop an AIDS-defining illness.
How HIV Affects the Body

HIV enters susceptible cells, especially CD4 T lymphocytes.
It uses cellular machinery to reproduce.
Without treatment, ongoing infection progressively damages immune function.
Reduced immune defenses increase vulnerability to opportunistic infections and certain cancers.

Stages of HIV Infection

Acute HIV Infection: Early period after infection. Some people develop fever, fatigue, rash, sore throat, or swollen lymph nodes; others have no symptoms.
Chronic HIV Infection: HIV remains active, but symptoms may be absent for years. Treatment can suppress viral replication.
AIDS: Advanced immune damage associated with high risk of serious complications.

Opportunistic Illnesses
Opportunistic illnesses occur more frequently or more severely when the immune system is weakened.
Examples include:

Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP/PJP): Serious fungal lung infection.
Esophageal candidiasis: Fungal infection affecting the esophagus.
Toxoplasmosis: Parasitic infection that can affect the brain.
Tuberculosis: May occur at any HIV stage and can be especially serious with immune suppression.
Certain cancers: Including Kaposi sarcoma and some lymphomas.

HIV Transmission
HIV spreads through certain body fluids containing infectious virus.
Fluids That Can Transmit HIV

Blood.
Semen and pre-seminal fluid.
Vaginal fluids.
Rectal fluids.
Breast milk.

For transmission to occur, these fluids must reach susceptible mucous membranes, damaged tissue, or the bloodstream.
Common Transmission Routes

Sexual contact involving exposure to infectious fluids.
Sharing needles, syringes, or other injection equipment.
Transmission during pregnancy, childbirth, or breastfeeding.
Occupational blood exposure, such as certain needlestick injuries.

HIV Is Not Transmitted Through

Hugging, handshakes, or ordinary touching.
Sharing toilets, utensils, or dishes.
Sweat, tears, or saliva alone.
Coughing or sneezing.
Insect bites.
Ordinary caregiving without a relevant exposure.

Important: HIV is not an airborne infection. HIV status alone does not require airborne, droplet, or contact isolation.
Testing for HIV
HIV tests look for antibodies, viral antigens, or viral genetic material.






























TestWhat It DetectsTypical Detection Window After ExposureAntibody TestAntibodies produced in response to HIV23–90 daysLaboratory Antigen/Antibody TestHIV p24 antigen and antibodies, using blood from a vein18–45 daysRapid Fingerstick Antigen/Antibody TestHIV antigen and antibodies18–90 daysNucleic Acid Test (NAT)HIV genetic material10–33 days
Window Period
The window period is the interval after infection before a particular test can reliably detect HIV.

A negative result soon after an exposure does not necessarily exclude infection.
Follow-up testing may be necessary.
Positive screening tests require appropriate confirmatory testing.
HIV testing and interpretation are performed by authorized healthcare professionals.

These typical windows assume the person is not taking antiretroviral medication, which can affect test detection.
HIV Treatment
Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) uses medications to suppress HIV replication.
ART is recommended for everyone diagnosed with HIV.
Effective treatment can:

Reduce viral load.
Preserve or restore immune function.
Prevent progression to AIDS.
Reduce HIV-related illness and death.
Prevent sexual transmission when viral suppression is maintained.

Viral Load & CD4 Count

Viral Load: Amount of HIV in the blood; used to monitor treatment effectiveness.
CD4 Count: Measure of immune-system status and vulnerability to opportunistic infections.

Undetectable = Untransmittable (U=U)
A person living with HIV who takes ART and maintains a suppressed viral load below 200 copies/mL does not transmit HIV through sex.
This is called Undetectable = Untransmittable (U=U).
U=U specifically refers to sexual transmission. Other routes, including breastfeeding, require separate medical guidance.
Preventing HIV Infection
General Prevention

Use condoms appropriately to reduce exposure during sex.
Avoid sharing needles or injection equipment.
Use sterile equipment for injections and invasive procedures.
Follow Standard Precautions in healthcare settings.
Obtain HIV testing and preventive care when appropriate.

Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP)
PrEP is medication used by people without HIV to reduce their risk before potential exposure.

May be taken orally or by scheduled injection.
Requires appropriate medical assessment and follow-up testing.
Does not protect against every sexually transmitted infection.

Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP)
PEP is a short course of antiretroviral medication used after a potentially significant HIV exposure.

Must be started as soon as possible, no later than 72 hours after exposure.
Typically involves a 28-day medication course.
Requires prompt medical evaluation.

Healthcare Worker Exposure
Following a possible occupational exposure:

Perform immediate first aid appropriate to the exposure, such as washing a needlestick site with soap and water or flushing exposed mucous membranes with water.
Report the exposure immediately.
Follow the facility’s occupational exposure procedures.
Obtain urgent medical evaluation for possible PEP.

Do not delay reporting or evaluation while waiting for information about the source patient’s HIV status.
CNA Considerations

Use Standard Precautions for all residents.
Follow facility PPE and sharps-safety procedures.
Report possible occupational exposures immediately.
Observe and report new fever, cough, unexplained weight loss, unusual fatigue, mouth lesions, or functional decline.
Support hydration, nutrition, hygiene, comfort, and prescribed care.
Do not independently diagnose HIV, interpret test results, or administer HIV medications outside authorized scope.
Protect confidentiality and treat residents without discrimination.

See Caring for Residents with HIV & AIDS.
Study Notes

Lymphatic & Immune System
Standard Precautions
Transmission-Based Precautions

Clinical Connections

Standard Precautions: Routine infection prevention applies regardless of known HIV status.
Chain of Infection: HIV requires specific transmission routes.
Recognizing Patient Distress: Opportunistic illness can cause serious clinical deterioration.
Caring for Residents with HIV & AIDS: Covers patient rights, stigma, communication, and individualized care.

diseases-and-conditions/heart-failure-(c.title: Heart Failure (CHF)
diseases-and-conditions/heart-failure-(c.content:
Overview
Heart failure (HF) occurs when the heart cannot pump or fill effectively enough to meet the body’s needs without abnormally elevated filling pressures.
Congestive Heart Failure (CHF) refers to heart failure associated with fluid congestion.
Heart failure can affect both circulation and fluid balance, potentially causing shortness of breath, swelling, and reduced exercise tolerance.
Common Causes & Risk Factors

Hypertension: Long-term high blood pressure increases the heart’s workload.
Coronary Artery Disease: Reduced blood supply can damage or weaken the heart muscle.
Previous Heart Attack: Damaged heart muscle may pump less effectively.
Heart Valve Disease: Abnormal valves can increase pressure or volume strain.
Cardiomyopathy: Disease of the heart muscle that affects its structure or function.
Arrhythmias: Abnormal rhythms can impair effective pumping.

Key Mechanisms

Reduced Cardiac Output: The heart may deliver insufficient blood to body tissues.
Fluid Retention: Reduced kidney perfusion and compensatory hormonal responses can promote sodium and water retention.
Pulmonary Congestion: Elevated pressures in the pulmonary circulation can cause fluid to accumulate in lung tissue.
Peripheral Congestion: Increased venous pressure can cause fluid to collect in the legs, ankles, or other tissues.

Common Signs & Symptoms













































FindingDescriptionWhy It HappensDyspneaShortness of breathPulmonary congestion or reduced ability to meet oxygen demandsOrthopneaDifficulty breathing while lying flatLying down increases venous return, potentially worsening lung congestionParoxysmal Nocturnal Dyspnea (PND)Sudden episodes of severe breathlessness that awaken a person from sleepRedistribution of fluid and changes in cardiac filling pressures during sleepPeripheral EdemaSwelling, particularly in the feet, ankles, and legsIncreased venous pressure and fluid retentionNocturiaIncreased urination during the nightFluid from dependent tissues may return to circulation when lying down, increasing nighttime urine productionFatigue / WeaknessReduced energy and exercise toleranceReduced cardiac reserve, impaired perfusion, and other factorsRapid Weight GainSudden increase in body weightFluid accumulation rather than an immediate increase in body fat
Important distinction: Orthopnea is breathlessness while lying flat. PND is sudden breathlessness that awakens someone after they have been asleep. They are related but different symptoms.
CNA Considerations

Observe and report new or worsening breathing difficulty.
Assist with upright positioning when appropriate and consistent with the care plan.
Record daily weights consistently when ordered.
Observe and report new or worsening edema.
Follow prescribed fluid-intake and output monitoring.
Observe activity tolerance, fatigue, and changes from baseline.
Follow prescribed mobility, diet, and fluid restrictions.
Report worsening symptoms promptly.

Emergency signs: Severe breathing difficulty, new chest pain, fainting, or sudden unresponsiveness require immediate emergency response.

Respiratory System
Cardiac Output
Fluid Balance

How can heart failure cause fluid retention?
Why does lying flat worsen breathing for some residents with heart failure?

What is heart failure?01-foundations / diseases-conditionsAnswerImpaired pumping or filling of the heart that can cause inadequate circulation or congestion.
What is orthopnea?01-foundations / diseases-conditionsAnswerDifficulty breathing while lying flat.
What is paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND)?02-mechanisms / diseases-conditionsAnswerSudden breathlessness that awakens a person from sleep.
Why does heart failure cause peripheral edema?02-mechanisms / diseases-conditionsAnswerIncreased venous pressure and fluid retention cause swelling.
Why can heart failure cause nocturia?02-mechanisms / diseases-conditionsAnswerFluid shifts into circulation when lying down, increasing nighttime urine production.

diseases-and-conditions/hypertension.title: Hypertension
diseases-and-conditions/hypertension.content:
What is it?
Hypertension is persistently elevated arterial blood pressure.

Blood pressure is recorded as systolic/diastolic in mmHg.
A diagnosis generally requires properly obtained measurements over time.
Hypertension often causes no noticeable symptoms.

Adult Blood Pressure Categories






























CategorySystolicDiastolicNormalBelow 120AND below 80Elevated120–129AND below 80Stage 1 Hypertension130–139OR 80–89Stage 2 Hypertension140 or higherOR 90 or higher
These are classification categories, not automatic CNA reporting thresholds.
How does it work?
Arterial pressure is influenced by:

Cardiac Output.
Systemic Vascular Resistance.
Circulating blood volume.
Kidney and hormonal regulation.
Hypertension may involve:
Increased vascular resistance.
Abnormal blood-pressure regulation by the kidneys.
Increased arterial stiffness.
Genetic, environmental, and other contributing factors.

Primary vs. Secondary Hypertension

Primary: No single identifiable cause; most common form.
Secondary: Elevated blood pressure caused by an underlying condition or substance.

Why does it matter clinically?
Long-term hypertension can damage blood vessels and organs.
Possible complications include:

Stroke.
Heart attack.
Heart failure.
Chronic kidney disease.
Vision problems.

What should I look for?
Common Presentation:

Often no symptoms.
Elevated blood pressure readings over time.
Possible Concerning Symptoms:
Severe headache.
Chest pain.
Difficulty breathing.
Sudden weakness or numbness.
New visual disturbances.
Confusion or other acute neurological changes.
Important: These symptoms can have many causes; they require appropriate evaluation rather than assuming hypertension is responsible.

What should I do?

Measure blood pressure using the correct technique.
Compare readings with the resident’s usual baseline and care-plan parameters.
Report unexpectedly elevated readings according to facility policy.
Follow instructions to repeat or confirm an unusual reading.
Recognize and immediately escalate symptoms suggesting an acute medical emergency.
Support prescribed lifestyle and treatment plans within CNA scope.
Emergency: Very high blood pressure accompanied by chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, or acute neurological symptoms requires emergency evaluation.

Related

Blood Pressure
Measuring Blood Pressure
Vital Sign Ranges
Cardiac Output
Systemic Vascular Resistance
Hypotension
Recognizing Patient Distress

Sources

American Heart Association — High Blood Pressure
CDC — About High Blood Pressure

Flashcards
Does hypertension usually cause noticeable symptoms?02-mechanisms / diseases-conditionsAnswerOften no; it can be asymptomatic.
What can long-standing hypertension damage?01-foundations / diseases-conditionsAnswerHeart, brain, kidneys, eyes, and blood vessels.
