diseases-and-conditions/hypotension.title: Hypotension
diseases-and-conditions/hypotension.content:
What is it?
Hypotension is blood pressure that is abnormally low for the person’s needs or circumstances.

Often described as systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg or diastolic pressure below 60 mmHg.
These values are general reference points, not universal treatment or reporting thresholds.
Some healthy people naturally have relatively low blood pressure without symptoms.

How does it work?
Blood pressure can fall because of:
Reduced Cardiac Output

Reduced circulating blood volume.
Decreased ventricular filling.
Heart dysfunction.

Reduced Systemic Vascular Resistance

Excessive vasodilation.
Certain medications.
Some types of shock.

Reduced Circulating Volume

Dehydration.
Blood Loss.
These mechanisms may occur together.

Why does it matter clinically?
Low blood pressure can reduce blood flow to vital organs.
Possible effects include:

Dizziness or lightheadedness.
Weakness.
Fainting.
Falls.
Reduced tissue perfusion.
Shock when circulation becomes critically inadequate.

What should I look for?
Possible Symptoms:

Dizziness or faintness.
Blurred vision.
Unusual fatigue or weakness.
Nausea.
Confusion.
Syncope (fainting).
Other Observations:
Lower-than-usual blood pressure.
Rapid or weak pulse.
Cool or clammy skin.
Changes in alertness.
Symptoms associated with sitting or standing.

Orthostatic Hypotension
A blood pressure decrease associated with moving upright.
Commonly defined as:

Systolic decrease of at least 20 mmHg, or
Diastolic decrease of at least 10 mmHg,
within three minutes of standing or head-up tilt.
See Orthostatic Hypotension for details.

What should I do?

Observe symptoms and changes from baseline.
Measure blood pressure according to training and facility policy.
Notify the nurse of symptomatic or unexpected low readings.
Assist residents with changing positions safely.
Stop ambulation or transfers if the resident becomes dizzy or faint.
Help the resident into a safe position and summon assistance.
Activate emergency response for unresponsiveness, severe symptoms, or suspected shock.
CNA Scope: CNAs identify concerning observations and report them. Causes, diagnosis, and treatment are determined by qualified clinicians.

Related

Blood Pressure
Measuring Blood Pressure
Orthostatic Hypotension
Cardiac Output
Systemic Vascular Resistance
Dehydration
Blood Loss
Fall Risk
Recognizing Patient Distress

Sources

American Heart Association — Low Blood Pressure
AAFP — Orthostatic Hypotension

Flashcards
What does hypotension describe?01-foundations / diseases-conditionsAnswerBlood pressure abnormally low for the person's circumstances.
Why might hypotension cause fainting?02-mechanisms / diseases-conditionsAnswerInsufficient blood flow to the brain.

diseases-and-conditions/incontinence.title: Incontinence
diseases-and-conditions/incontinence.content:
What is it?
Involuntary loss of bladder or bowel control.

Urinary incontinence: involuntary leakage of urine.
Fecal incontinence: involuntary passage of stool.

Why does it matter?

Increases risk of moisture-associated skin damage.
Can affect dignity, comfort, and independence.
May contribute to infection risk and social isolation.

What should I look for?

Urine or stool leakage.
Changes in elimination patterns.
Skin irritation or maceration.
Discomfort, embarrassment, or distress.

What should I do?

Provide timely hygiene and skin protection.
Encourage independence and scheduled toileting as directed.
Maintain privacy and dignity.
Report new or worsening incontinence or associated symptoms.

Related

Incontinence Care
Perineal Care
Skin Integrity & Breakdown Prevention
Skin Findings & Terminology

Sources

NIDDK — Bladder Control Problems (Urinary Incontinence)
NIDDK — Bowel Control Problems (Fecal Incontinence)
NIDDK — Treatment of Fecal Incontinence

Flashcards
What is urinary incontinence?01-foundations / diseases-conditionsAnswerInvoluntary leakage of urine.
What two important consequences can incontinence have?01-foundations / diseases-conditionsAnswerSkin moisture damage and loss of comfort or dignity.

diseases-and-conditions/latex-allergy.title: Latex Allergy
diseases-and-conditions/latex-allergy.content:
What is it?
An adverse reaction to natural rubber latex, found in some gloves, medical equipment, and other products.
Types of reactions:

Irritant Contact Dermatitis: Dry, itchy, irritated skin; not a true allergy.
Delayed Allergic Contact Dermatitis: Itchy rash, redness, or blisters, typically developing 24–96 hours after exposure.
Immediate Latex Allergy: Rapid allergic reaction, potentially causing hives, wheezing, or anaphylaxis.

Why does it matter?

Repeated exposure can contribute to sensitization.
Severe immediate reactions can be life-threatening.
Latex may be present in multiple healthcare products.

What should I look for?

Itching, redness, or rash after contact.
Hives or swelling.
Wheezing, breathing difficulty, or signs of anaphylaxis.

What should I do?

Check documented allergies and facility precautions.
Use approved latex-free equipment when indicated.
Stop exposure and report suspected reactions.
Activate emergency response immediately for severe symptoms.

Related

Occupational Exposure & Response
Standard Precautions
Emergency Preparedness & Response

Sources

CDC/NIOSH — Preventing Latex Allergies

Flashcards
What signs could indicate an immediate severe latex reaction?03-application / diseases-conditionsAnswerHives, wheezing, breathing problems, or anaphylaxis.
What is the distinction between irritant dermatitis and latex allergy?02-mechanisms / diseases-conditionsAnswerIrritant dermatitis is not itself an immune allergy.

diseases-and-conditions/multidrug-resist.title: Multidrug-Resistant Organisms (MDROs)
diseases-and-conditions/multidrug-resist.content:
What is it?
MDROs are microorganisms resistant to treatment with multiple antimicrobial medications.
Common examples:

MRSA: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
VRE: Vancomycin-resistant enterococci.
Colonization vs. Infection:
Colonization: Organism is present without causing illness.
Infection: Organism causes tissue damage or illness.

Why does it matter?

Resistant infections can be difficult to treat.
Vulnerable residents may develop serious complications.
MDROs can spread through contact with contaminated hands, equipment, and surfaces.
Risk factors:
Recent or prolonged antibiotic exposure.
Extended healthcare stays.
Wounds or indwelling medical devices.
Weakened immune system or chronic illness.

What should I look for?
MRSA:

May colonize skin or the nose without symptoms.
Infection may cause redness, swelling, pain, or drainage.
VRE:
May colonize the gastrointestinal tract without symptoms.
Can cause urinary, wound, or bloodstream infections.
General concerns:
Fever or new signs of infection.
Wound changes or unusual drainage.
New changes in resident condition.

What should I do?

Follow required infection-control precautions.
Perform hand hygiene consistently.
Use PPE according to facility instructions.
Clean and disinfect shared equipment appropriately.
Report concerning changes to the nurse.

Related

Enhanced Barrier Precautions
Transmission-Based Precautions
Standard Precautions
Chain of Infection

Sources

CNA Module 6 — Drug-Resistant Infections
CDC — MDRO Prevention Guidance

Flashcards
What is an MDRO?01-foundations / diseases-conditionsAnswerA microorganism resistant to multiple antimicrobial drugs.
Why do MDROs affect precautions?02-mechanisms / diseases-conditionsAnswerThey can spread in healthcare settings and complicate treatment.

diseases-and-conditions/orthostatic-hypo.title: Orthostatic Hypotension
diseases-and-conditions/orthostatic-hypo.content:
What is it?
A drop in blood pressure that occurs when a person changes to an upright position, especially from lying down to standing.

Blood temporarily pools in the lower body after standing.
Normally, the body compensates by increasing vascular tone and adjusting heart rate.
In orthostatic hypotension, this compensation may be inadequate.
Clinical definition: A sustained decrease in systolic blood pressure of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure of at least 10 mmHg within three minutes of standing or head-up tilt.

Why does it matter?

May reduce blood flow to the brain.
Can cause dizziness, fainting, and falls.
May limit safe transfers and ambulation.
Possible contributors:
Dehydration or blood loss.
Prolonged bed rest.
Certain medications.
Autonomic nervous system dysfunction.

What should I look for?
Common symptoms after sitting or standing:

Dizziness or lightheadedness.
Weakness or faintness.
Blurred vision.
Nausea.
Sweating or unusual pallor.
Syncope (fainting).
Important: Some residents may have orthostatic blood pressure changes without noticeable symptoms.

What should I do?

Follow the care plan for mobility assistance.
Help the resident change positions gradually.
Use Dangling at Bedside when indicated.
Observe tolerance before standing or walking.
If symptoms occur, help the resident into a safe position.
Do not continue ambulation while the resident is dizzy or faint.
Notify the nurse about new or worsening symptoms.
Measure positional blood pressure only when directed and trained.
Urgent: Loss of consciousness, chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, or other concerning symptoms require immediate escalation.

Related

Blood Pressure
Hypotension
Dehydration
Blood Loss
Dangling at Bedside
Fall Risk
Assisting with Ambulation

Sources

CNA Module 5 — Mobility & Transfers
CNA Module 12 — Emergency Procedures
AAFP — Orthostatic Hypotension

Flashcards
What is the clinical BP-drop definition of orthostatic hypotension?02-mechanisms / diseases-conditionsAnswerAt least 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes upright.
What should be done if standing causes dizziness?03-application / diseases-conditionsAnswerHelp the resident safely sit or lie down and report symptoms.

diseases-and-conditions/ostomies-and-div.title: Ostomies and Diversions
diseases-and-conditions/ostomies-and-div.content:
What is it?
An ostomy is a surgically created diversion that allows intestinal contents or urine to leave the body through an alternative pathway.
A stoma is the surgically created opening through which output passes.
Common Types

























TypeStructureOutputColostomyColon (large intestine)Stool; consistency varies with locationIleostomyIleum (small intestine)Typically liquid to pasty intestinal outputUrostomyUrinary tract diversion, often using a segment of intestineUrine, often draining continuously
Most conventional ostomies use an external collection pouch. Some diversions use internal reservoirs or other collection methods.
Why does it matter?

Allows elimination when the normal intestinal or urinary pathway has been diverted.
Requires attention to stoma appearance, output, and surrounding skin.
Leakage can cause skin irritation and breakdown.
Ileostomy output can cause significant fluid and electrolyte losses, increasing dehydration risk.
Ostomies can affect body image, comfort, and independence.

What should I look for?
Stoma and Skin:

Stoma appearance, typically moist and pink to red.
New discoloration, swelling, bleeding, or unusual pain.
Redness, irritation, or breakdown of surrounding skin.
Leakage or poor pouch fit.

Output:

Expected urine or intestinal output according to ostomy type.
Unexpectedly high, low, or absent output.
Unusual changes in consistency, appearance, or odor.
Associated abdominal pain, distention, nausea, or vomiting.

Urgent Concerns:

A stoma becoming dark purple, gray, or black.
Significant or uncontrolled bleeding.
Sudden absence of intestinal output with severe pain, distention, or vomiting.
High-volume watery ileostomy output with signs of dehydration.

Report urgent findings immediately according to facility emergency procedures.
What should I do?

Follow the resident’s individualized ostomy care plan.
Observe the stoma, surrounding skin, and output during assigned care.
Assist with pouch emptying only when trained and authorized.
Maintain hygiene and protect surrounding skin.
Record output when required.
Report new skin damage, changes in output, leakage, or discomfort.
Encourage resident independence and preserve privacy and dignity.
Do not independently insert devices into a stoma, change treatment plans, or diagnose complications.

Related

Ostomy Care
Elimination Care
Incontinence Care
Skin Integrity & Breakdown Prevention
Dehydration
Measuring Intake & Output

Sources

NIDDK — Types of Ostomy Surgery of the Bowel
NIDDK — Complications of Ostomy Surgery
NIDDK — After Ostomy Surgery
WOCN — Peristomal Skin Assessment Guide
Resident-specific ostomy care plan and facility procedure (verify at clinical site)

Flashcards
How does a colostomy differ from an ileostomy?03-application / diseases-conditionsAnswerColostomy diverts colon output; ileostomy diverts small-intestine output.
What is a urostomy used for?01-foundations / diseases-conditionsAnswerDiverting urine through a surgically created opening.
Why is dehydration a particular concern with high-output ileostomies?02-mechanisms / diseases-conditionsAnswerLarge fluid and electrolyte losses.
What concerning change in stoma color requires immediate reporting?03-application / diseases-conditionsAnswerA stoma becoming dark purple, gray, or black.

diseases-and-conditions/pressure-injurie.title: Pressure Injuries
diseases-and-conditions/pressure-injurie.content:
What is it?
Localized damage to the skin and underlying tissue caused by prolonged or intense pressure, often combined with shear.

Commonly occurs over bony prominences or beneath medical devices.
Previously called pressure ulcers, bedsores, or decubitus ulcers.

Why does it matter?

Sustained pressure can impair local blood flow and damage tissue.
Injuries may progress into deeper structures and increase infection risk.
Prevention requires pressure redistribution, skin care, nutrition, and mobility support.

What should I look for?
Pressure Injury Stages

































StageCharacteristicsStage 1Intact skin with persistent, nonblanchable redness or localized color change. May also have temperature, firmness, or sensation changes.Stage 2Partial-thickness skin loss exposing the dermis. Pink/red moist wound bed or a serum-filled blister. No visible fat, slough, or eschar.Stage 3Full-thickness skin loss; subcutaneous fat may be visible. Tunneling, undermining, or slough may occur. No exposed muscle, tendon, or bone.Stage 4Full-thickness skin and tissue loss with exposed or directly palpable deeper structures such as fascia, muscle, tendon, or bone.UnstageableFull-thickness injury where slough or eschar obscures the extent of tissue loss.Deep Tissue Pressure InjuryPersistent deep red, maroon, or purple discoloration, or a blood-filled blister suggesting underlying tissue damage.
Blanching

Blanchable: Redness temporarily lightens when pressure is applied.
Nonblanchable: Redness persists despite pressure being applied.
Darker skin may show changes in color, warmth, firmness, or sensation rather than obvious redness.

Common Locations


Sacrum and coccyx.
Heels and ankles.
Hips and sitting bones.
Elbows and shoulder blades.
Back of head and ears.
Areas beneath medical devices.

Risk Factors

Immobility or prolonged pressure.
Friction and shear.
Incontinence and excessive moisture.
Reduced sensation or consciousness.
Poor nutrition or hydration.
Fragile skin or poor circulation.
Increased local heat and humidity (microclimate).

What should I do?

Observe skin during routine care, especially pressure points.
Report new redness, discoloration, blisters, open areas, or pain promptly.
Follow individualized repositioning and pressure-relief schedules.
Use prescribed pillows, support surfaces, and offloading devices.
Keep skin appropriately clean and dry.
Minimize friction and shear during transfers and repositioning.
Encourage mobility and adequate nutrition within the care plan.
Avoid massaging reddened pressure areas.
Follow nursing instructions for skin products and wound protection.
CNA Scope: Observe and report skin changes. Formal pressure injury staging and wound treatment are performed by appropriately qualified clinical staff.

Related

Skin Integrity & Breakdown Prevention
Repositioning in Bed
Patient Positions
Limited Mobility
Skin Findings & Terminology
Integumentary System

Sources

CNA Module 8 — Patient Care Skills
NPIAP — Pressure Injury Stages
AHRQ — Pressure Injury Staging

Flashcards
What characterizes a stage 1 pressure injury?01-foundations / diseases-conditionsAnswerIntact skin with nonblanchable erythema or a comparable change in darker skin.
What is an unstageable pressure injury?01-foundations / diseases-conditionsAnswerDepth is obscured by slough or eschar.
Who determines pressure-injury staging?03-application / diseases-conditionsAnswerQualified licensed clinicians, not CNAs independently.

patient-care/care-of-residents-with-medi.filePath: Patient Care/Care of Residents With Medical Tubing.md
patient-care/care-of-residents-with-medi.title: Care of Residents With Medical Tubing
patient-care/care-of-residents-with-medi.content:
Patient Needs
Some residents rely on medical tubing to deliver fluids, medications, or supplemental oxygen.
The CNA helps maintain comfort, mobility, safety, and proper positioning while protecting the equipment from accidental disruption.
What Should I Assess?
Intravenous (IV) Therapy

Tubing pulling or becoming caught during movement.
Redness, swelling, leakage, or bleeding at the IV site.
Complaints of pain or discomfort.
IV equipment interfering with transfers or dressing.

Supplemental Oxygen

Acute conditions:

Asthma attack, trauma.
Highly concentrated


Chronic conditions:

COPD or Emphysema
Oxygen typically between 1-6 L/min


Nasal cannula or mask position.
Visible damage, disconnections, or kinks.
Dryness, irritation, or bleeding around the nose.
Skin redness or breakdown behind the ears.
Changes in breathing effort or respiratory distress.
Ensure flow rate is alongisde resident’s care plan, and adequate amount of oxygen is in portable tank.

Enteral Feeding Tubes (Gastrostomy & Nasogastric)

Visible pulling, kinks, displacement, or accidental disconnection.
Redness, swelling, leakage, drainage, or irritation near a gastrostomy insertion site.
Discomfort, coughing, gagging, vomiting, or breathing difficulty.
Tubing that interferes with positioning, transfers, or hygiene.
Residents will be in Fowler’s position at all time.

Report concerning findings promptly. Do not independently assess internal tube placement.
How Do I Provide Care?
Supporting Residents With IV Tubing

Keep the IV pole and tubing safely positioned during movement.
Prevent pulling during transfers, ambulation, and dressing.
Use appropriate gowns or clothing accommodations.
Follow the nurse’s instructions when changing clothing around IV equipment.
Report IV site concerns promptly.
Do not disconnect, adjust, or manipulate an IV infusion outside authorized duties.

Supporting Residents Receiving Oxygen

Confirm equipment and prescribed setup against the care plan, within assigned responsibilities.
Check for visibly displaced or kinked tubing.
Ensure tubing does not create a tripping hazard.
Observe breathing comfort and skin condition.
Follow approved procedures for portable oxygen equipment.
Encourage a comfortable position that supports breathing.
Reinforce coughing, deep breathing, or incentive spirometry instructions already taught by the nurse when directed.

Supporting Residents With Feeding Tubes

Protect tubing from accidental pulling during bathing, dressing, positioning, and transfers.
Follow the resident’s individualized positioning and aspiration precautions.
Observe the visible insertion site and surrounding skin during routine care as appropriate.
Provide routine hygiene within assigned duties.
Request nursing assistance for suspected tube displacement, leakage, blockage, or equipment problems.
Do not independently insert, reposition, flush, or administer feeding, water, or medication through a feeding tube.
Do not attempt to restart feeding equipment or determine tube placement independently.

Safety & Precautions
Oxygen Safety

Oxygen supports combustion.
Keep oxygen equipment away from smoking, flames, sparks, and heat sources.
Follow oxygen equipment safety rules.
Never change a prescribed oxygen flow rate independently.
Do not assume all residents require the same flow rate.
Follow the care plan for oxygen-related skin protection.

IV Safety

Do not alter IV pump settings or infusion rates.
Avoid disconnecting IV tubing.
Prevent tension on vascular access devices.
Seek nursing assistance before transfers if equipment management is uncertain.

What Should I Report?

New or worsening shortness of breath.
Chest pain or severe respiratory distress.
Oxygen equipment problems or discrepancies.
IV site redness, swelling, bleeding, or pain.
Accidental dislodgement or suspected device failure.
Skin breakdown associated with tubing.
Emergency: Severe respiratory distress or sudden deterioration requires immediate escalation.

Related

Recognizing Patient Distress
Vital Signs
Skin Integrity & Breakdown Prevention
Safe Patient Transfers
Assisting with Ambulation
Standard Precautions

Sources

CNA Module 9B — Care of Patients With Tubing
Facility IV equipment and oxygen therapy policies
California CDPH — Nurse Assistant Training Program Skills Checklist (CDPH 276A)
AHRQ — A Resident With a PEG Tube
CDC — Oxygen Therapy and Fire Safety
Facility enteral-feeding, IV, and oxygen-equipment policies (verify at clinical site)

Flashcards
What must a CNA not independently change on oxygen equipment?03-application / patient-careAnswerThe prescribed oxygen flow rate.
What signs at an IV site must be reported?03-application / patient-careAnswerRedness, swelling, leakage, bleeding, or pain.
What should a CNA do if a resident's feeding tube appears displaced?03-application / patient-careAnswerStop potentially disruptive care, protect the tubing, and notify the nurse promptly.
May a CNA independently administer formula, water, or medications through a feeding tube?03-application / patient-careAnswerNo. Refer feeding-tube administration to authorized clinical personnel.

patient-care/caring-for-residents-with-c.filePath: Patient Care/Caring for Residents with Cancer.md
patient-care/caring-for-residents-with-c.title: Caring for Residents with Cancer
patient-care/caring-for-residents-with-c.content:
Overview
Residents living with cancer may experience physical symptoms, treatment-related complications, emotional distress, and changes in their ability to perform daily activities.
Person-centered cancer care focuses on supporting comfort, safety, dignity, independence, and the resident’s individual goals.
Cancer experiences vary widely. Some residents continue their usual activities during treatment, while others need significant assistance.
Core Principle: Care for the person, not just the diagnosis. Follow the individualized care plan and report changes promptly.
Supporting Residents During Cancer Treatment
Fatigue
Cancer-related fatigue is persistent physical, emotional, or cognitive tiredness that may not improve fully with rest.
Possible contributors include cancer itself, anemia, treatment, disrupted sleep, poor intake, and emotional distress.
CNA Considerations:

Allow additional time for ADLs.
Schedule care around rest periods when possible.
Encourage permitted activity while respecting the resident’s limitations.
Help prioritize essential activities.
Observe changes in energy and functional ability.
Report new or worsening fatigue.

Pain
Cancer-related pain may result from tumors, inflammation, surgery, nerve damage, or treatment effects.
Pain can interfere with sleep, movement, appetite, and emotional well-being.
CNA Considerations:

Ask about pain using the facility’s approved approach.
Observe verbal and nonverbal signs of discomfort.
Assist with positioning and comfort measures according to the care plan.
Report uncontrolled, new, or worsening pain.
Reassess comfort and communicate observations to nursing staff.

Do not independently change pain medication or treatment plans.
Nausea, Vomiting & Poor Appetite
Cancer or its treatments may affect appetite, taste, smell, swallowing, and digestion.
CNA Considerations:

Offer assistance with meals as appropriate.
Follow prescribed food textures, diet instructions, and fluid restrictions.
Provide oral hygiene and comfort measures.
Record intake and output when assigned.
Observe vomiting, poor intake, and dehydration signs.
Report persistent symptoms.

Mouth Sores (Mucositis)
Certain cancer treatments can cause inflammation or sores in the mouth and throat.
This may make eating, swallowing, or speaking painful.
CNA Considerations:

Assist with gentle oral care according to the care plan.
Report sores, bleeding, discomfort, or difficulty swallowing.
Avoid irritating tissues during mouth care.
Follow prescribed oral-care products and restrictions.

Hair Loss & Changes in Appearance
Some treatments cause hair loss, skin changes, swelling, scars, or body-image concerns.
CNA Considerations:

Ask about personal preferences for grooming.
Handle sensitive skin and scalp gently.
Respect privacy during bathing and dressing.
Do not assume appearance changes are emotionally distressing to every resident.
Offer support without making unsolicited comments about appearance.

Infection & Bleeding Precautions
Cancer and its treatments may affect bone marrow and immune function.
Hazardous Medication Exposure Precautions
Some cancer treatments involve hazardous medications. Drug residues may be present in a resident’s body fluids or waste for a period after treatment.

Follow facility-specific procedures for handling contaminated linens, body fluids, spills, and waste.
Use the PPE required by the medication-specific and facility protocols.
Ask the nurse when additional handling precautions are needed.
Do not assume every cancer treatment requires the same precautions.

Neutropenia
Neutropenia is an abnormally low neutrophil count, increasing vulnerability to infection.

Perform consistent hand hygiene.
Follow the resident’s prescribed infection-prevention measures.
Report fever, chills, new cough, or other signs of infection promptly.
Avoid exposing vulnerable residents to people with contagious illnesses according to facility guidance.

Important: Fever during neutropenia can indicate a life-threatening infection, even when other symptoms are mild.
Thrombocytopenia
Thrombocytopenia is a reduced platelet count, increasing bleeding risk.

Handle residents gently during transfers and personal care.
Observe unusual bruising, petechiae, or bleeding.
Follow prescribed bleeding precautions.
Report blood in urine or stool, nosebleeds, or bleeding gums.

Anemia
Anemia is a reduction in red blood cells or hemoglobin, potentially decreasing oxygen delivery.
Possible symptoms include:

Fatigue.
Weakness.
Dizziness.
Pallor.
Shortness of breath during activity.

Observe and report significant changes, and provide assistance with mobility when appropriate.
Mobility, Skin & Daily Living
Cancer or cancer treatment may cause weakness, pain, neuropathy, or reduced endurance.
CNA Considerations

Assess the level of assistance described in the care plan.
Encourage independence where safe.
Assist with walking and transfers using appropriate equipment.
Follow fall-prevention precautions.
Report new numbness, weakness, or balance changes.
Observe skin integrity, especially in residents with immobility, edema, or poor nutritional intake.
Follow prescribed precautions for surgical sites, radiation-treated skin, and medical devices.

Important: Do not independently apply topical products to radiation treatment areas, manipulate oncology devices, or perform procedures outside authorized CNA duties.
Emotional & Social Support
Residents with cancer may experience uncertainty, fear, frustration, sadness, or concerns about independence.
They may also feel hopeful, emotionally stable, or focused on ordinary daily activities.
Avoid assuming how a resident feels based solely on their diagnosis.
Therapeutic Communication

Listen without judgment.
Ask what matters most to the resident.
Respect preferences regarding discussion of illness.
Avoid unsolicited reassurance or predictions about outcomes.
Maintain normal social interaction when desired.
Support privacy and independence.
Report significant changes in mood, behavior, or coping.

Helpful Communication Examples





























SituationSupportive ResponseResident expresses fear about treatmentListen, acknowledge their concern, and offer to connect them with the nurseResident does not want to discuss cancerRespect their preference and offer ordinary conversationResident feels frustrated about needing assistanceOffer choices and encourage participation in tasks they can performFamily asks about prognosisRefer medical questions to the nurse or authorized clinicianResident expresses concern about painListen, observe, and report the concern promptly
Palliative Care
Palliative care is specialized care that focuses on relieving suffering and improving quality of life during serious illness.
It can be provided alongside surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, and other cancer treatments.
Palliative care may address:

Pain and other physical symptoms.
Nausea, fatigue, and breathlessness.
Emotional and psychological distress.
Social and spiritual concerns.
Communication about goals of care.
Support for caregivers and family members.

Palliative Care Goals

Improve comfort.
Reduce symptom burden.
Preserve dignity and autonomy.
Support meaningful daily activities.
Align treatment and care with the person’s values.

Palliative Care vs. Hospice

























Palliative CareHospice CareCan begin at diagnosis of serious illnessTypically provided when a terminal illness is expected to be in its final monthsMay be given alongside curative treatmentFocuses on comfort rather than treatment intended to cure the terminal illnessSupports quality of life throughout illnessProvides comprehensive end-of-life supportNot limited to dying patientsIntended for people approaching the end of life
Important: Palliative care is not equivalent to giving up on treatment.
Supporting Residents Receiving Palliative or Hospice Care

Prioritize comfort and resident preferences.
Follow individualized positioning, hygiene, and mobility plans.
Observe and report pain, anxiety, agitation, breathlessness, and other symptoms.
Provide frequent gentle mouth care when appropriate.
Respect preferences for visitors, quiet, conversation, and spiritual support.
Avoid forcing food or fluids; follow the resident’s goals and care plan.
Support privacy, dignity, and family involvement as authorized.
Report uncontrolled symptoms promptly.

Do not independently decide to withhold or initiate treatment. Follow documented orders, the care plan, and nursing direction.
Patient Rights & Autonomy
Residents living with cancer retain their rights to:

Privacy and confidentiality.
Respectful, nondiscriminatory care.
Participation in care decisions.
Information about treatment options from qualified clinicians.
Consent to or refusal of treatment within applicable legal requirements.
Pain and symptom assessment.
Personal dignity and independence.
Appropriate family or support-person involvement according to their preferences and authorizations.

Advance Care Planning
Advance Directives: Legal documents that communicate healthcare wishes or identify someone authorized to make healthcare decisions when the person cannot.
Goals of Care: The treatments and outcomes that matter most to the resident, such as longevity, function, comfort, or time with family.
Code Status: Medical orders specifying resuscitation preferences.
CNA Role: Know where to obtain relevant care instructions, follow authorized orders and emergency procedures, and refer questions about treatment decisions to qualified staff.
When to Report

New or worsening pain.
Fever, chills, or signs of infection.
New bruising or bleeding.
Persistent nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Poor oral intake or dehydration.
New mouth sores or swallowing difficulty.
Sudden or significant functional decline.
New confusion or behavioral changes.
New weakness, numbness, or difficulty walking.
Uncontrolled symptoms during palliative care.
Concerns about dignity, confidentiality, or treatment preferences.

Emergency signs: Severe breathing difficulty, uncontrolled bleeding, seizures, sudden neurological deficits, or unresponsiveness require immediate attention according to the resident’s orders, goals of care, and facility emergency protocols.
Study Notes

Cancer
Lymphatic & Immune System
Patient Rights

Clinical Connections

Therapeutic Communication: Listening and respecting preferences support the resident’s well-being.
Recognizing Patient Distress: Cancer complications and treatment effects may require urgent recognition.
Standard Precautions: Neutropenia and other conditions increase infection vulnerability.
Assisting with Feeding: Nausea, mucositis, and appetite changes may affect nutritional intake.
Fluid Balance: Vomiting, diarrhea, and poor intake can affect hydration.
Skin Integrity & Breakdown Prevention: Reduced mobility and treatment effects can increase skin vulnerability.
Fall Risk: Weakness, anemia, and neuropathy can increase fall risk.
Patient Rights: Comfort, dignity, privacy, and informed choices remain essential.

Questions

How does cancer-related fatigue differ from ordinary tiredness?
What symptoms might indicate uncontrolled pain?
Why can chemotherapy increase infection risk?
Why does thrombocytopenia increase bleeding risk?
How does anemia affect activity tolerance?
What should a CNA observe when assisting a resident with mucositis?
What is palliative care?
How does palliative care differ from hospice?
How can a CNA preserve autonomy during serious illness?
What symptoms should be reported immediately?

Sources

National Cancer Institute — Side Effects of Cancer Treatment
National Cancer Institute — Palliative Care in Cancer
National Cancer Institute — Coping with Cancer
National Cancer Institute — Cancer Fatigue
National Cancer Institute — Infection and Neutropenia
Medicare — Hospice Care

Flashcards
What is the primary goal of person-centered cancer care?01-foundations / patient-careAnswerSupport comfort, safety, dignity, independence, and individual goals.
What is cancer-related fatigue?01-foundations / patient-careAnswerPersistent exhaustion that may not improve fully with rest.
What should a CNA do when cancer pain worsens?03-application / patient-careAnswerObserve, report promptly, and follow prescribed comfort measures.
What is mucositis?01-foundations / patient-careAnswerInflammation or sores affecting mucous membranes, often after cancer treatment.
What is neutropenia?01-foundations / patient-careAnswerAn abnormally low neutrophil count, increasing infection risk.
Why is fever concerning in a resident with neutropenia?03-application / patient-careAnswerIt may indicate a life-threatening infection.
What is thrombocytopenia?01-foundations / patient-careAnswerA low platelet count that increases bleeding risk.
What is anemia?01-foundations / patient-careAnswerReduced red blood cells or hemoglobin, potentially impairing oxygen delivery.
What common cancer treatment side effects may affect eating?02-mechanisms / patient-careAnswerNausea, taste changes, mouth sores, and poor appetite.
How can a CNA support a resident with cancer-related fatigue?03-application / patient-careAnswerAllow rest, assist with activities, and encourage permitted independence.
What is the primary goal of palliative care?01-foundations / patient-careAnswerRelieve suffering and improve quality of life.
Can palliative care accompany curative cancer treatment?01-foundations / patient-careAnswerYes. It can begin at any point during serious illness.
How does hospice differ from general palliative care?02-mechanisms / patient-careAnswerHospice focuses on end-of-life comfort when cure is no longer the goal.
What is an advance directive?01-foundations / patient-careAnswerA legal document describing healthcare wishes or designating a decision-maker.
What should a CNA do if a resident reports uncontrolled symptoms?03-application / patient-careAnswerReport promptly to the nurse and follow the individualized care plan.
How should a CNA discuss prognosis with a resident's family?03-application / patient-careAnswerRefer medical prognosis questions to authorized clinicians.

patient-care/caring-for-residents-with-h.filePath: Patient Care/Caring for Residents with HIV and AIDS.md
patient-care/caring-for-residents-with-h.title: Caring for Residents with HIV and AIDS
patient-care/caring-for-residents-with-h.content:
Overview
Residents living with HIV or AIDS deserve the same quality of care, respect, privacy, independence, and dignity as every other resident.
HIV is a manageable chronic condition for many people receiving effective treatment.
A resident’s HIV status should not change how healthcare workers treat them personally or whether they receive appropriate care.
Core Principle: Provide individualized, compassionate care while following Standard Precautions and respecting confidentiality.
Patient Rights
Equal Treatment & Non-Discrimination
People living with HIV are protected against discrimination under applicable federal and California laws.
Relevant federal protections include:

Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA): Prohibits disability-based discrimination in covered settings.
Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act: Protects people with disabilities in federally funded programs.
Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act: Prohibits specified discrimination in covered health programs and activities.

In nursing facilities and other healthcare settings, residents must not be denied appropriate care simply because they have HIV.
CNA Responsibilities:

Provide the same standard of respectful care.
Do not refuse ordinary care because of HIV status.
Do not stigmatize, ridicule, isolate socially, or shame residents.
Report discriminatory conduct according to facility procedures.

Privacy & Confidentiality
HIV status is protected medical information.
Federal HIPAA requirements and California confidentiality laws govern when protected health information can be accessed, used, or disclosed.
CNA Responsibilities:

Discuss HIV status only with authorized personnel who need the information for permitted care-related purposes.
Do not disclose HIV status to other residents, visitors, friends, or unauthorized family members.
Avoid discussing diagnoses in hallways, elevators, dining areas, or other public spaces.
Protect charts, electronic records, and other confidential information.
Refer requests for disclosure to the appropriate nurse or authorized professional.

Important: Confidentiality is not absolute. Certain legally authorized disclosures, including public-health reporting, can occur without ordinary patient authorization. CNAs should follow established procedures rather than independently deciding when disclosure is permitted.
Dignity & Autonomy
Living with HIV does not eliminate a resident’s rights to:

Privacy during bathing, dressing, and personal care.
Participation in care decisions.
Respectful communication.
Visitors and social relationships, subject to ordinary facility rules and safeguards.
Appropriate opportunities for independence.
Freedom from harassment and discrimination.
Consensual intimacy consistent with applicable resident protections and safety considerations.

The resident is a person with individual preferences, relationships, beliefs, and goals—not simply a diagnosis.
Stigma & Respectful Communication
HIV-related stigma involves negative attitudes, stereotypes, or discriminatory treatment toward people living with HIV.
Stigma may discourage people from seeking treatment, disclosing concerns to trusted clinicians, or accessing support.
Person-Centered Language





























AvoidPreferHIV-infected personPerson living with HIVAIDS victimPerson living with AIDSClean / Dirty HIV testNegative / Positive HIV testDangerous patientResident with specific care or infection-control needsBlaming someone for acquiring HIVNeutral, nonjudgmental discussion
Supportive Communication

Listen without judgment.
Avoid assumptions about how someone acquired HIV.
Ask permission before discussing sensitive topics.
Respect the resident’s preferences about discussing their diagnosis.
Offer privacy for personal conversations.
Report concerns about stigma, harassment, or discrimination.

Infection Prevention During Resident Care
Standard Precautions
Standard Precautions apply to all residents, regardless of HIV status.

Perform hand hygiene.
Wear gloves when contact with blood or potentially infectious body fluids is anticipated.
Use gowns, masks, and eye protection when the task presents an appropriate exposure risk.
Handle soiled linens and equipment safely.
Follow approved sharps and exposure-prevention procedures.

Important: HIV alone does not require an isolation room, negative-pressure room, or routine additional Transmission-Based Precautions.
If a resident has another infection requiring additional precautions, follow the appropriate isolation plan for that condition.
See Standard Precautions and Transmission-Based Precautions.
Supporting Physical & Emotional Well-Being
Daily Care

Assist with ADLs according to the care plan.
Encourage independence and respect personal preferences.
Support adequate food and fluid intake.
Observe for fatigue, weakness, fever, unexplained weight loss, or changes from baseline.
Report concerning skin changes, mouth discomfort, persistent cough, or new illness symptoms.
Support prescribed routines and appointments within CNA responsibilities.

Emotional & Social Support
Residents may experience anxiety, fear of disclosure, isolation, discrimination, or concerns about relationships.
Helpful approaches include:

Creating a welcoming and nonjudgmental environment.
Respecting the resident’s control over personal information.
Encouraging appropriate social interaction when desired.
Reporting emotional distress or withdrawal that represents a change from baseline.
Connecting concerns to the nurse or care team.

Do not assume every person living with HIV experiences emotional distress or requires special psychosocial support.
Common CNA Scenarios





































SituationAppropriate ResponseA resident tells you privately they have HIVListen respectfully; protect confidentiality and share information only when permitted and necessary for careAnother resident asks whether someone has AIDSDo not confirm or deny another person’s diagnosis; redirect respectfullyA coworker refuses to provide routine care because of HIVFollow facility procedures and report discriminatory or unsafe conductA resident with HIV needs bathing or toileting assistanceProvide routine care using Standard Precautions and task-appropriate PPEA resident develops persistent fever, cough, or significant functional declinePromptly report changes to the nurseYou experience a needlestick or blood exposurePerform appropriate first aid, report immediately, and seek urgent occupational health evaluationA visitor asks about the resident’s HIV medicationsDo not disclose protected information; refer to authorized staff
When to Report

Suspected discrimination, harassment, or mistreatment.
Possible breaches of confidential information.
Refusal or withholding of appropriate resident care.
Sudden physical or behavioral changes.
New signs of infection or functional decline.
Significant emotional distress or concerning withdrawal.
Potential occupational exposure to blood or infectious material.

Emergency signs: Severe respiratory distress, loss of consciousness, or other acute medical emergencies require immediate emergency response, regardless of HIV status.
Study Notes

HIV & AIDS
Patient Rights
Standard Precautions
Transmission-Based Precautions

Clinical Connections

Patient Rights: Privacy, dignity, autonomy, and freedom from discrimination are fundamental care principles.
Therapeutic Communication: Respectful communication helps establish trust.
Abuse, Neglect & Rights Violations: Discriminatory mistreatment or withholding appropriate care may raise rights and safety concerns.
Standard Precautions: Universal application of precautions protects residents and staff.
Recognizing Patient Distress: Report new or concerning clinical changes promptly.
HIV & AIDS: Explains HIV transmission, testing, treatment, and prevention.

Questions

What rights do residents living with HIV have?
Why is HIV status considered confidential medical information?
How should a CNA respond to another resident asking about someone’s HIV status?
What is HIV-related stigma?
How does person-centered language support dignity?
Are additional isolation precautions required solely because a resident has HIV?
How should a CNA respond to workplace discrimination?
How can a CNA support independence and emotional well-being?
What should happen after an occupational blood exposure?

Sources

HIV.gov — Civil Rights
HHS — HIV Civil Rights and Health Information Privacy
California — State Health Information Guidance, Sharing HIV/AIDS Information
CDC — Standard Precautions
HIV.gov — Talking About Your HIV Status

Flashcards
What is the primary principle of caring for a resident with HIV?01-foundations / patient-careAnswerProvide respectful, individualized, nondiscriminatory care.
Does HIV status alone justify additional isolation precautions?03-application / patient-careAnswerNo. Standard Precautions apply unless another condition requires additional precautions.
Can a CNA disclose a resident's HIV status to another resident?03-application / patient-careAnswerNo. HIV status is confidential medical information.
What federal law protects people with HIV against disability discrimination?03-application / patient-careAnswerAmericans with Disabilities Act (ADA).
How should a CNA respond to a coworker discriminating against a resident with HIV?03-application / patient-careAnswerReport the discriminatory behavior according to facility procedures.
What is HIV-related stigma?01-foundations / patient-careAnswerNegative attitudes or discriminatory treatment toward people living with HIV.
What is a respectful alternative to calling someone an AIDS victim?01-foundations / patient-careAnswerPerson living with HIV or AIDS.
Should a CNA use gloves for routine social contact with a resident who has HIV?03-application / patient-careAnswerNo. Gloves are based on exposure risk, not HIV status alone.
How should a CNA respond to questions about another resident's HIV status?03-application / patient-careAnswerProtect confidentiality and do not confirm or disclose the diagnosis.
What should a CNA do after an occupational blood exposure?03-application / patient-careAnswerPerform appropriate first aid, report immediately, and obtain urgent evaluation.

patient-care/communication-and-psychosoc.title: Communication Accommodations
patient-care/communication-and-psychosoc.content:
Patient Needs
Adapt communication to the resident’s sensory, speech, cognitive, and individual needs while maintaining dignity and independence.
What Should I Assess?

Hearing or vision limitations.
Difficulty speaking or understanding language.
Preferred communication methods.
Need for assistive devices or interpretation.

How Do I Provide Care?
Hearing Impairment

Face the resident at eye level.
Speak clearly at a natural pace and pitch.
Keep your mouth visible.
Reduce background noise.
Use hearing aids or written communication as appropriate.
Speech & Language Impairment
Expressive Aphasia: Difficulty producing language; allow extra time and use communication aids.
Receptive Aphasia: Difficulty understanding language; use short, clear statements and confirm understanding.
Use picture boards, writing, or assistive technology when appropriate.
Vision Impairment
Identify yourself when entering.
Explain before touching or moving objects.
Give specific directions (e.g., “2 o’clock on your tray”).
Offer your arm when guiding; describe obstacles.
Cognitive & Neurodevelopmental Differences
Use clear, literal language when helpful.
Maintain predictable routines when preferred.
Allow additional processing time.
Respect sensory needs and individual communication preferences.

Safety & Precautions

Never assume a communication disability means impaired intelligence.
Avoid shouting unless specifically needed.
Do not force eye contact.
Never move or guide a resident without explanation and agreement.

What Should I Report?

New or worsening communication difficulties.
Sudden speech or comprehension changes (urgent evaluation needed).
Communication barriers affecting safety or care.

Related

Therapeutic Communication
Aphasia
Dementia Care

Flashcards
What adjustments help residents with hearing difficulty?03-application / patient-careAnswerFace them, reduce noise, speak clearly, and use aids.
What is important when communicating with someone with receptive aphasia?03-application / patient-careAnswerUse short statements and confirm comprehension.

patient-care/communication-and-psychosoc.filePath: Patient Care/Communication and Psychosocial/Culturally Responsive Care.md
patient-care/communication-and-psychosoc.title: Culturally Responsive Care
patient-care/communication-and-psychosoc.content:
Patient Needs
Provide respectful, individualized care that recognizes cultural beliefs, personal values, identity, and preferences.
What Should I Assess?

Preferred name, pronouns, and forms of address.
Language and communication preferences.
Religious or spiritual practices.
Dietary preferences and restrictions.
Personal care, modesty, and privacy preferences.
Family involvement and decision-making preferences.

How Do I Provide Care?

Ask First: Learn the resident’s preferences rather than assuming.
Avoid Stereotypes: Treat each resident as an individual.
Respect Identity: Use preferred names and pronouns.
Adapt Care: Accommodate dietary, religious, and personal routines when possible.
Communicate Clearly: Use qualified interpreters when needed.
Remain Open: Accept feedback and adjust your approach.

Safety & Precautions

Never assume beliefs or preferences based on appearance or background.
Do not use family members as substitutes for qualified medical interpreters when professional interpretation is required.
Balance individual preferences with safety requirements and the care plan.
Provide equitable care regardless of background or identity.

What Should I Report?

Preferences or needs that require care-plan adjustments.
Communication barriers affecting care.
Concerns involving discrimination, dignity, or unmet cultural needs.

Related

Patient Rights
Therapeutic Communication
Informed Consent

Flashcards
How should cultural preferences be addressed in care?03-application / patient-careAnswerAsk the individual rather than making assumptions.

patient-care/communication-and-psychosoc.filePath: Patient Care/Communication and Psychosocial/De-escalation and Conflict Resolution.md
patient-care/communication-and-psychosoc.title: De-escalation and Conflict Resolution
patient-care/communication-and-psychosoc.content:
Patient Needs
Reduce distress and maintain safety when a resident becomes upset, agitated, or potentially aggressive.
What Should I Assess?

Signs of agitation, fear, frustration, or escalating behavior.
Possible triggers: pain, confusion, unmet needs, overstimulation, or communication difficulties.
Immediate safety risks to the resident, staff, or others.

How Do I Provide Care?

Stay Calm: Speak slowly and use a respectful tone.
Listen Actively: Allow the resident to express concerns without interruption.
One Speaker: Avoid multiple people speaking at once.
Avoid Confrontation: Do not argue, blame, threaten, or make personal attacks.
Offer Choices: Provide reasonable alternatives to restore a sense of control.
Give Space: Maintain personal space and avoid unnecessary physical contact.

Safety & Precautions

Prioritize personal and resident safety.
Maintain access to an exit; avoid blocking the resident’s movement.
Do not attempt physical restraint unless specifically authorized, trained, and acting under applicable emergency procedures.
Request assistance when behavior escalates or safety is threatened.

What Should I Report?

Threats, aggression, or unsafe behavior.
New or worsening agitation or confusion.
Suspected causes of distress.
Actions taken and the resident’s response.

Related

Therapeutic Communication
Dementia Care
Patient Refusal of Care

Sources

CNA Module 3 — Interpersonal Skills
NICE — Dementia: Assessment, Management and Support
Facility de-escalation, behavioral-response, and workplace-safety procedures (verify at clinical site)

Flashcards
What is an initial de-escalation priority?01-foundations / patient-careAnswerRemain calm, listen, reduce stimulation, and maintain safety.

patient-care/communication-and-psychosoc.title: Dementia Care
patient-care/communication-and-psychosoc.content:
Patient Needs
Residents with dementia may experience changes in memory, orientation, communication, judgment, and ability to perform daily activities.
Care Goals:

Preserve dignity, independence, and personal preferences.
Maintain familiar routines when helpful.
Reduce avoidable confusion and distress.
Support safe participation in daily activities.
Adapt care to the resident’s current abilities rather than assuming all residents with dementia need the same assistance.

What Should I Assess?
Observe and report changes in:

Alertness, orientation, and responsiveness.
Communication and ability to express needs.
Mood, agitation, anxiety, withdrawal, or unusual behavior.
Mobility, balance, and ability to complete daily activities.
Eating, drinking, toileting, sleep, and comfort.

Potential Causes of Distress:

Pain or discomfort.
Hunger, thirst, or toileting needs.
Fear or difficulty understanding what is happening.
Excessive noise, unfamiliar surroundings, or overstimulation.
Illness, infection, or sudden changes in mental status.

Important: Sudden confusion or an abrupt change from baseline requires prompt reporting. Do not assume it is simply a progression of dementia.
How Do I Provide Care?
Communication

Approach calmly, introduce yourself, and explain what you are doing.
Use short, clear statements and allow time for responses.
Offer simple choices when appropriate.
Use gestures, visual cues, or demonstrations when helpful.
Avoid arguing, criticizing, or repeatedly correcting the resident.
Listen to verbal and nonverbal expressions of needs.
Identify perseveration, which is when they repeat the same task over and over. Redirect to something else.

Supporting Daily Activities

Encourage the resident to perform tasks they can safely manage.
Break complicated activities into smaller steps.
Offer guidance without rushing.
Follow familiar routines and preferences whenever possible.
Maintain privacy during bathing, dressing, and toileting.

Responding to Distress

Remain calm and maintain a respectful tone.
Check for immediate safety concerns.
Consider possible unmet needs or environmental triggers.
Reduce unnecessary stimulation when appropriate.
Offer reassurance, choices, or a change in activity.
Stop nonurgent care if the resident becomes significantly distressed.
Seek nursing assistance when distress persists or safety is threatened.

Safety & Precautions

Follow the individualized care plan and required supervision level.
Maintain a safe environment without unnecessarily restricting independence.
Do not use threats, punishment, confrontation, or coercion.
Respect refusal of care and follow facility procedures for reporting and reassessment.
Never assume a resident lacks all decision-making ability because they have dementia.
Follow approved procedures for wandering, falls, and other identified risks.

Wandering tends to be okay, so long as they are on-premises.


Do not use restraints for staff convenience.

What Should I Report?

Sudden or significant changes in cognition or behavior.
New confusion, unusual drowsiness, or difficulty waking.
Persistent agitation or distress.
New difficulty eating, drinking, swallowing, walking, or completing daily activities.
Suspected pain, illness, injury, or unmet needs.
Safety concerns, falls, or changes requiring a different level of assistance.
Resident preferences or approaches that successfully reduce distress.

Related

Dementia
Nervous System — delirium and sudden changes in cognition
De-escalation & Conflict Resolution
Therapeutic Communication
Communication Accommodations
Patient Refusal of Care
Fall Risk

Sources

CNA Module 3 — Interpersonal Skills
NICE — Dementia: Assessment, Management and Support
NICE — Managing Distress in Dementia
Facility dementia-care and behavioral-response procedures (verify at clinical site)

Flashcards
What should be considered when a resident with dementia becomes agitated?03-application / patient-careAnswerUnmet needs such as pain, fear, toileting, or overstimulation.
Why use predictable routines for dementia care?03-application / patient-careAnswerThey may reduce confusion and distress.
Why must sudden confusion in a resident with dementia be reported?03-application / patient-careAnswerIt may indicate delirium, illness, or another acute change.
How should instructions be adapted for residents with dementia?03-application / patient-careAnswerUse clear language, simple steps, and adequate response time.

patient-care/communication-and-psychosoc.filePath: Patient Care/Communication and Psychosocial/Emotional and Family Support.md
patient-care/communication-and-psychosoc.title: Emotional and Family Support
patient-care/communication-and-psychosoc.content:
Patient Needs
Support emotional well-being, independence, meaningful relationships, and a sense of dignity during illness or long-term care.
Rehabilitation & Family Involvement

Encourage meaningful family and friend interactions when desired by the resident.
Support participation in appropriate recreational and restorative activities.
Family members may provide useful information about resident preferences and previous abilities.
Encourage independence rather than completing every task for the resident.
Protect resident confidentiality and follow authorization requirements.
Report changes in motivation, mood, or participation.

What Should I Assess?

Mood, behavior, and changes in emotional state.
Signs of sadness, loneliness, anxiety, or withdrawal.
Desire for independence and participation in daily activities.
Resident preferences for family involvement.
Availability of meaningful social support.

How Do I Provide Care?
Emotional Support

Listen with empathy and without judgment.
Maintain a kind, patient, and respectful attitude.
Encourage independence and participation in care.
Acknowledge difficult emotions rather than forcing positivity.
Family Interaction
Welcome appropriate family involvement according to resident preferences.
Listen to family concerns and observations.
Encourage meaningful contact when desired by the resident.
Refer medical questions and care-plan decisions to licensed staff.

Safety & Precautions

Respect the resident’s right to limit family involvement.
Maintain confidentiality and verify authorization before sharing health information.
Avoid making promises about recovery or outcomes.
Do not dismiss sadness, grief, or emotional distress.

What Should I Report?

Persistent sadness, withdrawal, or behavioral changes.
Statements suggesting hopelessness or self-harm (report immediately).
Family concerns affecting resident care.
Changes in emotional well-being or social participation.

Related

Therapeutic Communication
Patient Rights
End-of-Life Care
Dementia Care

Flashcards
What helps a distressed resident feel heard?03-application / patient-careAnswerActive listening and acknowledgment without dismissing concerns.

patient-care/communication-and-psychosoc.title: End-of-Life Care
patient-care/communication-and-psychosoc.content:
Patient Needs
Provide comfort, dignity, emotional support, and respect for the patient’s wishes during the final stages of life.
Types of care:

Palliative Care: Relieves symptoms and improves quality of life at any stage of serious illness.
Hospice Care: Focuses on comfort and quality of life near the end of life rather than curing the terminal illness. Usually less than 6 months left to live.
Advance Directives: Document healthcare preferences and/or identify a healthcare decision-maker.
DNR Order: Directs healthcare professionals not to attempt CPR if cardiac or respiratory arrest occurs.

Grief and Emotional Responses
The five commonly taught grief responses are:





























ResponsePossible ExperienceDenialShock, numbness, or disbeliefAngerFrustration, blame, or feelings of unfairnessBargaining”What if” or “if only” thoughtsDepressionSadness, withdrawal, or feeling overwhelmedAcceptanceAcknowledging and learning to live with a loss
Important: Grief is individual and does not necessarily follow these stages in order. Do not pressure someone to reach acceptance.
CNA Care:

Listen without judgment.
Allow residents and loved ones to express emotions.
Avoid minimizing grief or making promises about outcomes.
Report severe distress or expressed thoughts of self-harm.
Offer access to additional support through the nurse.

Spiritual and Family Support

Ask about preferences rather than assuming religious beliefs.
Respect the resident’s spiritual, cultural, and personal practices.
Offer meaningful religious or comfort objects when appropriate.
Ask the nurse to help arrange a chaplain, faith representative, or other requested support.
Do not impose personal beliefs.
Include family and loved ones according to the resident’s preferences and applicable privacy rules.
Offer visitors privacy, seating, and opportunities to rest.
Do not automatically require family to leave during routine care; ask the resident and follow privacy and safety requirements.

Signs of Approaching Death
Changes vary and may include:
Respiratory

Irregular breathing or pauses between breaths.
Cheyne-Stokes breathing.
Noisy respiratory secretions, sometimes called a “death rattle.”
Changes in breathing depth and effort.

Cardiovascular

Cool or mottling (purple marbling on skin from poor blood flow) extremities.
Lower blood pressure.
Changes in heart rate or circulation.
Blue or gray discoloration of peripheral skin.

Nervous System

Increased sleeping or reduced responsiveness.
Confusion, agitation, or altered awareness.
Occasional involuntary movements.

Digestive and Urinary

Reduced appetite and thirst.
Difficulty swallowing.
Decreased bowel activity.
Reduced urine output or darker urine.
Possible incontinence.

Important: These findings can also occur with potentially treatable complications. Notify the nurse about new, distressing, or unexpected changes rather than independently attributing them to dying.
Comfort Measures

Reposition gently according to comfort, tolerance, and the individualized plan.
Maintain clean, dry linens and comfortable clothing.
Provide prescribed mouth care and lip moisturizer.
Support safe positioning when breathing is difficult.
Offer blankets or adjust the environment according to comfort.
Observe nonverbal signs of pain, anxiety, or respiratory distress.
Offer food and fluids only when consistent with swallowing safety, orders, and resident wishes.
Speak respectfully even if the resident cannot respond.
Inform the nurse when discomfort persists or worsens.

Important: Do not force food or fluids, assume fixed repositioning schedules, or independently administer medication or oxygen adjustments.
What Should I Assess?
Common end-of-life changes:

Increased sleeping, fatigue, or reduced responsiveness.
Decreased appetite and fluid intake.
Difficulty swallowing.
Changes in breathing patterns.
Cool or discolored extremities.
Changes in bowel and bladder control.

Signs of discomfort:

Grimacing, restlessness, or moaning.
Anxiety, fear, or agitation.
Difficulty breathing.
Nonverbal indications of pain.

How Do I Provide Care?
Physical Comfort:

Reposition gently according to comfort and the care plan.
Provide oral care and lip moisture as directed.
Maintain hygiene and protect skin integrity.
Adjust blankets, lighting, and room temperature.
Allow rest and avoid unnecessary disturbances.

Emotional Support:

Speak calmly and respectfully, even when the patient is unresponsive.
Listen without judgment.
Respect spiritual, religious, and cultural preferences.
Support family presence according to patient wishes and facility policy.

Dignity & Autonomy:

Respect personal preferences and advance care plans.
Explain care before touching or moving the patient.
Encourage choices and independence when possible.

Safety & Precautions

Follow documented care goals and applicable medical orders.
Do not force food or fluids when swallowing becomes difficult.
Never assume reduced responsiveness means the patient cannot hear.
A DNR order applies to resuscitation; it does not mean withholding routine comfort care.
Report new or uncontrolled symptoms promptly.

What Should I Report?

Signs of pain, distress, or breathing difficulty.
Significant changes in responsiveness or condition.
New skin breakdown or discomfort.
Patient requests or concerns about treatment.
Family concerns requiring licensed staff assistance.

Related

Patient Rights
Informed Consent
Patient Refusal of Care
Skin Integrity & Breakdown Prevention
Pain Assessment

Sources

MedlinePlus — Hospice Care
MedlinePlus — Palliative Care
MedlinePlus — The Final Days of Life

Flashcards
What is the focus of comfort-oriented end-of-life care?01-foundations / patient-careAnswerDignity, symptom comfort, preferences, and family support.
Do the five stages of grief occur in a required order?03-application / patient-careAnswerNo. Grief is individual and does not follow a predictable sequence.
What is Cheyne-Stokes breathing?01-foundations / patient-careAnswerCycles of changing breathing depth with periods of apnea.
What is a death rattle?01-foundations / patient-careAnswerNoisy breathing caused by pooled respiratory secretions near death.
What physical changes may occur as death approaches?03-application / patient-careAnswerIrregular breathing, mottled skin, reduced alertness, and decreased intake or urine output.
Should a CNA force food or fluids on a dying resident?03-application / patient-careAnswerNo. Follow resident wishes, swallowing safety, and the care plan.
What should a CNA do when a dying resident shows new signs of discomfort?03-application / patient-careAnswerReport the symptoms promptly and follow the comfort-care plan.
How should a CNA support a resident's spiritual needs?03-application / patient-careAnswerRespect their beliefs and arrange requested support through the nurse.

patient-care/communication-and-psychosoc.filePath: Patient Care/Communication and Psychosocial/Patient Refusal of Care.md
patient-care/communication-and-psychosoc.title: Patient Refusal of Care
patient-care/communication-and-psychosoc.content:
Patient Needs
Patients generally have the right to refuse care or treatment, even when refusal may affect their health.
Common reasons for refusal:

Pain, discomfort, or fatigue.
Fear, embarrassment, or anxiety.
Cultural, religious, or personal preferences.
Confusion, dementia, or communication difficulties.
Desire for independence or control.

What Should I Assess?

What care is being refused?
Why might the patient be refusing?
Is the patient experiencing pain, distress, or confusion?
Does the patient understand what is being offered?
Are there communication barriers or unmet needs

How Do I Provide Care?

Respect: Stop or pause the care being refused. Remain calm and respectful.
Understand: Ask why the patient does not want the care.
Explain: Briefly describe the purpose of care within your scope.
Adapt: Offer appropriate alternatives, choices, or a different time.
Report: Notify the nurse of refusals according to policy, especially when safety is at risk.
Document: Record the refusal and relevant observations as required.

Safety & Precautions

Never force, threaten, shame, or coerce a patient.
Do not assume dementia automatically removes the right to make decisions.
Respect the patient’s autonomy while maintaining immediate safety.
Do not independently determine decision-making capacity.
Follow care plans, facility policy, and applicable consent requirements.

Refusal of Care: Safety & Escalation
Routine Refusal

Respect the resident’s decision; do not force or coerce care.
Ask about discomfort, concerns, or preferences.
Offer appropriate alternatives or another time when reasonable.
Report the refusal according to facility policy.
Document the care as refused or not completed, rather than recording it as performed.

Refusal With Immediate Safety Concerns

Recognize concerning symptoms, such as severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, sudden confusion, or significant bleeding.
Summon nursing assistance immediately and activate emergency response when indicated.
Explain what you are doing calmly and respectfully.
Do not independently determine decision-making capacity or override a resident’s refusal.
Follow licensed staff direction and applicable consent, emergency, and facility procedures.

Important: A refusal does not automatically establish that a resident lacks decision-making capacity. Likewise, a diagnosis of dementia does not automatically invalidate a resident’s wishes.
What Should I Report?

Refusal of essential care, nutrition, hydration, or treatment.
Repeated refusals affecting health or hygiene.
New confusion, pain, distress, or behavioral changes.
Concerns about the patient’s ability to understand or communicate.
Any immediate safety risks.

Related

Patient Rights
Informed Consent
Dementia Care
End-of-Life Care

Sources

42 CFR §483.10 — Resident Rights
Facility resident-rights, informed-consent, refusal-of-care, and emergency-response policies (verify at clinical site)

Flashcards
What should a CNA do if a resident refuses care?03-application / patient-careAnswerRespect refusal, ensure safety, and report per policy.
Can a CNA force routine care because it is in the care plan?03-application / patient-careAnswerNo; respect resident rights and escalate concerns appropriately.
What should a CNA do if a resident refuses care while showing signs of a medical emergency?03-application / patient-careAnswerRespect consent, summon urgent help, and follow emergency procedures without independently overriding refusal.

patient-care/communication-and-psychosoc.title: Therapeutic Communication
patient-care/communication-and-psychosoc.content:
Patient Needs
Effective communication builds trust, reduces stress, promotes comfort, and helps residents express their needs.

Verbal: Spoken words, tone, and clarity.
Nonverbal: Facial expressions, gestures, posture, and body language.

What Should I Assess?

Can the resident understand and respond?
Are there language, hearing, speech, or cognitive barriers?
Does their body language suggest distress or discomfort?

How Do I Provide Care?

Active Listening: Give attention without interrupting.
Empathy: Acknowledge feelings without judgment.
Eye Contact: Maintain culturally and individually appropriate eye contact.
Body Language: Use a calm, open posture.
“I” Statements: Express concerns without blame.
Clarity: Use simple language and allow time for responses.

Safety & Precautions

Avoid rushing, arguing, or dismissing concerns.
Respect communication preferences and cultural differences.
Do not assume silence means understanding or consent.

What Should I Report?

New difficulty communicating.
Sudden changes in behavior or understanding.
Unexpressed needs, distress, or communication barriers affecting care.

Related

Communication Accommodations
Patient Refusal of Care
Dementia Care

Flashcards
Why use open-ended questions when possible?03-application / patient-careAnswerThey encourage the resident to express concerns in their own words.

patient-care/developmental-and-neurologi.title: Developmental and Neurological Conditions
patient-care/developmental-and-neurologi.content:
Patient Needs
Residents with developmental, neurological, or mental health conditions may need individualized assistance with mobility, communication, self-care, safety, and social participation.
Care should reflect the resident’s actual abilities and preferences, not assumptions based on a diagnosis.
Intellectual Disability
A developmental condition involving limitations in intellectual functioning and adaptive skills.
Possible needs:

Additional time to understand instructions.
Clear, concrete communication.
Assistance with selected ADLs.
Support for independence and decision-making.

Cerebral Palsy
A group of disorders affecting movement, posture, and muscle coordination, caused by changes or injury to the developing brain.

May affect balance, movement, muscle tone, and speech.
Some residents may have difficulty swallowing.
Intellectual ability varies; cerebral palsy does not automatically imply intellectual disability.
Symptoms are generally nonprogressive in origin, although functional needs can change over time.

Epilepsy
A neurological condition involving recurrent unprovoked seizures or other recognized epilepsy criteria.

Seizures may involve convulsions, altered awareness, unusual movements, or temporary behavioral changes.
Some individuals have identifiable seizure triggers.
Antiseizure medications may help control seizures.

Parkinson’s Disease
A progressive neurological condition involving loss of dopamine-producing neurons and other nervous-system changes.
Possible features:

Tremor, rigidity, and slowed movement.
Difficulty walking or initiating movements.
Swallowing difficulties.
Changes in sleep, thinking, or mood.

Not every resident develops dementia, hallucinations, or severe disability.
Mental Health Conditions
Conditions that can affect mood, thoughts, perceptions, behavior, and daily functioning.
Examples include depression, anxiety disorders, and other mental illnesses.
Residents deserve the same dignity, privacy, safety, and participation in care as anyone else.
What Should I Assess?
Observe and report:

Changes in mobility, balance, or muscle control.
New swallowing or communication difficulties.
Seizure activity or changes in usual seizure patterns.
New confusion or changes in responsiveness.
Withdrawal, distress, or major behavioral changes.
Reduced ability to complete usual ADLs.
Statements indicating possible self-harm or suicide risk.

How Do I Provide Care?

Learn how the resident prefers to communicate.
Speak directly to the resident rather than assuming another person must answer.
Use simple, clear instructions when helpful.
Allow sufficient time for responses and movements.
Offer choices and promote independence.
Follow prescribed mobility, positioning, swallowing, and seizure precautions.
Support meaningful activities appropriate to the person’s interests and capabilities.
Protect privacy and respect informed decisions.
Report changes from the resident’s usual baseline.

Safety & Precautions

Do not assume a resident lacks decision-making capacity based on a diagnosis.
Do not physically force movement or rush a resident with impaired coordination.
Follow the existing Seizure Response procedure during a seizure.
Do not restrain a seizing resident or put anything in their mouth.
Observe for signs of aspiration when swallowing difficulties are present.
Treat new severe confusion, stroke-like symptoms, or loss of responsiveness as potentially urgent.
Escalate self-harm or suicide concerns immediately according to facility procedures.

What Should I Report?

New seizures or changes in seizure activity.
Falls or unexpected changes in mobility.
New choking or swallowing difficulties.
Sudden confusion, weakness, or speech changes.
Severe emotional distress or self-harm concerns.
Changes affecting safety or daily functioning.

Related

Seizure Response
Dementia Care
Therapeutic Communication
Recognizing Patient Distress
Assisting with Ambulation
Restorative & Rehabilitative Care

Sources

CNA Module 13 — Developmental, Neurological & Mental Health Conditions
CDC — Cerebral Palsy
CDC — Epilepsy
NINDS — Parkinson’s Disease
Resident-specific care plan

Flashcards
Does cerebral palsy automatically mean a resident has an intellectual disability?02-mechanisms / patient-careAnswerNo. Intellectual ability varies independently of movement difficulties.
What is epilepsy?01-foundations / patient-careAnswerA neurological condition characterized by a tendency to have recurrent seizures.
What are common motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease?01-foundations / patient-careAnswerTremor, rigidity, slowed movement, and walking difficulties.
How should a CNA communicate with a resident with an intellectual disability?03-application / patient-careAnswerUse clear communication, allow time, and adapt to the resident's needs.
What should a CNA do during a seizure?03-application / patient-careAnswerProtect the resident from injury and follow the seizure response protocol.
Does a mental health diagnosis remove a resident's right to make choices?03-application / patient-careAnswerNo. Support consent, dignity, and individual decision-making.

patient-care/dysphagia-and-aspiration-pr.title: Dysphagia and Aspiration Precautions
patient-care/dysphagia-and-aspiration-pr.content:
Patient Needs
Dysphagia is difficulty swallowing.
Residents with dysphagia may be at increased risk of:

Aspiration (material entering the airway).
Choking.
Dehydration and malnutrition.
Aspiration-related respiratory complications.

Aspiration: Food, liquid, saliva, or other material passing into the airway below the vocal folds.
What Should I Assess?
Observe and report:

Coughing or choking while eating or drinking.
Wet or gurgling voice after swallowing.
Difficulty chewing or controlling food.
Food remaining in the mouth.
Drooling or difficulty managing saliva.
Unusually prolonged meals.
Reduced intake or signs of distress.
Changes in breathing during meals.

Important: Aspiration can sometimes occur without obvious coughing (silent aspiration).
How Do I Provide Care?

Check the prescribed food texture, liquid consistency, positioning, and assistance level.
Verify that the correct meal and drinks have been provided.
Position the resident as directed.
Offer food and drinks at the prescribed pace and in the approved manner.
Use adaptive equipment only when permitted.
Observe tolerance and swallowing throughout the meal.
Stop and request assistance for new swallowing difficulties.
Provide or assist with prescribed oral hygiene.
Report and document concerns according to facility procedures.

Texture-Modified Foods & Thickened Liquids
Your CNA coursework uses:

Cut-up or easy-to-chew foods.
Ground foods.
Pureed foods.
Nectar-, honey-, and pudding-thick liquids.

The International Dysphagia Diet Standardisation Initiative (IDDSI) uses defined levels for drink thickness (0–4) and food textures (3–7).
The resident’s prescribed consistency takes priority. Do not independently substitute one level for another.
Safety & Precautions

Follow NPO orders and all swallowing restrictions.
Never independently thicken or thin liquids to a different prescribed level.
Don’t assume that thickened liquids eliminate aspiration risk.
