reference-and-guidelines/infection-preve.title: Bloodborne Pathogens
reference-and-guidelines/infection-preve.content:
Quick Reference
Bloodborne pathogens are infectious microorganisms present in human blood that can cause disease.
Common Bloodborne Pathogens

























PathogenDiseaseImportant ConsiderationsHBVHepatitis BCan damage the liver; vaccination is availableHCVHepatitis CCan damage the liver; no vaccine is availableHIVHuman Immunodeficiency VirusAffects the immune system; effective treatments are available
Routes of Exposure
Bloodborne pathogens may enter the body through:

Needlesticks or injuries involving contaminated sharps.
Contact with nonintact skin, such as cuts or abrasions.
Exposure to mucous membranes of the eyes, nose, or mouth.

Potentially Infectious Materials

Blood.
Body fluids visibly contaminated with blood.
Certain other body fluids and tissues classified as potentially infectious under occupational safety rules.
Important: Not every bodily fluid has the same bloodborne pathogen risk. However, Standard Precautions apply broadly because different infectious agents can be transmitted through different materials.

Prevention

Perform Hand Hygiene.
Select appropriate PPE for anticipated exposure.
Handle contaminated linens and equipment safely.
Never recap used needles or handle sharps unnecessarily.
Dispose of sharps in approved containers.
Follow facility exposure-control procedures.
Obtain recommended occupational vaccinations, including hepatitis B.

Responding to an Exposure

Stop the activity safely.
Wash needlestick injuries, cuts, or exposed skin with soap and water.
Flush exposed mucous membranes with water or saline as appropriate.
Report the incident immediately.
Obtain prompt medical evaluation for possible post-exposure treatment.
Complete required exposure documentation.

Important Considerations

HIV, HBV, and HCV are not spread through ordinary casual contact.
Gloves reduce exposure risk but do not eliminate it.
Post-exposure medical evaluation is time-sensitive.
Do not wait for symptoms before reporting an exposure.
Use the facility’s exposure-control plan.

Related

Standard Precautions
Transmission-Based Precautions
Hand Hygiene
Donning & Doffing PPE
Occupational Exposure & Response
Chain of Infection
Employee Rights

Sources

CNA Module 4 — Emergency Preparedness & Safety
CNA Module 6 — Infection Prevention & Control
CDC/NIOSH — Bloodborne Infectious Disease Risks
OSHA — Bloodborne Pathogens

Flashcards
Name three major occupational bloodborne pathogens.01-foundations / reference-guidelinesAnswerHepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV.
What exposures may transmit bloodborne pathogens?01-foundations / reference-guidelinesAnswerContaminated sharps, mucous membranes, or nonintact skin exposure.

reference-and-guidelines/infection-preve.filePath: Reference and Guidelines/Infection Prevention/Chain of Infection.md
reference-and-guidelines/infection-preve.title: Chain of Infection
reference-and-guidelines/infection-preve.content:
Quick Reference
The chain of infection describes the six links necessary for an infection to spread. Breaking any link interrupts transmission.








































LinkDescriptionHow to Break ItInfectious AgentPathogen capable of causing diseaseCleaning, disinfection, appropriate treatmentReservoirWhere pathogens live or multiplyEnvironmental cleaning, food safetyPortal of ExitHow pathogens leave the reservoirCover wounds, contain drainage, respiratory hygieneMode of TransmissionHow pathogens spreadHand hygiene, PPE, safe equipment handlingPortal of EntryHow pathogens enter another hostProtect skin, aseptic techniqueSusceptible HostPerson vulnerable to infectionVaccination, nutrition, appropriate preventive measures
Types of Infectious Agents:

Bacteria
Viruses
Fungi
Parasites

Important Considerations

Hand hygiene interrupts transmission.
Intact skin and mucous membranes provide important protection.
Infection can spread through direct contact, indirect contact, droplets, or airborne routes.
A person can carry certain pathogens without showing symptoms.
Prevention requires multiple measures, not just PPE.

Related

Standard Precautions
Transmission-Based Precautions
Hand Hygiene
Medical & Surgical Asepsis

Sources

CNA Module 6 — Infection Prevention & Control

Flashcards
Why break a link in the chain of infection?02-mechanisms / reference-guidelinesAnswerTo interrupt transmission to a susceptible host.

reference-and-guidelines/infection-preve.filePath: Reference and Guidelines/Infection Prevention/Enhanced Barrier Precautions.md
reference-and-guidelines/infection-preve.title: Enhanced Barrier Precautions
reference-and-guidelines/infection-preve.content:
Quick Reference
Enhanced Barrier Precautions (EBP) reduce transmission of multidrug-resistant organisms (MDROs) in nursing homes.
Used for residents with:

Known MDRO infection or colonization when Contact Precautions are not otherwise required.
Wounds or indwelling medical devices, regardless of known MDRO status, when indicated by guidance.
Required PPE during high-contact care:
Gown
Gloves
High-Contact Activities:
Bathing and dressing.
Transferring residents.
Providing hygiene or toileting care.
Changing linens.
Changing briefs or assisting with device care.
Wound care and indwelling device care.
Lower-Contact Activities:
Delivering meals.
Providing medication without extensive contact.
Brief conversation or social visits.
Adjusting personal items without significant resident contact.

Important Considerations

EBP is used in addition to Standard Precautions.
EBP differs from Contact Precautions because gown and gloves are targeted to high-contact activities.
Residents under EBP are generally not restricted to their rooms solely because of EBP.
Perform hand hygiene before and after required PPE use.
Follow posted signage and facility infection-control policies.

Related

Standard Precautions
Transmission-Based Precautions
Donning & Doffing PPE
Multidrug-Resistant Organisms (MDROs)

Sources

CDC — Enhanced Barrier Precautions in Nursing Homes
CNA Module 6 — Enhanced Barrier Precautions

Flashcards
What is the purpose of enhanced barrier precautions in nursing homes?01-foundations / reference-guidelinesAnswerReduce spread of certain MDROs during high-contact resident care.

reference-and-guidelines/infection-preve.filePath: Reference and Guidelines/Infection Prevention/Medical and Surgical Asepsis.md
reference-and-guidelines/infection-preve.title: Medical and Surgical Asepsis
reference-and-guidelines/infection-preve.content:
Quick Reference
Asepsis: Practices used to prevent contamination by microorganisms.
Medical Asepsis (Clean Technique)
Reduces the number and spread of microorganisms.

Perform hand hygiene.
Use appropriate PPE.
Clean and disinfect equipment and surfaces.
Handle soiled linens and waste safely.
Avoid cross-contamination between clean and dirty items.

Surgical Asepsis (Sterile Technique)
Prevents microorganisms from contaminating a sterile field or sterile equipment.

Use sterile instruments and supplies.
Maintain sterile barriers and fields.
Prevent contamination during sterile procedures.
Replace supplies if sterility is compromised.

Important Considerations

Clean does not mean sterile.
Disinfection reduces or inactivates many pathogens; sterilization destroys all forms of microbial life, including bacterial spores.
Sterile procedures require specific training and authorized responsibilities.
CNAs primarily use medical asepsis during routine patient care.
Follow facility policies for contaminated equipment, specimens, and spills.

Related

Hand Hygiene
Standard Precautions
Donning & Doffing PPE
Chain of Infection

Sources

CNA Module 6 — Medical & Surgical Asepsis

Flashcards
What is the basic difference between medical and surgical asepsis?02-mechanisms / reference-guidelinesAnswerMedical reduces organisms; surgical seeks to maintain sterility.

reference-and-guidelines/infection-preve.title: Standard Precautions
reference-and-guidelines/infection-preve.content:
Quick Reference
Standard Precautions are infection-prevention practices applied to all residents, regardless of known or suspected infection.
Core Practices

Hand Hygiene: Before and after resident contact, after potential contamination, and after removing gloves.
PPE: Select gloves, gowns, masks, and eye protection based on anticipated exposure.
Respiratory Hygiene: Cover coughs and sneezes, dispose of tissues, and perform hand hygiene.
Equipment & Environment: Clean and disinfect shared equipment and contaminated surfaces.
Linen & Waste: Handle contaminated materials to minimize exposure and transmission.
Sharps & Injection Safety: Follow safe injection and sharps-handling procedures when applicable to authorized duties.
Resident Placement: Follow infection-control guidance when additional transmission risks exist.

PPE Selection





















Anticipated ExposureProtectionBlood, body fluids, mucous membranes, nonintact skin, or potentially contaminated materialsGlovesPossible contamination of clothing or exposed skinGownRisk of splashes or sprays affecting eyes, nose, or mouthAppropriate mask and eye or face protection
Additional PPE may be necessary depending on isolation requirements.
Important Considerations

Standard Precautions apply to every resident.
Gloves never replace hand hygiene.
Change gloves between residents and when moving from contaminated to clean tasks as appropriate.
Use soap and water when hands are visibly soiled.
Follow facility policies and posted precautions.
Use Transmission-Based Precautions when indicated in addition to Standard Precautions.

Additional Precautions

Transmission-Based Precautions
Enhanced Barrier Precautions
Multidrug-Resistant Organisms (MDROs)
C. difficile Infection

Related

Hand Hygiene
Donning & Doffing PPE
Chain of Infection

Sources

CNA Module 6 — Infection Prevention & Control
CDC — Standard Precautions

Flashcards
To whom do Standard Precautions apply?01-foundations / reference-guidelinesAnswerAll patients, regardless of known infection status.
When should PPE selection be based on anticipated exposure?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerBefore care, based on expected contact with blood, fluids, or infectious materials.

reference-and-guidelines/infection-preve.title: Transmission-Based Precautions
reference-and-guidelines/infection-preve.content:
Quick Reference
Transmission-Based Precautions are additional infection-prevention measures for residents with known or suspected transmissible infections.
Always used in addition to Standard Precautions.





























TypeTransmissionCore PPERoom RequirementsContactDirect contact or contaminated surfacesGown and glovesPrivate room when indicated; no special air pressureDropletInfectious respiratory dropletsSurgical/procedure maskPrivate room when indicated; no special air pressureAirborneInfectious particles that can remain suspended in airFit-tested N95 or higher-level respiratorNegative-pressure room (AIIR) when required
Contact Precautions
Prevent transmission through direct contact with residents or contaminated surfaces.

PPE: Gown and gloves, as directed.
Room: Private room preferred when indicated; placement depends on the setting.
Examples: C. difficile, norovirus, certain MDROs.
Equipment: Dedicated or properly disinfected shared equipment.

Droplet Precautions
Prevent transmission through infectious respiratory droplets.

PPE: Surgical/procedure mask upon room entry; additional PPE based on exposure risks.
Room: Private room preferred when indicated.
Examples: Influenza, pertussis, meningococcal infection.
Transport: Resident wears a mask if tolerated and appropriate.

Airborne Precautions
Prevent transmission through infectious airborne particles.

PPE: Fit-tested N95 respirator or higher-level respiratory protection, as required.
Room: Airborne Infection Isolation Room (AIIR), also called a negative-pressure room.
Examples: Infectious pulmonary or laryngeal tuberculosis, measles, chickenpox (varicella), and disseminated shingles.
Transport: Limit unnecessary movement; resident wears a surgical/procedure mask when appropriate and tolerated.

Negative-Pressure Rooms (AIIR)
A negative-pressure room is designed to keep infectious airborne particles from spreading into surrounding areas.

Airflow: Air flows from the hallway into the room, rather than from the room into the hallway.
Purpose: Protects other residents, healthcare workers, and visitors from airborne infection.
Ventilation: Air is exhausted outdoors or filtered through appropriate HEPA filtration before recirculation.
Door: Keep closed except when entering or exiting.
Monitoring: Facilities monitor airflow and pressure to ensure the room operates correctly.
PPE: Negative pressure does not replace the need for a fit-tested N95 or other required respirator.

CNA Considerations:

Follow the isolation signage and facility’s PPE requirements before entering.
Keep the room door closed.
Report open doors, airflow alarms, or suspected ventilation problems to the nurse.
Do not change ventilation settings or disable alarms.

Negative vs. Positive Pressure




















Room TypeDirection of AirflowPurposeNegative PressureHallway → RoomKeeps airborne infectious particles containedPositive PressureRoom → HallwayHelps protect vulnerable patients from outside contaminants
Remember: Negative pressure protects people outside the room. Positive pressure protects the patient inside the room.
Transporting Residents Under Precautions

Limit transport outside the room when required by the isolation plan.
Perform hand hygiene and prepare the resident according to the required precautions.
Use appropriate source control, such as a mask for respiratory infections when indicated.
Cover or contain wounds, drainage, and contaminated areas.
Ensure clean clothing or coverings as needed.
Notify receiving personnel of required precautions before transport.
Follow facility policy for transport staff PPE.
Clean and disinfect transport equipment appropriately.
Important: Transport precautions depend on the infectious agent and the resident’s needs.

Additional PPE Safety

Inspect PPE before use.
Change gloves when torn, contaminated, or when moving from dirty to clean tasks.
Avoid touching contaminated PPE surfaces.
Remove PPE carefully to prevent self-contamination.
Perform hand hygiene after removal and whenever hands become contaminated.
Follow approved reprocessing instructions for reusable protection.

Important Considerations

Contact: Gown + gloves.
Droplet: Surgical/procedure mask.
Airborne: Fit-tested N95 or higher respirator.
Some infections require multiple precaution types.
For C. difficile and norovirus, follow facility guidance regarding soap-and-water handwashing.
Follow isolation signage and facility-specific requirements.
Maintain resident dignity and minimize unnecessary isolation-related distress.

Related

Standard Precautions
Enhanced Barrier Precautions
Hand Hygiene
Donning & Doffing PPE
Chain of Infection

Sources

CNA Module 6 — Infection Prevention & Control
CDC — Transmission-Based Precautions
CDC — Isolation Precautions

Flashcards
What are the three main transmission-based precaution categories?01-foundations / reference-guidelinesAnswerContact, droplet, and airborne.
Why are transmission-based precautions used in addition to standard precautions?02-mechanisms / reference-guidelinesAnswerCertain organisms need extra measures based on their transmission route.
What is the purpose of a negative-pressure room?01-foundations / reference-guidelinesAnswerPrevent airborne infectious particles from escaping into surrounding areas.
In which direction does air flow in a negative-pressure room?01-foundations / reference-guidelinesAnswerFrom the hallway into the patient room.
Which transmission-based precaution typically requires a negative-pressure room?01-foundations / reference-guidelinesAnswerAirborne Precautions.
What does AIIR stand for?01-foundations / reference-guidelinesAnswerAirborne Infection Isolation Room.
Why should the door of a negative-pressure room remain closed?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerTo maintain controlled airflow and help contain infectious particles.
Does a negative-pressure room replace the need for an N95 respirator?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerNo. Required respiratory PPE must still be worn.
What is the difference between negative-pressure and positive-pressure rooms?02-mechanisms / reference-guidelinesAnswerNegative pressure contains airborne infection; positive pressure protects vulnerable patients from outside contaminants.

reference-and-guidelines/medical-termino.content:
Overview
Medical terminology provides a standardized way to communicate clinical information.
Many terms are formed using Greek or Latin elements:
Prefix + Root + Suffix

Prefix: Modifies meaning, often indicating location, number, or intensity.
Root: Identifies the main structure or concept.
Suffix: Indicates a condition, process, or specialty.

Examples

For example, AD may have multiple meanings and should not be used without clarification.
Directional Terms

































TermDirectionMedialToward, or nearer, the midline of the bodyLateralAway from the midline of the body; the side of the bodyAnteriorToward the front side of the bodyPosteriorToward the backside of the bodyProximalClosest to; the nearer of two points on the bodyDistalFarthest from; the farther of two poitns on the body.
Abbreviation Safety
The Joint Commission identifies several abbreviations and medication notations that create significant error risks.
Examples to Avoid in Orders and Medication-Related Documentation









































AvoidWrite InsteadU or uunitIUinternational unitQD, q.d.dailyQOD, q.o.d.every other dayMSWrite the complete intended medication nameMSO4 / MgSO4Write the complete intended medication nameTrailing zero, e.g. 5.0 mg5 mgMissing leading zero, e.g. .5 mg0.5 mg
These restrictions apply to the contexts specified by the relevant standards and organizational policies. They are not a blanket prohibition against every medical abbreviation.
CNA Responsibilities

Learn abbreviations used by your facility.
Use only accepted terminology in documentation.
Ask for clarification when an abbreviation is unclear.
Avoid ambiguous shortcuts in verbal reports.
Do not guess when instructions may affect resident safety.

reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.filePath: Reference and Guidelines/Professional Practice and Legal/Abuse, Neglect and Rights Violations.md
reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.title: Abuse, Neglect and Rights Violations
reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.content:
Quick Reference
Residents have the right to freedom from abuse, neglect, exploitation, involuntary seclusion, and unauthorized restrictions on movement.
Types of Violations




























































ViolationDescriptionExampleAbuseHarmful or threatening conduct, including physical, verbal, sexual, or psychological abuseDeliberately striking or humiliating a residentNeglectFailure to provide necessary care or servicesRepeatedly failing to provide required toileting or repositioningNegligenceFailure to exercise legally required reasonable careFailing to follow applicable safety standardsMisappropriationDeliberately misusing or taking resident propertyStealing money or personal belongingsInvasion of PrivacyImproper interference with personal privacyReading private mail without permissionAbandonmentImproperly leaving a resident without required care or coverageLeaving an assignment without arranging necessary careFalse ImprisonmentUnlawfully restricting freedom of movementPreventing a resident from leaving without lawful justificationInvoluntary SeclusionSeparating or confining a resident against their will without lawful justificationLocking a resident alone in a room as punishmentAssaultThreatening harmful or offensive contactThreatening to hit a residentBatteryIntentional unlawful harmful or offensive contactHitting a resident
Preventing Violations

Respect dignity, privacy, and personal choices.
Follow individualized care plans.
Maintain professional boundaries.
Provide care promptly and consistently.
Never threaten, punish, humiliate, or coerce residents.
Protect resident belongings and financial information.

Recognizing Violations
Possible warning signs:

Unexplained injuries or bruising.
Fearfulness around particular individuals.
Sudden behavioral changes or withdrawal.
Poor hygiene or unmet basic needs.
Missing money or belongings.
Reports of mistreatment or inappropriate restraints.

Reporting Violations
California CNA Responsibilities
CNAs caring for elders or dependent adults are generally mandated reporters under California Welfare and Institutions Code §15630.

Protect immediate safety. Obtain emergency assistance when necessary.
Report suspected abuse promptly. A reasonable suspicion is sufficient; proof is not required.
Notify the supervising nurse according to facility policy, without delaying a legally required external report.
Report to the required outside agency. The appropriate agency and deadline depend on the care setting and circumstances.
Document objective facts. Record observations, relevant times, and the resident’s statements accurately, following facility requirements.
Do not conduct your own investigation. Cooperate with authorized investigators.

California Reporting Requirements

General elder or dependent adult abuse reporting: Report immediately or as soon as practicably possible by telephone or an authorized confidential online reporting tool. When reporting by telephone, submit the required written or authorized online follow-up within two working days.
Abuse in long-term care facilities: Special reporting rules generally require a verbal report to local law enforcement within two hours and written reports to designated agencies within 24 hours.
Exception: For certain resident-on-resident incidents involving a resident with physician-diagnosed dementia and no serious bodily injury, a different 24-hour written-report procedure applies.
Other settings: Reports generally go to Adult Protective Services or local law enforcement, as applicable.

Important: Exact recipients, time limits, and required forms vary by setting and incident type. Follow the applicable law and facility reporting procedures; do not assume every incident uses the same deadline.
Individual Responsibility
Reporting to a supervisor does not automatically discharge a CNA’s personal mandated-reporting duty. A supervisor cannot prevent or prohibit a required report.
Never delay a required report while waiting for permission or conducting an independent investigation.
California Mandatory Reporting — CNA Responsibilities
California CNAs caring for elders or dependent adults are generally mandated reporters.
When Abuse Is Known or Suspected:

Ensure immediate resident safety and summon emergency assistance when necessary.
Promptly notify the nurse or appropriate supervisor.
Fulfill applicable external reporting obligations; internal reporting alone may not satisfy the law.
Report factual observations, resident statements, and relevant circumstances.
Do not independently investigate, interrogate witnesses, or confront the suspected perpetrator.
Follow facility procedures that are consistent with legal reporting duties.

California Long-Term Care Reporting
Mandated reporters must report known or reasonably suspected abuse without waiting to prove that abuse occurred.
California Welfare and Institutions Code §15630 and federal nursing-facility requirements may apply simultaneously.
California WIC §15630 — Long-Term Care Facilities
For most covered incidents:

Verbal report: To local law enforcement immediately or as soon as practicable, no later than 2 hours.
Written report: To the Long-Term Care Ombudsman, local law enforcement, and corresponding state licensing agency within 24 hours.

Specific exception: Certain resident-to-resident incidents involving a resident with physician-diagnosed dementia and no serious bodily injury require written reports to the ombudsman and law enforcement within 24 hours, without the usual 2-hour verbal-report requirement.
Additional Federal Nursing-Facility Requirements — 42 CFR §483.12
Facilities must ensure allegations are reported to the administrator and required authorities:

Within 2 hours: Allegations involving abuse or resulting in serious bodily injury.
Within 24 hours: Other covered allegations that do not involve abuse or result in serious bodily injury.

CDPH guidance directs federally regulated facilities to use the stricter 2-hour reporting process, including written or electronic reports to the required agencies, for abuse or serious-bodily-injury incidents.
Important:

These are different legal reporting requirements; the applicable deadlines may overlap.
Do not assume that a 24-hour state written-report deadline permits delaying a report required sooner under federal rules.
The reporter’s individual legal obligations remain in effect even after notifying a supervisor.
Never delay emergency assistance or required reporting while completing routine documentation.
Confirm facility type, reporting recipients, and current procedures during clinical orientation.

Important Considerations

You do not need to prove abuse before reporting a reasonable suspicion.
Do not independently investigate or confront an alleged abuser.
Do not promise confidentiality that conflicts with reporting obligations.
Report retaliation

Sources

CNA Module 2 — Patient Rights, Abuse & Neglect
California Welfare and Institutions Code §15630 — Mandated Reporting
California Department of Social Services — Information for Mandated Reporters
California Department of Justice — Mandated Reporter Training
California Department of Public Health — AFL 21-26
Facility abuse-reporting policy and mandated-reporter training (verify at clinical site)

Flashcards
What should a CNA do when abuse or neglect is suspected?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerProtect safety and promptly report via required channels.
Can reporting suspected abuse to a supervisor replace a CNA's legally required external report?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerNo. Mandated-reporting duties are individual.
Is proof of elder or dependent adult abuse required before making a mandated report?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerNo. Reasonable suspicion is sufficient.
Does a CNA need proof of abuse before making a mandated report?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerNo. Reasonable suspicion can trigger a reporting duty.
Does reporting suspected abuse to a supervisor always satisfy California law?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerNo. External reporting may also be required.
Can a supervisor prevent a mandated reporter from filing a legally required report?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerNo. Reporting duties are individual.
What should a CNA do first when witnessing resident abuse?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerProtect immediate safety and summon help without putting anyone at further risk.
Should a CNA personally investigate suspected abuse?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerNo. Report observations and leave formal investigation to authorized personnel.
What is the usual California LTC verbal abuse-reporting deadline under WIC §15630?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerImmediately or as soon as practicable, no later than 2 hours, with specified exceptions.
Under federal nursing-facility rules, when must abuse allegations be reported?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerImmediately, no later than 2 hours, to the administrator and required authorities.
Can an internal incident report replace required external abuse reporting?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerNo.

reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.filePath: Reference and Guidelines/Professional Practice and Legal/CNA Info, Scope and Requirements.md
reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.title: CNA Info, Scope and Requirements
reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.content:
Quick Reference
Scope of Practice
CNAs provide basic patient care under the supervision of licensed nursing professionals.
Responsibilities include:

Assisting with activities of daily living (ADLs).
Providing hygiene, mobility, and comfort care.
Measuring and recording vital signs and intake/output.
Supporting emotional, cognitive, and restorative care needs.
Observing and reporting changes in patient condition.
Reinforcing instructions provided by licensed staff.

Certification Requirements (California)

Complete a CDPH-approved training program.
Complete 160 training hours:

60 hours classroom theory.
100 hours supervised clinical training.


Pass the required knowledge and clinical skills competency examinations.
Complete criminal background clearance.

Certification Renewal

Renew certification every 2 years.
Complete 48 hours of approved in-service training/CEUs:

At least 12 hours each year.
Maximum 24 hours through approved online programs.


Perform qualifying paid nursing or nursing-related work under licensed supervision during the certification period.
Maintain criminal record clearance.

Nurse Aide Registry

California maintains a certification registry through CDPH.
Employers can verify certification status.
The registry may display active, denied, suspended, or revoked certification statuses.

Important Considerations

Work within your training, authorized scope, and facility policies.
CNAs do not independently diagnose, prescribe treatments, or develop nursing care plans.
Clarify unfamiliar or unauthorized tasks with the supervising nurse.
Report patient changes and safety concerns promptly.
Maintain records of completed continuing education.

California SNF Orientation
California Title 22 §71833 requires 16 documented hours of orientation for certified and noncertified nurse assistants, completed within the first 40 hours of employment.
First 8 Hours:

Completed before direct patient care.
Facility layout, resident population, and routines.
Equipment and communication systems.
Emergency and disaster procedures.
Remaining 8 Hours:
Completed within the first 40 employment hours.
Additional required facility-specific training, including patient care policies, resident rights, and CNA responsibilities.
Important: Facility orientation is separate from initial CNA certification training.

Teaching vs. Reinforcing

CNAs reinforce care instructions provided by licensed professionals.
Introducing new clinical teaching or independently changing treatment instructions is outside routine CNA responsibilities.
Refer clinical questions requiring nursing judgment to the supervising nurse.

Professional Accountability

Know and follow your authorized scope of practice.
Clarify delegated tasks before performing them.
Report changes in resident condition promptly.
Communicate when assigned tasks cannot be completed safely.

Related

Patient Rights
Employee Rights
Standard Precautions
Vital Signs

Sources

California Department of Public Health — CNA Certification
California Title 22 — Nurse Assistant Training
CDPH 283A — Continuing Education Requirements
CDPH 283C — CNA Renewal Requirements

Flashcards
Does CNA training permit independent nursing diagnosis or treatment planning?01-foundations / reference-guidelinesAnswerNo; CNAs observe, perform authorized tasks, and report.

reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.filePath: Reference and Guidelines/Professional Practice and Legal/CNA Professionalism and Ethics.md
reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.title: CNA Professionalism and Ethics
reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.content:
Quick Reference
Professionalism means providing reliable, respectful, ethical, and safe care while maintaining appropriate boundaries.
Core Responsibilities









































QualityWhat It Looks LikeDependabilityFollowing through on assigned responsibilitiesPromptnessArriving on time and responding to resident needsCompassionTreating residents with kindness and empathyCommunicationSharing accurate information and listening activelyAdaptabilityResponding professionally to changing situationsAccountabilityReporting errors, concerns, and incomplete tasksPersonal HygieneMaintaining cleanliness and infection-control practicesIntegrityBeing honest and documenting accurately
Ethical Principles

Autonomy: Respect the resident’s choices.
Beneficence: Act to promote the resident’s well-being.
Nonmaleficence: Avoid causing harm.
Justice: Provide fair and unbiased care.
Confidentiality: Protect personal and health information.

Professional Boundaries

Maintain appropriate caregiver-resident relationships.
Protect confidentiality and privacy.
Do not accept inappropriate gifts or financial arrangements.
Avoid discussing residents outside authorized care settings.
Communicate respectfully with residents, families, and coworkers.

Important Considerations

Report mistakes and safety concerns honestly.
Do not perform unauthorized tasks.
Complete documentation accurately and promptly.
Respect cultural, religious, and individual differences.
Follow professional standards even during stressful situations.

Related

Patient Rights
Employee Rights
Chain of Command & Delegation
Therapeutic Communication
Culturally Responsive Care

Sources

CNA Module 1 — Professionalism and Ethics

Flashcards
Why maintain confidentiality?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerTo protect resident privacy and trust.

reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.filePath: Reference and Guidelines/Professional Practice and Legal/Chain of Command and Delegation.md
reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.title: Chain of Command and Delegation
reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.content:
Quick Reference
Chain of Command: The established reporting structure used to communicate concerns, receive instructions, and escalate problems.
Typical Structure:

Certified Nursing Assistant (CNA)
Supervising Nurse (RN or LVN/LPN)
Director of Nursing (DON)
Facility Administrator
Actual reporting structures vary by facility.

Delegation
Delegation occurs when an authorized healthcare professional assigns an appropriate task to another worker.
Before Accepting:

Is the task within my authorized scope?
Am I trained and competent to perform it?
Is the task appropriate for this resident and situation?
Do I understand the instructions and expected outcome?
Do I know when and what to report?
After Accepting:
Complete the task safely and promptly.
Report unexpected findings or inability to complete it.
Document according to facility policy.

Refusing or Clarifying Tasks

Do not perform tasks outside your authorized scope or competence.
Explain concerns professionally.
Ask for clarification or additional training.
Follow the chain of command when concerns remain unresolved.

Teaching vs. Reinforcing

Teaching: Introducing new clinical information or patient education requiring licensed professional judgment.
Reinforcing: Reminding or helping a resident practice previously taught instructions.
Example: “Let’s practice the technique your nurse showed you.”

Important Considerations

Delegation does not automatically expand CNA scope of practice.
Do not accept a task you cannot perform safely.
Never silently abandon an accepted task.
Report urgent safety concerns immediately rather than delaying for routine reporting channels.
Follow facility procedures when an unresolved concern requires escalation.

Related

CNA Info, Scope & Requirements
CNA Professionalism & Ethics
Patient Rights
Employee Rights

Sources

CNA Module 1 — Chain of Command and Delegation
Facility delegation and reporting policies


Flashcards
What must a CNA do if delegated a task beyond training or permitted scope?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerSeek clarification and decline unsafe or unauthorized performance.

reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.filePath: Reference and Guidelines/Professional Practice and Legal/Employee Rights.md
reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.title: Employee Rights
reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.content:
Quick Reference
Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
Established under the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 to protect workers from workplace hazards.
Employee rights:

A safe and healthy workplace.
Appropriate PPE and safety training.
Protection from occupational exposure to infectious materials.
Ability to report workplace hazards without retaliation.

Healthcare-specific protections:

Hepatitis B vaccination at no cost for eligible workers with occupational exposure.
Training on bloodborne pathogens.
Appropriate exposure prevention measures and post-exposure evaluation.

California: Cal/OSHA enforces state workplace safety regulations.
Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA)
Provides eligible employees up to 12 workweeks of job-protected leave in a 12-month period for qualifying reasons.
Qualifying reasons include:

Birth, adoption, or foster placement of a child.
Employee’s serious health condition.
Caring for a spouse, child, or parent with a serious health condition.
Certain military family circumstances.

Protections:

Return to the same or an equivalent job.
Continuation of group health insurance under applicable conditions.
Protection from retaliation for exercising FMLA rights.

Professional Responsibilities

Follow workplace safety and infection-control requirements.
Use employer-provided PPE appropriately.
Report unsafe working conditions and occupational exposures.
Communicate concerns through established workplace procedures.
Understand applicable leave protections and employment policies.

Important Considerations

FMLA is generally unpaid and has eligibility requirements.
OSHA protections include the right to report unsafe conditions without retaliation.
California may provide additional leave and workplace protections.
Report workplace exposures and injuries promptly according to facility policy.

Related

Patient Rights
CNA Info, Scope & Requirements
Standard Precautions
Bloodborne Pathogens

Sources

OSHA — Occupational Safety and Health Act
OSHA — Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030)
U.S. Department of Labor — Family and Medical Leave Act
California Division of Occupational Safety and Health (Cal/OSHA)

Flashcards
What should staff do after an occupational exposure?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerReport promptly and follow exposure-control procedures.

reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.filePath: Reference and Guidelines/Professional Practice and Legal/Healthcare Settings and Levels of Care.md
reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.title: Healthcare Settings and Levels of Care
reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.content:
Quick Reference
Healthcare settings differ in patient needs, length of stay, and level of medical supervision.








































SettingFocusTypical CNA ResponsibilitiesAcute CareShort-term treatment of illness or injuryVital signs, mobility, intake/output, personal careSubacute CareOngoing skilled care and recovery after serious illnessADLs, ambulation, rehabilitation supportLong-Term Care (LTC)Ongoing nursing and personal careHygiene, feeding, positioning, restorative careAssisted LivingSupporting independence with daily activitiesADLs, meals, personal assistanceHome HealthcareCare within the patient’s homePersonal care, mobility, observation, supportHospiceComfort and quality of life near the end of lifeHygiene, comfort, emotional support
Continuing Care Retirement Communities (CCRCs)
Provide multiple levels of care within a community, allowing residents to transition as their needs change.
Healthcare Team

RN: Nursing assessment, care planning, treatment, and supervision.
LVN/LPN: Nursing care and treatment within authorized scope.
CNA: Basic care, observations, reporting, and assistance with ADLs.
PT: Movement, strength, balance, and mobility.
OT: Daily activities and functional independence.
SLP: Communication, cognition, and swallowing.
Medical Assistant: Clinical and administrative support, commonly in ambulatory settings.

Important Considerations

CNA responsibilities vary by setting, certification, training, and facility policy.
Skilled nursing care differs from assistance with ADLs.
Long-term care emphasizes continued support, resident rights, and quality of life.
Medicare, Medicaid, private insurance, and private payments may fund different services.
Facility licensure, accreditation, and survey requirements vary by setting.

Related

CNA Info, Scope & Requirements
Rehabilitation & Therapy Services
Restorative & Rehabilitative Care
End-of-Life Care

Sources

CNA Module 1 — Healthcare Settings

Flashcards
What is the main purpose of skilled nursing care?01-foundations / reference-guidelinesAnswerProvide nursing and rehabilitation services requiring skilled personnel.

reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.filePath: Reference and Guidelines/Professional Practice and Legal/Informed Consent.md
reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.title: Informed Consent
reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.content:
Quick Reference
Informed consent is the process of ensuring a patient understands and voluntarily agrees to a proposed treatment or procedure.
Key Elements:

Disclosure: Explain the treatment, risks, benefits, and alternatives.
Understanding: Patient understands the information provided.
Capacity: Patient can make the specific healthcare decision.
Voluntary: Decision is made without coercion.
Authorization: Patient or legally authorized representative agrees.

Patient Rights:

Ask questions and receive understandable explanations.
Accept or refuse care and treatment.
Withdraw consent, subject to applicable legal limitations.
Participate in decisions about their care.

CNA Responsibilities:

Explain routine care before performing it.
Ask permission and respect resident choices.
Stop or pause when a resident refuses or withdraws cooperation.
Report refusals or questions about treatment to the nurse.
Do not independently obtain informed consent for medical procedures outside CNA responsibilities.

Important Considerations

A signed form alone does not establish meaningful informed consent.
Consent must be voluntary and informed.
Decision-making capacity is specific to the decision and may fluctuate.
An authorized representative may make decisions when legally appropriate.
Consent to one procedure does not imply consent to others.
Emergencies and certain legal circumstances may create exceptions.

Related

Patient Rights
Patient Refusal of Care
End-of-Life Care
CNA Info, Scope & Requirements

Sources

CDPH — Nursing Home Residents’ Rights
California Title 22, §72528 — Informed Consent
42 CFR §483.10 — Resident Rights

Flashcards
What does informed consent require?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerAn informed, voluntary decision by an authorized person.

reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.filePath: Reference and Guidelines/Professional Practice and Legal/Patient Rights.md
reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.title: Patient Rights
reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.content:
Quick Reference
Residents have the right to receive safe, respectful, individualized care that preserves their dignity, autonomy, privacy, independence, and quality of life.
These rights apply regardless of a resident’s diagnosis, abilities, or payment source.
Legal & Regulatory Foundations





























RegulationPurposeCalifornia Title 22State licensing regulations, including skilled nursing facility resident rightsCalifornia Health & Safety CodeState laws governing healthcare facilities and protecting residentsOBRA of 1987Federal nursing home reforms strengthening resident rights, quality of care, and quality of life42 CFR Part 483Federal nursing home participation requirements, including resident rightsHIPAA Privacy RuleProtects health information held or transmitted by covered entities and business associates
Core Resident Rights
Dignity & Respect

Receive respectful, individualized care.
Be free from discrimination, humiliation, and punishment.
Maintain personal identity, preferences, and relationships.
Receive reasonable accommodations for individual needs.

Autonomy & Independence

Participate in developing and revising the care plan.
Make informed choices about care and daily routines.
Consent to or refuse treatment, subject to applicable law.
Maintain independence in activities of daily living when possible.
Choose personal clothing, grooming, and activities.

Privacy & Confidentiality

Receive personal care with appropriate privacy.
Have personal and medical information kept confidential.
Maintain privacy in personal communications.
Keep personal belongings protected.
Access personal and medical records under applicable rules.

Personal Property & Finances

Retain and use personal belongings as permitted by safety and space requirements.
Manage personal finances.
Choose whether to authorize the facility to manage personal funds.
Receive protection against misuse or theft of personal property.

Safety & Freedom from Mistreatment

Receive care in a safe, clean, and comfortable environment.
Be free from abuse, neglect, and exploitation.
Be free from improper physical or chemical restraints.
Be free from involuntary seclusion.

Communication & Complaints

Communicate with family, friends, advocates, and authorized representatives.
Access the long-term care ombudsman.
Raise grievances without retaliation.
Receive information about rights and available complaint procedures.

End-of-Life Decisions

Participate in decisions about treatment goals.
Exercise applicable rights concerning advance directives.
Receive care consistent with authorized treatment preferences and medical orders.

CNA Responsibilities
Respect Choices:

Explain care before beginning.
Offer appropriate choices.
Encourage independence.
Respect preferences, privacy, and dignity.
Protect Confidentiality:
Discuss resident information only with authorized individuals for legitimate care-related purposes.
Protect records and personal belongings.
Never photograph or share resident information on personal devices or social media without proper authorization.
Respond to Refusals:
Do not force routine care.
Clarify concerns and offer appropriate alternatives.
Notify the nurse when care is refused or cannot be completed.
Recognize & Report Violations:
Watch for possible abuse, neglect, exploitation, or rights violations.
Protect immediate resident safety.
Report suspected violations promptly through required channels.
Follow applicable mandated reporting requirements.

Transfer & Discharge Protections
Residents of federally regulated nursing facilities have protections against improper transfers and discharges.

Transfer or discharge must meet legally permitted grounds.
Written notice generally must be provided at least 30 days in advance, subject to specified exceptions.
Notices must include reasons, timing, destination, appeal information, and ombudsman contact details as applicable.
Residents must receive appropriate preparation for safe, orderly transfers or discharges.
Bed-hold and readmission rights depend on the applicable requirements.

All residents in long-term care have the right to stay at their chosen facility unless:

Facility cannot meet the needs of the resident;
the resident no longer needs SNF services,
the resident is threatening the safety or health of staff or otehr residents, or
the resident cannot pay for services.

Notice of transfer must include where resident is going, contact info for state ombudsman, and info on the bed-hold and readmission policies.
CNA Responsibility: Respect resident rights, maintain dignity, support safe preparation, and refer questions about legal notices or discharge decisions to the appropriate licensed staff.
Source: 42 CFR § 483.15 — Admission, Transfer, and Discharge Rights
Long-Term Care Ombudsman & Complaints
The Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program advocates for residents of long-term care facilities.
Ombudsmen may:

Explain resident rights.
Receive and help address resident complaints.
Advocate for residents’ wishes and interests.
Help residents understand available complaint procedures.
Support improvements in long-term care quality.

Ombudsman complaint handling generally respects resident direction, consent, and confidentiality requirements.
California Department of Public Health
The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) licenses and regulates certain healthcare facilities, including skilled nursing facilities.
Residents, family members, employees, or other concerned individuals may submit complaints to CDPH.
Important: An ombudsman complaint or internal grievance process does not replace a CNA’s independent mandatory-reporting duty when abuse-reporting laws apply.
CNA Responsibilities

Inform residents about available help according to facility procedures.
Respect their right to make complaints without retaliation.
Promptly report concerns through required channels.
Do not discourage or interfere with a complaint.
Do not promise secrecy when mandatory reporting is legally required.

Important Considerations

Resident rights continue even when a resident requires extensive assistance.
Cognitive impairment does not automatically eliminate decision-making rights.
A resident’s authorized representative may participate in certain decisions as permitted by law.
Protecting safety does not justify unnecessary restrictions on autonomy.
Facility convenience is not a valid reason to disregard resident rights.
CNAs support resident decision-making but do not independently determine legal capacity or obtain informed consent for procedures requiring licensed clinical responsibility.

Related

Abuse, Neglect & Rights Violations
Informed Consent
Patient Refusal of Care
Restraints & Alternatives
CNA Professionalism & Ethics
End-of-Life Care
Culturally Responsive Care
CNA Info, Scope & Requirements

Sources

CNA Module 2 — Patients’ Rights
California Title 22 §72527 — Patients’ Rights
42 CFR §483.10 — Resident Rights
HHS — HIPAA Privacy Rule

Flashcards
Does a resident retain the right to refuse care?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerYes, subject to applicable legal and clinical processes.
What should CNAs protect during personal care?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerPrivacy, dignity, preferences, and autonomy.
What is the primary purpose of a Long-Term Care Ombudsman?01-foundations / reference-guidelinesAnswerAdvocate for residents' rights and help address complaints.
Can residents make complaints without retaliation?01-foundations / reference-guidelinesAnswerYes. Residents have the right to raise concerns without retaliation.
What does informed consent require?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerAppropriate information and a voluntary decision by the person authorized to consent.
Does HIPAA protect spoken health information?01-foundations / reference-guidelinesAnswerYes. The Privacy Rule protects qualifying oral, written, and electronic information.

reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.filePath: Reference and Guidelines/Professional Practice and Legal/Restraints and Alternatives.md
reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.title: Restraints and Alternatives
reference-and-guidelines/professional-pr.content:
Quick Reference
A restraint restricts a resident’s freedom of movement or ability to access their body.
Types:

Physical/Mechanical: Devices restricting movement, such as wrist, waist, or vest restraints.
Chemical: Medication used to restrict movement or behavior when not required to treat a medical symptom.
Environmental: Restrictions involving the environment that prevent freedom of movement.
Resident Rights:
Residents have the right to freedom from unnecessary restraints.
Restraints cannot be used for staff convenience or punishment.
When medically necessary and legally authorized, use the least restrictive approach for the shortest appropriate time.

Risks of Restraints
Physical:

Pressure injuries and skin damage.
Reduced mobility and muscle weakness.
Incontinence and constipation.
Respiratory complications.
Entrapment, falls, or serious injury.
Emotional:
Fear, agitation, and distress.
Loss of dignity and independence.
Depression and reduced self-worth.

Alternatives

Address pain, hunger, thirst, and toileting needs.
Provide frequent observation and reassurance.
Use therapeutic communication.
Reduce overstimulation.
Encourage appropriate mobility and activities.
Use individualized environmental and safety measures.

Important Considerations

Never independently decide to apply a restraint.
Follow authorized orders, the care plan, monitoring requirements, and facility policy.
Observe and report discomfort, skin changes, and circulation concerns.
Side rails may constitute restraints depending on their purpose and effect.
Bed and chair alarms are not substitutes for individualized fall-prevention care.
Restraint monitoring and release schedules depend on applicable regulations, orders, and facility policy.

Related

Patient Rights
Informed Consent
Fall Risk
Patient Refusal of Care
De-escalation & Conflict Resolution

Sources

CNA Module 12 — Restraints
42 CFR §483.12 — Freedom from Abuse, Neglect, and Exploitation

Flashcards
Why should restraints not be used for staff convenience?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerThey restrict rights and pose physical and psychological risks.
What is preferable to unnecessary restraints?01-foundations / reference-guidelinesAnswerIndividualized nonrestrictive safety alternatives.

reference-and-guidelines/safety-and-emer.filePath: Reference and Guidelines/Safety and Emergencies/Body Mechanics and Injury Prevention.md
reference-and-guidelines/safety-and-emer.title: Body Mechanics and Injury Prevention
reference-and-guidelines/safety-and-emer.content:
Quick Reference
Ergonomics: Adapting work environments and tasks to reduce physical strain and prevent injury.
Core Principles:

Assess the task before moving a resident.
Use appropriate mechanical assistance to minimize manual lifting.
Maintain a stable stance and avoid twisting.
Keep objects close to your body when handling them.
Adjust bed and equipment heights for safe working conditions.
Coordinate movements and communicate clearly with assisting staff.
Equipment:
Gait belts: Support appropriate assisted transfers and ambulation.
Sit-to-stand lifts: Assist eligible residents with some weight-bearing ability.
Full-body lifts: Support residents requiring greater transfer assistance.
Grab bars and handrails: Improve stability and independence.
Fall Prevention:
Keep walkways clear.
Remove hazards and obstacles.
Ensure appropriate footwear.
Check brakes and equipment before transfers.

Important Considerations

Good posture alone cannot make manual patient lifting safe.
Never attempt a transfer beyond your ability, training, or available assistance.
Follow the resident’s mobility and weight-bearing restrictions.
Anticipate unexpected movements and loss of balance.
Report unsafe equipment or environmental hazards.

Related

Safe Patient Transfers
Using a Gait Belt
Using a Mechanical Lift
Fall Risk

Sources

CNA Module 5 — Body Mechanics, Transfers & Ambulation
OSHA — Safe Patient Handling
OSHA — Ergonomics Guidelines for Nursing Homes
NIOSH — Safe Lifting and Movement of Nursing Home Residents
Facility safe-patient-handling policy and equipment-specific competency checklist (verify at clinical site)

Flashcards
Why use assistive transfer devices?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerTo reduce injury risk for residents and staff.

reference-and-guidelines/safety-and-emer.filePath: Reference and Guidelines/Safety and Emergencies/Emergency Preparedness and Response.md
reference-and-guidelines/safety-and-emer.title: Emergency Preparedness and Response
reference-and-guidelines/safety-and-emer.content:
Quick Reference
An emergency is a sudden event requiring immediate action to prevent harm.
Emergency Preparedness:

Know facility emergency plans and evacuation routes.
Locate alarms, exits, emergency equipment, and assembly areas.
Understand backup power and communication procedures.
Participate in required training and drills.
CNA Responsibilities:
Remain calm and identify immediate dangers.
Activate the appropriate emergency response.
Follow the chain of command and assigned responsibilities.
Communicate resident needs and safety concerns.
Assist with evacuation or sheltering as trained and directed.
Disasters & Evacuation:
Know evacuation routes and alternative routes.
Identify residents needing mobility or medical assistance.
Follow instructions for sheltering, horizontal evacuation, or full evacuation.
Help maintain resident identification, safety, and continuity of care.
Bomb Threats:
Remain calm and gather details if safe.
Note exact wording, timing, and background sounds.
Notify authorities and supervisors according to the emergency plan.
Follow evacuation or sheltering directions.

Emergency Codes & Chain of Command

Know the facility’s emergency codes and how to activate them.
Follow assigned CNA responsibilities during an emergency.
Communicate the location, nature, and urgency of the event.
Obtain clear instructions before performing unfamiliar tasks.
Report changes in patient condition immediately.
Participate in required emergency response drills.
Remember: Emergency code names and meanings may differ between facilities.

Important Considerations

Protect yourself before attempting to assist others.
Do not attempt unsafe transfers or rescues.
Know whom to contact and how to summon help.
Facility-specific emergency procedures take priority over generalized study notes.
Emergency plans must address hazards, communication, procedures, and staff training.

Related

Fire Safety & Response (RACE, PASS)
Workplace Violence & Active Threats
Facility & Environmental Safety
Employee Rights

Sources

CMS — Emergency Preparedness
OSHA — Emergency Preparedness

Flashcards
What is the first priority during a facility emergency?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerEnsure safety and follow the facility response plan.

reference-and-guidelines/safety-and-emer.filePath: Reference and Guidelines/Safety and Emergencies/Facility and Environmental Safety.md
reference-and-guidelines/safety-and-emer.title: Facility and Environmental Safety
reference-and-guidelines/safety-and-emer.content:
Quick Reference
A safe healthcare environment reduces injuries, infection risks, and resident distress.
Physical Environment:

Clear, accessible hallways and exits.
Functional handrails and call-light systems.
Safe drinking water and adequate ventilation.
Appropriate lighting, privacy, and accessible toileting.
Safe resident rooms and common areas.
Fire & Equipment Safety:
Functional fire alarms, sprinklers, and fire doors.
Safe electrical cords, outlets, and equipment.
Emergency power and evacuation supplies.
Noise Control:
Reduce unnecessary noise and overhead paging.
Respond promptly to alarms and resident needs.
Provide quiet activities and calming environments.
Cleanliness & Odor Control:
Promptly remove soiled linen and waste.
Clean and disinfect shared equipment as directed.
Provide timely toileting and incontinence care.
Keep bathrooms and commodes clean.

Important Considerations

Follow individualized toileting schedules rather than assuming every resident requires toileting every two hours.
Keep exits, fire doors, and emergency equipment accessible.
Report damaged equipment and environmental hazards.
Follow facility procedures for handling soiled linens and waste.

reference-and-guidelines/safety-and-emer.title: Workplace Violence and Active Threats
reference-and-guidelines/safety-and-emer.content:
Quick Reference
Workplace violence includes threats, harassment, physical aggression, and other dangerous behavior.
Risk Factors:

Agitated or aggressive individuals.
Working alone or during low-staffing periods.
Public-facing and community-based work.
Poor lighting, unsecured areas, or inadequate communication.
De-escalation:
Remain calm and speak respectfully.
Allow one person to speak at a time.
Listen and acknowledge concerns.
Avoid arguing, threats, or personal attacks.
Maintain distance and access to an exit.
Request assistance before the situation becomes unsafe.
Active Threat — Run, Hide, Fight:
Run: Evacuate if a safe route exists.
Hide: Shelter and secure your location if evacuation is unsafe.
Fight: As a last resort when in immediate danger, defend yourself.

Important Considerations

Personal and resident safety take priority.
Follow facility-specific active threat procedures.
Do not confront an armed person or attempt a rescue that creates additional danger.
Call emergency services when safe.
Report threats, assaults, and concerning incidents.
Healthcare evacuation requires planning for patients who cannot independently escape.

Related

De-escalation & Conflict Resolution
Therapeutic Communication
Emergency Preparedness & Response
Employee Rights

Sources

OSHA — Emergency Preparedness
Facility workplace violence prevention policy

Flashcards
What should staff prioritize during an active threat?03-application / reference-guidelinesAnswerImmediate safety, alerting others, and following facility emergency procedures.

    17 cards

      Digestive System

index.title: Nursing Knowledge Base
index.content:
A collection of nursing education notes covering anatomy and physiology, clinical concepts, patient care, and practical nursing skills.
Getting Started

Browse by subject: Use the Explorer sidebar to navigate notes organized by topic.
Follow connections: Click links between notes or use Graph View to discover related concepts.
Practice active recall: Use the Flashcard Library to review questions drawn from my notes.
Search for a topic: Use the search bar to find terminology, procedures, and clinical concepts.

Explore the Knowledge Base
Anatomy and Physiology
Understand how the human body is organized, how its systems function, and how those systems work together.
Start here:

Basic Structures — Cells, tissues, organs, and body organization.
Cardiovascular System — Blood circulation, heart function, and tissue perfusion.
Respiratory System — Breathing, gas exchange, and oxygenation.
Digestive System — Digestion, nutrient absorption, and elimination.

Additional body systems are available through the Explorer sidebar.
Clinical Skills & Patient Care
Practical nursing-assistance skills and the principles behind safe, respectful, person-centered care.
Topics include:

Hygiene, grooming, dressing, and personal care
Mobility, transfers, and patient positioning
Infection prevention and control
Vital signs, measurements, and observation
Recognizing changes in patient condition
Communication, documentation, and reporting

Use the Explorer sidebar to browse available clinical skills and patient care notes.
Clinical Concepts & Conditions
Explore how underlying physiology connects to patient symptoms, risks, and care needs.
These notes focus on:

Understanding the mechanisms behind diseases and conditions
Recognizing important signs and symptoms
Connecting observations to potential clinical concerns
Understanding prevention, safety, and appropriate escalation

Study Flashcards
Open the Flashcard Library →
Flashcards are generated automatically from questions embedded in published notes and organized by source note.
Questions generally focus on:

Foundations: Definitions, terminology, anatomy, and core facts.
Mechanisms: How and why physiological processes occur.
Clinical application: Recognition, patient care, safety, and reporting.

Click individual flashcards to reveal their answers and practice active recall.
Website flashcard review history is not synchronized with Obsidian.
How These Notes Are Organized
Each note is designed to address several questions:

What is it? — A clear explanation of the concept or skill.
How does it work? — Relevant physiology or underlying principles.
Why does it matter? — Connections to patient health, safety, and care.
What should I recognize or do? — Practical observations and care considerations within the appropriate scope of practice.
How does it connect? — Links to related concepts and skills.
